item.title: Ukraine Is Wiping Out Data Centers Across the Border
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
Ukrainian drone strikes have damaged three major Yandex data centers as well as facilities serving Sberbank and VKontakte (the country's equivalent to Facebook), disrupting cloud services, banking, e-commerce, ride-hailing and other digital services across Russia. The attacks may deal a longer-lasting blow to Russia's AI ambitions: Yandex's affected facilities housed its three top-500 supercomputers, and experts say sanctions and shortages of high-end Nvidia chips could make repairs difficult or even take years. "This effectively sets Russia far behind in the AI race, "said Mikhail Klimarev, head of the Internet Protection Society activist group. Fortune reports: Data centers are the latest targets of aerial campaigns waged by both sides against each other's vital infrastructure. [...] Kyiv's attacks on Russian data centers closely followed Moscow's recent strikes on data centers in Ukraine, which disrupted the internet and TV broadcasts. On Oct. 8, Ukrainian drones hit a Yandex data center in Sasovo in the Ryazan region that houses two of the company's three supercomputers. A data center in Kaluga was hit a day later and the one in Vladimir was struck Oct. 11.
The data center and AI hub for Sberbank was hit Oct. 14 in Balakovo in the Saratov region, and four days later, Kyiv struck a data center in St. Petersburg serving VKontakte. While oil refineries and warehouses are easy prey, data centers are even softer targets -- massive buildings packed with servers and supporting power and cooling infrastructure. Lasting damage can result from a drone carrying a relatively light load of explosives.
[...] Ukraine has stored critical data on servers in allied European countries, helping limit the damage from Russian attacks. But Moscow's strict digital sovereignty policy requires all data storage at home, making it extremely vulnerable. "Because all the infrastructure and all the data is located inside Russia, it's relatively easier to take down," [said Nick Reiners, senior geotechnology analyst at Eurasia Group]. Klimarev predicted the data center attacks could encourage many top Russian companies to move data abroad, while the authorities could ease their efforts to tighten internet controls to minimize the damage.

item.title: Don’t Let AI Steal Your Personality
item.author: Editing Protocol
item.content:encoded: We are well and truly in the AI era; there’s no point in denying it. Industries, by and large, have had to adjust, rethink hiring, their products and services, and even the nature of work itself over the last few years to accommodate this new reality. And so have we, albeit to some extent kicking and screaming.Because even though there’s a very logical, very solid argument that the applications of AI’s magical abilities are a net positive (if handled responsibly and not treated like many other transformational technologies before it, as yet another way for the powers that be to wage war across lines drawn in the sand), we, from an editorial point of view, have had a more complicated response to it.When the first waves of AI-generated content hit our queue, we mostly shunned it vehemently. In our eyes, AI-generated text was immediately synonymous with fluff and had no place in our painstakingly curated corner of the internet. We rejected indiscriminately, and it was easy to do so (AI-generated content was, and in many obvious ways still is, very easy to spot if you know what to look for). But, and it is important to take this with caveats, our stance has evolved over the years.Summarily: Write by yourself. Use AI as a brainstorming assistant. Use AI as a research assistant. But since then, our queue has grown by hundreds of articles every week, propelled in no small part by AI-generated text and our collective obsession with speed. To the point where even some of our favorite writers have begun sacrificing elements of their personality on the altar of quantity.Now, we can’t sit on a high horse and point a finger at anyone. When the world moves at breakneck speed, powered by AI supercars, there’s a real chance of being left behind. But we maintain that keeping up with the times cannot come at the expense of your personality, of your voice!If yours and every other thought leader’s article has the exact same structure, rhythm, and cadence, how do we tell you apart? How do we build a relationship with your thought process, your unique context? How do we pick you out of a crowd?HackerNoon was founded to accommodate a global community of contributors and readers, to platform a myriad of voices, all with unique POVs, all valuable, interdependent parts of a whole that paint a fuller picture of our ecosystem, our world. And that’s still something we live by to this day.That said, we also understand the paradoxical nature of things. Sometimes human-written content is bad, and AI-assisted content can be good, and we’re ready to compromise.But before we talk about what good AI-assisted content looks like to us, we must first say that when it ticks all the boxes of our editing protocol, WE WILL ALWAYS PRIORITIZE HUMAN-WRITTEN, PERSONALITY-RICH CONTENT.But if you must generate content with AI, then we must see signs that you’re fully in the driver’s seat.If You Absolutely Must, Here's How to Use AI Without Losing Your Voice EntirelyThis is, by some distance, our preferred approach. Get your thoughts on the page first, however messy, disjointed, or grammatically questionable they might be. Then, if you must, bring in AI to clean things up.Ask it to identify redundancies, improve sentence structure, flag inconsistencies, or point out where your arguments could use more work. But be careful not to let it polish away everything that makes your writing yours.The peculiar way you choose your words, your sometimes convoluted analogies, and even your tendency to ramble a little before you arrive at your point aren’t necessarily bugs that need to be fixed. Sometimes, they’re the whole point.1b. Let the first paragraph ALWAYS sound like youYour opening paragraph is your first opportunity to establish a relationship with the reader. Don't waste it on a generic introduction about how the world is rapidly evolving, how some industry is undergoing an unprecedented transformation, or how something is no longer a luxury but a necessity, or any of the newer variations of AI text templates.We’ve read hundreds of those introductions and, honestly, we’re tired of them.Start with an observation, a personal experience, an unpopular opinion, a question you've been wrestling with. Something, anything, that gives us a reason to believe there's a human being with something interesting to say behind the byline.And if AI helps you with the rest of the piece, make sure the personality you establish in that opening carries through.2. Think first, AI Later!Before you even think about opening ChatGPT or your AI assistant of choice, spend some time figuring out what you actually want to say.What's your central argument? What points do you want to make? What conclusions have you arrived at independently?You don't necessarily need a fully formed outline or a perfectly articulated thesis, but you should have enough of an idea that you're directing the conversation, not the other way around.Once you've done that, there's plenty AI can help with. Organizing your scattered thoughts into an outline, suggesting ways to connect two ideas, or even identifying areas that could use more research. You could even take it a step further and ask if AI can find some trends that support your rhetoric or if you need to rethink it.What we don't want is for you to hand over a topic, ask for 1,500 words, and copy the result into our editor.We can usually tell, and it casts a skeptical shadow over your work in our eyes.3a. Bring Your Personal Context to the TableThis one’s especially important for our technical writers and thought leaders. We’ve been pretty clear about what we generally expect from either group:To reiterate, if you're writing about a product you've built, tell us about YOUR experience. What decisions did you make? What surprised you? What did you try that didn't work? What would you do differently?If you're writing about an industry trend, tell us what you've observed, what informs your opinion, and why readers should care about your interpretation of events.AI can help you organize these experiences, but it cannot have them for you. And please, don't let it invent personal anecdotes, technical results, or sources to make your article sound more convincing. We will always ask to see verifiable proof on the page.3b. Don’t Let AI Dictate Your Article’s RhythmNot every article needs three key takeaways, five actionable strategies, and a conclusion that begins with "The future of..."Not every paragraph needs to be the same length. Not every section needs a subheading. And not every idea needs to be neatly packaged into a bullet point. Sometimes the best way to make an argument is to take the scenic route.Play around with your structure. Honor your train of thought. Use humor, skepticism, frustration, excitement, whatever comes naturally to you and serves the story.There’s no universal template for good writing!The Point is to Sound Like YouTo be clear, we’re not advocating for bad writing in the name of authenticity, nor are we suggesting that your article should be rife with imperfections just to prove that it’s human. Good editing matters. So do structure and clarity. We wouldn’t have a team of human editors if we thought otherwise.All we’re asking is that you don’t sacrifice your personality on the altar of faux efficiency.By all means, use the tools at your disposal. Experiment with them to your heart’s content. Let them make the writing process easier, and perhaps even better. But don’t surrender the very thing that makes your perspective worth publishing in the first place.Because if we can swap your byline with twenty others and nobody notices the difference, something has gone terribly wrong.Ready to put these tips to use?If you’re looking for a more guided way to build the habit of real thought leadership more consistently. Then the is for you.The HackerNoon Blogging CourseThe HackerNoon Blogging Course breaks down how to ideate, structure, draft, and publish high-quality technical stories, using the same editorial standards we apply every day.So instead of guessing what works, you’re building from a system that’s already been tested at scale.If your goal is to write clearer, sharper, more publishable content in 2026, this is a strong next step.

item.title: Comcast Loses More Customers, Claims Other ISPs' Cheap Prices Are 'Irrational'
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from Ars Technica: Comcast reportedly plans significant job cuts in its cable division as the firm continues to lose residential broadband and TV customers. Comcast lost 144,000 residential broadband customers in Q3 2026, up from a 91,000-customer loss in the same quarter a year ago, the company said in its earnings report today. Comcast historically capitalized on a lack of competition for high-speed wired broadband. But now it faces stronger competition from fixed wireless providers and from fiber providers in parts of its cable territory. "Fixed wireless remains aggressive and continues to take share, while fiber construction remains elevated, with pockets of irrational pricing and promotional activity," Comcast co-CEO Mike Cavanagh said today in an earnings call.
Comcast CFO Jason Armstrong said "irrational pricing" from fiber operators includes $30 to $40 monthly broadband offers "in specific markets in the third quarter." He said $30 to $40 pricing is irrational because deploying fiber costs $1,500 or more per home, and is "getting more expensive with construction costs up as you get into more suburban and rural areas." "As we look at the return profile of that, to us, that is irrational competition," Armstrong said. While he didn't name any specific competitors, Verizon has been pitching FiOS fiber plans that start at $30 a month. Comcast's network is a mix of fiber and cable, and it offers fiber-to-the-home in only small portions of its cable territory.
Armstrong said more Comcast customers are leaving when they face "pricing transitions," apparently referring to the price hikes customers get when promotional offers expire. "We've been refining our offers and retention strategies to better manage these transitions and strengthen customer retention," he said. Cavanagh said that "satellite is not yet a material factor" in the competition Comcast faces, but that Comcast is focused on "anticipating emerging forms of competition and positioning our business to respond as the market evolves."

item.title: Agent Guardrails Belong in Config, and Config Needs Tests
item.author: Mike Dabydeen
item.content:encoded:
When an AI agent can run shell commands in your pipeline, its permissions are infrastructure. They should be declared where reviewers look, versioned with the agent, and tested on every change. Docker Agent gets the first two right. The third is up to you, and when I wrote the tests, one widely used permission pattern failed in a way worth knowing about.Docker Agent is Docker's open-source runtime for teams of agents. A team is a config file: models, agents, which agents each one may delegate to, which tools each may use, and the policy around all of it. You run it with docker agent run crew.yaml.My test project, release-gate-crew, is a release gate for container services. A lead agent delegates to a container auditor and a pipeline auditor, then hands their findings to a scribe that writes a PASS/BLOCK report. The sample service under review is deliberately bad: an unpinned base image, a secret in , a privileged container with the Docker socket mounted, and a workflow that checks out untrusted code with write permissions.Every control sits in the same file as the agents:agents: container_auditor: model: worker instruction_file: prompts/container_auditor.md toolsets: - type: filesystem allow_list: ["./target"] # read scope - type: shell
runtime: safety: restricted # unattended: deny anything not allowed
permissions: allow: ["read_file", "shell:cmd=grep -n *"] deny: ["shell:cmd=*curl*", "shell:cmd=*&&*", "shell:cmd=*;*", "shell:cmd=*|*"]
budget: max_cost: 0.50 # one pot shared by every agent max_time: 10m A file hides and key files from every agent. The same team also exists as , because Docker Agent reads HCL too, and platform teams that live in Terraform may prefer it.Testing guardrails without a modelGuardrails are deterministic, so they should be testable without paying for tokens or tolerating model variance. I wrote a scripted, OpenAI-compatible stub model in Go and pointed every agent at it through a config flavor. The stub plays a fixed sequence per agent. It delegates, reads files, and then deliberately tries things the config should refuse.A Go integration test drives the real binary against both config files and checks nine written requirements. The runtime's own responses:excluded by .agentsignorePipeline auditor reads a file outside outside the allowed directories (./target)Scribe writes denied by restricted safety mode, no promptgrep -n FROM target/Dockerfile && curl --versiondenied by permissions configurationAll of that held, for YAML and HCL alike.The pattern that didn't holdPermission rules are globs matched against the whole command string, and matches spaces. So consider the prefix style common in examples:permissions: allow: ["shell:cmd=grep -n *"] deny: ["shell:cmd=curl *"] The command grep -n FROM target/Dockerfile && curl --version begins with , so the allow rule matches. It does not begin with , so the deny rule misses. Deny is evaluated first, finds nothing, then allow approves. In my test, curl ran and printed its version banner. The safety mode did not stop it, because an explicit allow outranks the mode.Docker's documentation says permissions are client-side and not a security boundary, and it recommends sandbox mode for isolation. I agree with that framing. The risk is practical: prefix rules look precise, and they are what most people will copy.Four changes close the gap:Deny shell operators: , , , backticks and .Match denied binaries anywhere: , not .Allow one narrow command per agent that needs a shell.Use , which runs the team in a Docker Sandboxes VM, for anything you don't fully trust.My suite keeps a test that reproduces the bypass. If a future release starts parsing compound commands, that test will fail and tell me to revisit the advice.The filesystem toolset is unrestricted by default. Set on every one.A config pulled from a registry can declare runtime.safety: autonomous. Your own flag or user settings take precedence only if you set them.Sub-agents receive only the task text the lead writes, inside a block. Good isolation, but the lead must pass along everything a specialist needs.The project moves quickly: 17 releases in September 2026. Pin the version in CI and disable telemetry there with .What the stub can't tell youNone of this measures review quality. A scripted stub proves the harness, not the judgement. The repository includes three cases for that: block the flawed sample, refuse to reveal the secret, and refuse to claim an edit. They need real model keys and a container runtime, and I haven't run them yet.That split is the main lesson I'd take to any agent platform. Test the guardrails deterministically on every push. Evaluate the model's judgement separately, with repeated runs, before you trust a gate decision.

item.title: Using Cypress Cloud CLI and Test Replay for AI-Assisted CI Debugging
item.author: Raju Dandigam
item.content:encoded:
A checkout test fails in CI with this message:expected '[data-cy="cart-total"]' to have text '$45.00' The screenshot shows . An AI assistant can invent several plausible explanations: the discount request failed, React rendered stale state, the selector found the wrong cart, or the assertion ran early.Plausible is not the same as supported.The quality of AI-assisted debugging depends less on how confidently the assistant explains the screenshot and more on whether it can inspect the evidence that produced it.Recorded CI and live local debugging are different surfacesCypress now exposes two useful but distinct agent workflows: A live, local open-mode Cypress session; Run and verify a change during development Completed Cloud runs and Test Replay data; Reconstruct an existing CI failureI have written separately about giving an agent access to a live Cypress session. This workflow starts at the opposite end: the failure already happened, perhaps only in CI, and the recorded attempt is the evidence.The Cypress Cloud CLI returns JSON for runs, specs, tests, commands, network requests, and console events. The local Test Replay viewer is available through in CLI version or newer.Start with a deliberately small evidence packetThe current documentation requires Node.js or newer and recommends using the latest CLI. Install it, record the resolved version, and pin that exact version in repeatable CI automation after validation:npm install --global @cypress/cloud@latest cy-cloud version cy-cloud status For a failed run, the shortest useful path is:cy-cloud run list \ --projectId <projectId> \ --branch main \ --status failed \ --limit 1
cy-cloud test list \ --projectId <projectId> \ --runNumber <runNumber> \ --status failed
cy-cloud replay timeline \ --testId <testId> \ --commands \ --aroundFailure 5 \ --network \ --logs That packet answers four questions:Which commands immediately preceded it?Which XHR or fetch activity overlapped the failure?Did the application log a related error?Do not begin by dumping an entire organization's run history into an agent. Scope the query to one project, run, test, attempt, and timeline window.Suppose the test failed on attempt one and passed on attempt two. A screenshot from the failed attempt tells us the symptom. Comparing the attempts can expose the first causal difference.cy-cloud replay timeline \ --testId <testId> \ --attempt 1 \ --commands --network --logs \ > attempt-1.json
cy-cloud replay timeline \ --testId <testId> \ --attempt 2 \ --commands --network --logs \ > attempt-2.json Imagine the relevant entries reduce to:, response at 1,240 ms; , response at 310 ms 820 ms; 760 ms; none; noneThe evidence does not yet prove whether the product or test is wrong, but it eliminates several guesses. The assertion can run before the successful response. The next review question is whether the UI should block until the response arrives, or whether the test failed to wait for an application event that defines completion.The timeline gives structure. The local replay viewer lets you inspect the recorded DOM and styles around one command:cy-cloud replay view open --testId <testId>
cy-cloud replay view move \ --testId <testId> \ --attempt 1 \ --pin '<commandId>|before'
cy-cloud replay view inspect \ --testId <testId> \ --selector '[data-cy="cart-total"]'
cy-cloud replay view move \ --testId <testId> \ --attempt 1 \ --pin '<commandId>|after' This is more diagnostic than asking an agent to infer causality from the final screenshot. It can see whether an earlier command changed an attribute, collapsed a container, or left the DOM stale. requires a Chromium-family browser and Cloud CLI or newer. Because Cloud CLI is Beta, scripts should pin a compatible version and treat output schemas as versioned dependencies.Give the agent a diagnostic contractAn unrestricted prompt such as “fix this test” encourages the assistant to optimize for a green run. It may add a hard wait, broaden a selector, remove an assertion, or mask a product regression.A better task is bounded:Analyze attempt-1.json and attempt-2.json for test <testId>.
1. Identify the first material difference before the failed assertion. 2. Cite the relevant command, network, or console event IDs. 3. Classify the likely cause as product, test synchronization, test data, environment, or unknown. 4. Propose the smallest code change, but do not edit files. 5. Do not add fixed waits or weaken the business assertion. 6. List the local verification commands and one negative control. The request separates observation, diagnosis, proposal, and execution. A human can reject the classification before any code changes.Credential locality is not the whole security modelCloud CLI access follows the organizations, teams, projects, and roles available to the authenticated Cypress Cloud user. OAuth is recommended locally; a personal access token can be supplied through in CI. Stored credentials are owner-readable on the local machine.Those are useful controls, but they do not mean every AI environment is automatically safe. If an agent can read arbitrary environment variables, home-directory files, or shell output, it may reach more than intended.Use the ordinary least-privilege questions:Which Cypress Cloud user or service identity is authenticating?Which projects can it read?Can the agent execute arbitrary shell commands?Where are downloaded replay data and screenshots cached?Can captured network bodies contain secrets or personal data?When are local artifacts deleted?Cypress supports masking and redaction for Test Replay network data; configure those boundaries before making replay evidence broadly available.Verification remains a separate stepAfter reviewing a proposed fix, run the affected spec locally. A useful sequence is:reproduce with the same fixture or a sanitized equivalent;apply the smallest reviewed change;run the original failure case;run a negative control that should still fail;inspect the behavior, not just the exit code;push only after the evidence agrees.The negative control matters. If changing the selector makes the test pass even when the discount is not applied, the “fix” destroyed the test.Remove runner drift with a pinned containerBefore blaming the test or product, rerun the candidate change in the same declared Node and browser environment. An official or image can make that boundary repeatable, but only when you pin a full version tag or digest:export CYPRESS_IMAGE='cypress/browsers@sha256:<approved-digest>' docker compose run --rm \ -e CYPRESS_SPEC='cypress/e2e/checkout.cy.ts' \ cypress The Compose service should run the same repository revision and application fixture used in the investigation. Record docker image inspect "$CYPRESS_IMAGE", , , and the selected browser with the evidence packet. A green result in a different image is not a reproduction; it is a new experiment.What this workflow does not proveRecorded Test Replay evidence describes one captured run. It does not prove that a failure is statistically representative or that the proposed patch is correct. A passing retry can differ because of data, timing, infrastructure, or an actual product race.Cloud CLI is also not an autonomous remediation system. It is a read-oriented evidence interface. Code changes, approval, and verification remain responsibilities of your development workflow.Ask AI to explain bounded evidence before asking it to change code.That turns the assistant from a confident guesser into a supervised participant in a debugging process whose claims can be reviewed

item.title: Agent Security & Identity (Part 2): Who Are You, Who's Your Agent, And What Should They Be Allowed?
item.author: Alejandro Saucedo
item.content:encoded:
This is a 2-part series on agent identity and security: who the user is, who the agent is, and what each of them should be allowed to reach. Part 2 runs the design end to end on a cluster, with two users, two agents, a tool, a model and a third-party service.In Part 1, I designed how agent identity can work on a platform where agent-delegation is enabled, and how we decide (+ enforce) what they and their users are allowed to reach. In this second and final part I deploy that design on a cluster and check whether it actually holds up.In this Part 2 blog post, I go through a hands-on use-case with 2 users of the same agent platform at the same company: Alice is in the group and Bob is in the group. Throughout this I will show the good, the bad and the ugly of agentic identity and security, especially when dealing with autonomous agents, and with users delegating permissions to an agent.The walkthrough answers 4 questions:Does an agent requesting a tool for a user in the wrong group actually get refused?When an agent calls its own tool and model, how do we authorize (+ verify) the hops?What happens to an autonomous agent that has no user behind it at all?When Alice asks for a 3rd party service (i.e. github) via an agent, does the request go out as Alice?Most of what I learnt came from the requests that got denied (+ from the complexities and lessons learned), so you'll see plenty of those below.Everything below runs on a local KIND cluster against the public Agentic Identity Broker release, pinned at . On a local cluster GitHub is a mock, so the consent screen gets completed automatically instead of in a browser, but every identity and access-control decision you'll see is real.Here's a quick refresher of what we covered in Part 1 before we run it.I started with the challenges we all phase when agents have to access 3rd party services on behalf of a user. Here I showed how just giving an API token falls short, as you can't tell which user an action was for, it has more access than any single user needs, and you can't revoke it for just one user.Fixing that needed a component that holds each user's own third-party credential, obtained with their consent. The Agentic Identity Broker does exactly that, so I adopted it instead of writing my own.Then I separated the 2 identities that every protected call carries. The is the human the work is being done for, and the is the agent doing the work. This is how the system enforces resource access on the actor and use the subject for what the user personally delegated, which keeps permissions correct when agents call other agents.Finally I made 6 architecture decisions, and 3 of them matter most for what follows:One gateway on every hop, plus a NetworkPolicy so nothing can go around itChecks in the agent runtime, a sidecar per workload, a service meshHow authorization is modelledOne explicit for who may enter an agent, with the agent's own dependencies derived from its spec, all evaluated by KAOS's own Open Policy Agent decision pointA policy language as the authoring surface, or the broker answering the decisionKAOS owns the integration; the broker and the identity provider run as their own releasesThe platform installing and lifecycle-managing its own brokerThat third row is why this walkthrough has both a broker and Keycloak in it. The broker holds the delegated third-party credentials and performs the exchange, and the gateway attaches the returned credential to the outbound request. Keycloak proves who the human is, carries the group membership the rules match on, and registers each agent as its own client so the broker can tell which agent is asking.Now let's build the cluster and see it work.The is the set of components that establish identity and decide the rules. Apart from the gateway, none of them carry your agents' actual traffic; they answer the 3 questions from part 1 about it. Here they are on one map. The greyed pieces belong to section 5 and can be ignored for now.There are quite a few components in this overview, so let's walk through them:: This is the single gateway every request passes through, including agent-to-tool, agent-to-model and agent-to-agent calls, which is what makes it a mesh.: Authenticates users, proves who they are and which groups they belong to; supports OIDC compatible services so we use Keycloak here.: Gives each agent their identity through secure credentials; the default uses k8s Service Accounts, but also supports OIDC compatible services; we also configure Keycloak in this example.: This is the authorization (authz) service that KAOS uses to allow/deny requests based on the "user" calling the "agent" accessing the "resource".Agent Impersonation Service: Lets an agent act on an outside service (like GitHub) as the user by exchanging third-party tokens (github/slack/etc) through a consent mechanism. The concrete tool I use is the Agent Identity Broker (AIB), and it gets its own section, section 5.: This component synchronises auth & identity bidirectionaly; it registers the KAOS resources on upstream auth services, and injects identities and secrets across KAOS resources.Before I show how this all fits together with an example, let's configure the kubernetes cluster with this setup.1.1 Install it in one commandI use the KAOS CLI to install the Gateway Mesh, User Auth, Agent Auth, the KAOS Authz Service, the KAOS Operator, and the Agent Identity Broker (AIB).This command wires everything together in a new cluster:kaos system install \ --gateway-strict \ # Traffic can only go through gateway --authz-enabled \ # KAOS Authorization service enabled --user-auth keycloak \ # Use Keycloak for User auth (alt: OIDC) --agent-auth keycloak \ # Use Keycloak for Agent Auth (alt: Service Accts. or OIDC) --token-exchange-enabled \ # Use AIB for token exchange
# Other flags --wait \ # Block until everything is ready --create-cli-config # In-folder config file for cli kaos system install --help lists everything else (image tags, resource limits, replica counts, realm names, observability backends); the Helm values behind each flag are shown per-component in section 4.Let's confirm the pieces are healthy:gateway ready login service ready (keycloak) access-control ready (2/2 replicas) sync service ready And let's make sure that everything is configured correctly:gateway: address: http://kaos-gateway.kaos-system.svc.cluster.local through_gateway: true auth: issuer: http://keycloak.keycloak.svc.cluster.local:8080/realms/kaos client_id: kaos realm: kaos broker_url: http://aib-agentic-identity-broker.aib-system.svc.cluster.local:8000 broker_admin_url: http://aib-agentic-identity-broker.aib-system.svc.cluster.local:14000/api namespace: kaos-system sessions: {} The is the actual agent traffic, meaning users invoking agents and agents calling tools and models. Every one of those calls travels through the Gateway Mesh and is checked before it is let through.The hands-on example uses the following resources:two users: (group ) and (group )two agents: (user-activated) and (autonomous agent)one model: (a model endpoint both agents may use)one external service: , covered in section 5The rules are that the group may use the agent, the agent may reach and , and the autonomous may reach . Everything else is denied, including bob (poor bob).Here's a chart that shows what we'll try to accomplish:2.1 How identity flows through a requestEvery call, a user/agent reaching an agent, or a user/agent reaching a tool or model, travels , which does two checks before letting it through:A is like an ID card issued by the identity provider, and both the user and the agent hold one.User Auth issues signed tokens for human users and it carries their groups ( isn't a core OIDC claim, so the identity provider maps it in; with Keycloak that's a group-membership protocol mapper).Agent Auth also issues signed tokens, but an agent starts from a credential it was given (a mounted ServiceAccount token, or a client secret) and exchanges that for one.The gateway does the two checks in order; first it confirms the token is genuine and unexpired (identity), then it asks the KAOS Authz Service whether that identity is allowed to do this (permission), and only if both pass does the request reach its destination.If the authz service the request is denied. There's no config knob to loosen this, since the operator sets on every policy it generates, and it's the reason the authz service runs highly available.2.2 Deploy the agents and toolsEverything the example needs (both agents, the tool, the model, and the access rule for who may use them) is bundled as a single sample. I deploy it with one command, then walk through each object and create it step by step.Here's the one line deploy command:kaos samples deploy 8-authorization-walkthrough -n kaos-system modelapi.kaos.tools/model-api serverside-applied mcpserver.kaos.tools/echo-mcp serverside-applied agent.kaos.tools/researcher serverside-applied agent.kaos.tools/autobot serverside-applied accessgrant.kaos.tools/researchers-to-researcher serverside-applied
Deployed sample '8-authorization-walkthrough' The tool's single function is an echo, and the model's responses are mocked, so every result is deterministic and the walkthrough only exercises . The four resources first, each a plain Kubernetes object (the access rule follows in 2.3):A model endpoint both agents may call.A tool (an MCP server) exposing a single function the may use.A user-facing agent. It needs a person behind it and carries that person's identity through to whatever it calls.An agent. No user behind it; it runs on a schedule and acts as itself.Each resource has its own command, so you can build a similar setup by hand and see the shape of each object. The model and tool first:# a small in-cluster model endpoint kaos modelapi create model-api \ --mode hosted \ --model "smollm2:135m"
# an echo tool exposed as an MCP server kaos mcp create echo-mcp \ --runtime python-string \ --params 'def echo(message: str) -> str: """Echo a note for the authorization walkthrough.""" return f"Echo: {message}"' Then the two agents. The user-facing one references the model and tool it should use:kaos agent create researcher \ --modelapi model-api \ --mcp echo-mcp \ --instructions "Echo the user's request and use echo-mcp when asked." The autonomous one adds an goal so it runs on its own interval instead of waiting for a person:kaos agent create autobot \ --modelapi model-api \ --autonomous-goal "Produce the automated echo report." \ --autonomous-interval 3600 writes ordinary KAOS objects; this is what the sample applies. The runs in mode and each agent carries , so the echo replies are deterministic. Note differs from mainly by its block. That single field is what makes it act as itself rather than needing a user.apiVersion: kaos.tools/v1alpha1 kind: ModelAPI metadata: name: model-api spec: mode: Proxy proxyConfig: models: - '*' --- apiVersion: kaos.tools/v1alpha1 kind: MCPServer metadata: name: echo-mcp spec: runtime: python-string params: | def echo(message: str) -> str: """Echo a note for the authorization walkthrough.""" return f"Echo: {message}" --- apiVersion: kaos.tools/v1alpha1 kind: Agent metadata: name: researcher spec: modelAPI: model-api model: echo mcpServers: - echo-mcp config: description: User-facing echo agent for authorization checks instructions: Echo the user's request and use echo-mcp when asked. container: env: - name: DEBUG_MOCK_RESPONSES value: '["{\"tool_calls\": [{\"id\": \"call_1\", \"name\": \"echo\", \"arguments\": {\"message\": \"authorization note\"}}]}", "Researcher echo response"]' agentNetwork: expose: true --- apiVersion: kaos.tools/v1alpha1 kind: Agent metadata: name: autobot spec: modelAPI: model-api model: echo config: description: Autonomous echo agent for authorization checks instructions: Echo a short automated report. autonomous: goal: Produce the automated echo report. intervalSeconds: 3600 container: env: - name: DEBUG_MOCK_RESPONSES value: '["Autobot echo response"]' agentNetwork: expose: true The sample deployed one more object alongside the resources, an , which is the rule for who may reach what. Access control is on, so nothing is reachable until it's authorized, and this grant is what lets alice's group in. It binds a (who) to one or more (what). Like the resources, you can write it yourself with , and you the object instead of applying it:kaos auth grant create --group researchers --resource agent/researcher --dry-run apiVersion: kaos.tools/v1alpha1 kind: AccessGrant metadata: name: researchers-to-researcher spec: subjects: - kind: Group name: researchers resources: - kind: Agent name: researcher A has a of (matched against the groups in the user's token), (matched against the user's subject or email), or . A names a (, , , or ) and a , or a label to match many at once. Apply it (drop ):kaos auth grant create --group researchers --resource agent/researcher [OK] created AccessGrant researchers-to-researcher That's the grant I write, which may surprise you, since the agent reaches and , and reaches , and I grant neither. An agent's access to its own tools and model is derived from the agent itself. When you declared with and , the KAOS Operator projected those links straight into the enforcement data, so the declaration the authorization. There's no separate AccessGrant to write for it, and none shows up in . The one thing that has no home in the agent spec is which may enter an agent, so that's the single grant you create.The declaration is the authorization.So the grant list is short:NAME SUBJECTS RESOURCES ENFORCED researchers-to-researcher researchers researcher True The column is the KAOS Operator reporting back, and means it has projected the rule into the Authz Service and the gateway is enforcing it. would name the reason, for example that access control is not enabled or that no user login provider is configured.If you ever need an agent to reach something it did declare, you can add an grant (kaos auth grant create --agent <agent> --resource ...). That AccessGrant is merged the derived access. For the common case, declaring the dependency is all you need.Those permissions (the one grant you wrote plus the ones derived from the agent specs) are the access that exists. Here's the same map, each green edge labelled with where its permission comes from, and everything not green is denied: gets a token from the login service and remembers it, printing what that login proves:kaos auth login alice --password kaos-password kaos auth login bob --password kaos-password [OK] logged in as alice - groups: researchers [OK] logged in as bob - groups: support The "groups" it prints are the exact claim the gateway will read out of the token on every request, and the exact thing an AccessGrant's subject matches against. alice carries and bob carries . alice as an individual isn't granted anything, her is. sends the call through the gateway as that person, and the CLI prints the plain result:kaos agent invoke researcher --user alice -m "summarise repo X" kaos agent invoke researcher --user bob -m "summarise repo X" Researcher echo response [OK] allowed - request permitted [X] denied - user not in a granted group Same agent and same request, and the only difference is who's behind it. alice's token carries , which the researchers-to-researcher grant allows, and bob's carries , which nothing grants, so he's refused at the door. alice's request lights up the granted path:...while bob's request never gets past the first edge:The agent using its granted tool and model:kaos agent invoke researcher --user alice -m "read echo-mcp and ask model-api" Researcher echo response [OK] allowed - request permitted This exercises the kind of rule. alice got in (first check), and now the agent reaches out to and . Each of those hops is itself a request through the gateway, checked against the access on its own spec (, ). Both are declared, so both succeed, and they're the two right-hand green edges on alice's diagram above.The autonomous agent acts as (no user), allowed only what was granted:kaos agent invoke autobot -m "run the automated report" Autobot echo response [OK] allowed - request permitted There's no here, yet the call is allowed, while the very next example (a user-facing agent with no ) is denied. Both are fail-closed working as intended. The autonomous agent presents its identity, which is valid, and the third rule lets that identity reach . A user-facing agent invoked with no has no identity behind it, and it needs one:kaos agent invoke researcher -m "summarise repo X" # no --user [X] denied - no valid identity And the fail-closed guarantee itself. kaos system access-control scales the KAOS Authz Service up or down, and with it gone the gateway denies:kaos system access-control --off kaos agent invoke researcher --user alice -m "hi" kaos system access-control --on [OK] access-control off [X] denied - access-control unavailable (failing closed) [OK] access-control on That's every rule from section 2 proven with plain commands, and nothing was configured by hand in User Auth or the Authz Service; the KAOS Operator kept them aligned with the objects you declared.The example above shows happens, and this section explains , one capability at a time. Each sub-section ends with the actual configuration behind it (declared objects and Helm values).4.1 Agent identity: how does an agent prove who it is?How does the gateway know which agent is calling, even when no person started it? That's Agent Auth's job, and it's the one place on the section 1 map where the KAOS Operator's out-of-band work is easiest to see. Here's the same map from the operator's point of view, with the sync work drawn in:Every agent gets an identity so the gateway knows who is calling. By default that identity is a Kubernetes ServiceAccount. When an agent's pod starts, KAOS mounts a short-lived ServiceAccount token into it, scoped so it's only valid for the gateway (its is ). Every call the agent makes carries that token; the gateway reads it to learn which agent is calling, then checks that agent's grants. The token expires and is refreshed automatically, so there's no long-lived secret sitting in the pod. This is Kubernetes' standard bound, audience-scoped ServiceAccount token mechanism (KEP-1205), not anything KAOS invents. The operator registers each agent so the Authz Service recognises it.I selected at install instead, because delegated third-party access (section 5) needs each agent to hold a login-service identity. With , the operator registers each agent as its in User Auth automatically, using dynamic client registration (DCR), which is the "registers each agent as a client" edge on the chart. No one creates those clients by hand. The stored Kubernetes Secret holding the agent's client credentials is the idempotency key, so if the Secret is present the agent is already registered, and deleting it forces a clean re-registration on the next reconcile. Timing differs by subject too, as the chart's other edges show; users and groups are provisioned once at install, while each agent's client is created when the agent is reconciled. For everything in sections 1 to 4, is simpler and I'd prefer it; only section 5 requires .An agent (like ) has no user behind it, so it acts . Its own identity is the "who asked", and it can reach only what that identity was granted. A user-facing agent (like ) instead carries the identity through to whatever it calls, so downstream checks see the real person.Agent identity is a single choice under security.agentAuth.identity. The default provider is Kubernetes-native:security: agentAuth: gatewayJwtOptional: true identity: provider: serviceaccount # the default serviceAccount: audience: kaos-gateway expirationSeconds: 3600 tokenPath: /var/run/secrets/kaos-agent/token means that for agent tokens, the Authz Service performs the full identity check; the gateway's own user-token check does not block agent calls. Autonomous agents need this, because their Kubernetes-issued ServiceAccount token isn't a user login token, and the user login provider would otherwise reject it before the access check ever runs. The block is the short-lived mounted token described above, valid only for the gateway (), auto-refreshed () and read from .Switching the provider is the whole difference between the two modes, and this is what sets:security: agentAuth: identity: provider: keycloak # each agent becomes its own login-service client With this provider the operator registers each agent's client via dynamic client registration and stores its credentials in a Kubernetes Secret (the idempotency key described above; delete it to force re-registration on the next reconcile). This is heavier than , and needed only when the agent must present a login-service identity to the Agent Identity Broker (section 5).4.2 User identity: who is this person, and what groups are they in?Who is this person, and which groups are they in? When a person is behind a request, User Auth (Keycloak in this example) proves who they are and they're in. That group membership is what access rules match on, so isn't granted access personally, her is. The intuition in one picture: ran the standard login exchange and cached alice's token; the groups it printed are the same ones the gateway will read on every request. The one thing KAOS requires of the login service is that issued tokens carry a claim (and a stable claim naming the user). Everything else about your identity provider, how people actually authenticate, where the groups come from, is up to you.The installer creates a realm with the users, the / groups, and a set of that stamp the right claims onto every issued token. Without the groups mapper, tokens wouldn't carry group membership and group-based AccessGrants couldn't match. This is the shape KAOS provisions (trimmed to the relevant pieces):{ "realm": "kaos", "enabled": true, "groups": [{ "name": "researchers" }, { "name": "support" }], "users": [ { "username": "alice", "email": "alice@example.com", "enabled": true, "groups": ["researchers"], "credentials": [{ "type": "password", "value": "...", "temporary": false }] }, { "username": "bob", "email": "bob@example.com", "enabled": true, "groups": ["support"], "credentials": [{ "type": "password", "value": "...", "temporary": false }] } ], "clients": [ { "clientId": "kaos", "publicClient": false, "secret": "kaos-dev-secret", "directAccessGrantsEnabled": true, "standardFlowEnabled": true, "protocolMappers": [ { "name": "kaos-groups", "protocolMapper": "oidc-group-membership-mapper", "config": { "claim.name": "groups", "full.path": "false", "access.token.claim": "true" } }, { "name": "kaos-subject", "protocolMapper": "oidc-usermodel-property-mapper", "config": { "user.attribute": "id", "claim.name": "sub", "access.token.claim": "true" } }, { "name": "kaos-audience", "protocolMapper": "oidc-audience-mapper", "config": { "included.client.audience": "kaos", "access.token.claim": "true" } } ] } ] } The gateway is told where to find this realm and what audience to expect through two Helm values:security: userAuth: issuer: http://keycloak.keycloak.svc.cluster.local:8080/realms/kaos audience: kaos # tokens must be minted for this audience In production you point at your own OIDC provider instead, and map your existing directory groups into the claim. KAOS doesn't care the claim gets populated, only that it's there.4.3 Access control: the rules and their enforcementThis is where "is it allowed?" gets answered, and there are two kinds of rule: An binds a (or user) to a resource: may use ." This gates a person reaching an agent. An binds an to tools/models: may reach and ." This gates movement between components.Both are the same object type, and only the subject differs (a group/user vs. an agent). I kept it uniform so there's one rule format to learn, one place to look, and one that shows every explicit grant in the cluster.Enforcement lives at the gateway, which asks the on every request. That service runs in-cluster as its own always-on service with multiple replicas, so it's highly available. It , so if it says no or can't be reached the request is denied (you saw this with ). And resources are only reachable when is set, so a workload can't sidestep it by calling a resource directly.The Authz Service never reads your AccessGrant objects directly. The KAOS Operator is the go-between, so it watches the objects, compiles them into the data the Authz Service evaluates, and keeps that projection current as you add and remove grants. The column you saw earlier is the operator confirming the rule is live.Autonomous agents fit the same model. Their identity is the subject, so needs a grant for anything it touches, exactly like a user does.Enforcement is the KAOS Authz Service (stock OPA behind Envoy's authorization plugin) plus the operator's projection of your grants into it:security: pdp: enabled: true # the KAOS Authz Service image: openpolicyagent/opa:1.18.1-envoy-static replicas: 2 # highly available agentAuth: authorization: # "automated": the KAOS Operator projects grant data from your # AccessGrant objects. You never author decision-service policy by hand. policyDataSource: automated projection: # prune removes stale grant data when an Agent or AccessGrant is deleted, # so permissions never outlive the object that declared them. prune: true # the "gateway is the only path" posture, so the check can't be bypassed strictGatewayApi: enabled: true networkPolicy: enabled: true # deny direct workload-to-workload traffic gatewayRouting: enabled: true # route agent -> tool/model/peer calls via the gateway The fail-closed behaviour is how the gateway treats an authorization backend that says no doesn't answer, and denying on "no answer" is the default and can't be relaxed into "allow on error". Fail-closed means treating "no answer" from the authz service as a . That safe default costs availability, which is exactly why the Authz Service runs HA.Further reading on the enforcement model. Checking every hop at a gateway is a standard shape, a policy enforcement point (the gateway) consulting a policy decision point (the Authz Service), in the vocabulary NIST SP 800-207 formalised. The concrete mechanism, an Envoy external-authorization filter calling out to a policy engine, is documented in the OPA-Envoy plugin. And while agents here default to Kubernetes ServiceAccounts, the same workload-identity idea generalises beyond the cluster through SPIFFE/SPIRE and the emerging IETF WIMSE work.5. Agents acting on behalf of users - on outside servicesWhat happens when the researcher agent needs to access GitHub on behalf of the user? Whose GitHub account does it act on?Everything so far focuses on identity for access control, and nothing yet lets an agent reach external oauth services like GitHub as the specific user instead of through a shared bot account.The naive way to let an agent use GitHub is to give it a single bot account's token and let every user's request ride on it (I did exactly this the first time round). People build it because it's the thing to build, one token in a Secret, one HTTP client, done. But it's a shared credential, so GitHub sees one identity for everyone, you can't tell whose request was whose, and revoking one person's access means rotating the token for all of them. Worse, that durable token now lives somewhere the agent can read.Nothing from sections 1-4 can fix it, because an in-cluster can't express "GitHub as alice". The cluster has no authority over GitHub's tokens, so it can decide a request leaves, but it can't make GitHub see alice instead of the bot. Bridging that gap needs a component that holds each user's GitHub credential (issued by GitHub, consented to by the user) and puts the right one on each outbound call.KAOS does the opposite of the shared bot on all 3 counts. When alice asks the researcher to touch GitHub, GitHub receives token and sees alice, and bob's requests go out as bob, so permissions and audit on the GitHub side are per-person, exactly as if each user called GitHub directly. The agent only ever holds its own short-lived in-cluster identity, because the real GitHub token is swapped onto the outbound request at the gateway and the agent code never touches it. And alice can withdraw her approval at any time without affecting anyone else.5.2 Enter the Agent Identity Broker (AIB)The component that holds each user's real credential is the (AIB; deployed from the chart). It runs as its own self-managed Helm release alongside the cluster, much like Keycloak, and the KAOS operator deploys none of it. It holds each user's real third-party tokens in a vault, put there when the user consents (5.4), and the one thing it does with them is . Present it proof of who the user is and which agent is acting, and it returns that user's stored third-party token. It never issues anyone's identity; agents get theirs from Agent Auth, users from User Auth, and the AIB only ever trades one proven identity for a stored credential.Nothing new gets installed here. Every component in this section went in with the single install command in 1.1 (, ). On the section 1 map the greyed pieces light up, and everything goes grey:This is also why the install needed . The AIB must be able to tie an exchange request to a specific agent, and for that the agent needs a login-service identity, which a ServiceAccount can't give it. The KAOS Operator keeps the connection current from the other side, registering each agent in the AIB under a stable () and keeping that record's client id up to date across re-registrations (the greyed operator edge on the 4.1 chart).5.3 Register GitHub and create a permission set is a tool the cluster, a KAOS resource gated by AccessGrants, and GitHub is a service it. You could wrap GitHub in an internal MCP server with a shared bot token, which is exactly the anti-pattern from 5.1. Instead, GitHub is declared , and each call goes out as the real user.Outside services are administered in the AIB itself and not as cluster objects, because the AIB is what actually holds the user's third-party tokens. The declaration has 3 parts: the (GitHub, meaning its API hostname and OAuth endpoints), a (the scopes an agent may request on it), and the (which agent may use that permission set, keyed by the agent's stable logical name). The operator keeps that logical name and the agent's login-service client current, and the declaration into the cluster plumbing it implies. The token swap exists only on the GitHub route, so internal traffic never touches the AIB. This is the same boundary the MCP security best practices draws when it forbids and requires audience validation; a token minted for one hop must never be silently reused on another, which is the classic trap.The declaration is AIB-native. There's no third-party YAML in your Git repo, since the AIB is the config authority and it's where third-party access is audited (the trade-off I accepted for keeping it out of the cluster API).# Administered in the AIB, not as a Kubernetes object. service: name: github hostnames: ['api.github.com'] oauth: authorization_url: https://github.com/login/oauth/authorize token_url: https://github.com/login/oauth/access_token scopes: ['repo', 'read:user']
permission_set: service: github scopes: ['repo', 'read:user']
agent: logical_name: kaos/kaos-system/researcher client_id: <keycloak-dcr-uuid> permission_sets: ['github'] The is the stable agent name the operator maintains; is the agent's login-service client (the DCR UUID from 4.1), kept current across re-registrations. From this declaration the operator materializes the egress route to , attaches the AIB's token-swap filter to that generated route, and injects the exchange target into the bound agent. Nothing here touches the internal access-control path.Inside the cluster nothing about the earlier checks changes, so alice still has to be allowed to use the researcher, and the researcher still has to be granted its tools. The new part is only the , the outbound call to GitHub.5.4 The request and consent flowThe user's identity travels all the way through the agent to GitHub, so every call goes out as the real user and GitHub sees alice.The very first time alice asks for something on GitHub there's no approval on file, so the request is refused with an instruction. alice approves once, the AIB stores her token, and from then on it just works until she revokes it:Walk it for real. The first time, there's no approval yet:kaos agent invoke researcher --user alice -m "list my GitHub repos" [X] needs approval - run: kaos auth connect github --user alice alice approves. The CLI opens GitHub's approval screen, she clicks allow, and the AIB stores her token:kaos auth connect github --user alice [OK] connected - alice can now use github through their agents (On a local demo cluster the approval is completed automatically against a mock GitHub, so the notebook runs without a real browser; in production alice clicks "allow" in her browser. That's the only difference.)Retry. Now it works, :kaos agent invoke researcher --user alice -m "list my GitHub repos" Third-party tool completed. [OK] allowed - acting as alice on github Approval is revocable, and revocation simply returns you to step 1 of the flow, so after a disconnect the agent is refused again until re-approved:kaos auth disconnect github --user alice kaos agent invoke researcher --user alice -m "list my GitHub repos" [OK] disconnected [X] needs approval - run: kaos auth connect github --user alice , that successful call is three moves:The agent runtime re-mints alice's own token so it also names the acting agent. This is a standard OAuth 2.0 token exchange (RFC 8693) against User Auth, authenticated with the agent's own client credentials, and it produces a token with , , aud=token-exchange-broker, one token that proves both who the user is and which agent is acting. This is what it means for the agent to the user, or act (the terms are used interchangeably); the exchanged token keeps identities, so the action stays auditable as and not as an anonymous bot.On the outbound GitHub route, and on that route, the gateway presents the re-minted token, together with the agent's own credential, to the AIB. The AIB validates both, checks that alice consented, and returns alice's real GitHub token from its vault.The gateway swaps alice's GitHub token onto the outbound request. GitHub receives it and sees alice (steps 7-10 on the 5.2 map).The token swap can never leak onto internal paths, because the swap filter is attached only to the egress route the operator generated for the declared service. Only alice's own token ever reaches GitHub, and the agent never sees a long-lived credential. But you don't have to think about any of that, since you once and then as normal.Further reading on acting on behalf of a user. Nothing in this pattern is bespoke to KAOS, and the same shape shows up in a few places:Closing Thoughts: Making Agent Identity BoringBack to Alice and Bob sending the same request and deserving different answers, and Alice asking for GitHub and deserving to be the one GitHub sees. I asked 4 questions at the top, and I can answer all of them now.A user in the wrong group is refused at the door. Same agent and same message, and the only difference is who's behind it. alice's token carries , which the one grant I wrote allows, and bob's carries , which nothing grants, so he never reaches the agent at all.The agent's own hops were authorized by its declaration. I wrote exactly one AccessGrant in the entire walkthrough. The researcher reaching and was authorized by the dependencies I declared on the agent, which the operator projected straight into the enforcement data, so that's one less thing to keep in sync.The autonomous agent acted as itself and was still checked. has no user behind it and is allowed anyway, because it presents its own identity, which is valid, and it can reach only what that identity was granted. The user-facing agent invoked with no user is refused, because that one has no identity behind it at all.And the GitHub endpoint received alice. She consented once, the broker stored her token, and every call after that went out carrying her delegated identity. When she disconnected, the very next request was refused again. The agent never held her credential at any point in that sequence, because the exchange happens at the gateway on one specific egress route and nowhere else. On this cluster the endpoint on the far end is a mock, so what I proved is the delegation path and not GitHub's own behaviour.What I'd take away from building this is that almost none of it is exotic. It's OAuth token exchange, an OIDC provider, a gateway doing external authorization, a NetworkPolicy, and one component holding consented credentials that I can now install instead of writing. What made this expensive for everyone was that the credential vault and the consent surface were homework each team had to do alone, and that piece has just been open sourced.If your agents can act as your users without ever holding their credentials, identity has become the dull part of the platform, and I think that's exactly where it belongs.Part 1: the problem, what to build on, and the broker. The three questions every agent request has to answer, the standards and tools that already exist, what the Agentic Identity Broker does, and the architecture decisions I made on top of it.Part 2 (this post): agent identity in action. A worked example that runs end to end on a cluster, with two users, two agents, a tool, a model and a third-party service, and real allow and deny outputs.This is a 2-part series on agent identity and security: who the user is, who the agent is, and what each of them should be allowed to reach. Part 2 runs the design end to end on a cluster, with two users, two agents, a tool, a model and a third-party service.In Part 1 I designed how agent identity can work on a platform where agent-delegation is enabled, and how we decide (+ enforce) what they and their users are allowed to reach. In this second and final part I deploy that design on a cluster and check whether it actually holds up.In this Part 2 blog post, I go through a hands-on use-case with 2 users of the same agent platform at the same company: Alice is in the group and Bob is in the group. Throughout this I will show the good, the bad and the ugly of agentic identity and security, especially when dealing with autonomous agents, and with users delegating permissions to an agent.The walkthrough answers 4 questions:Does an agent requesting a tool for a user in the wrong group actually get refused?When an agent calls its own tool and model, how do we authorize (+ verify) the hops?What happens to an autonomous agent that has no user behind it at all?When Alice asks for a 3rd party service (i.e. github) via an agent, does the request go out as Alice?Most of what I learnt came from the requests that got denied (+ from the complexities and lessons learned), so you'll see plenty of those below.Everything below runs on a local KIND cluster against the public Agentic Identity Broker release, pinned at . On a local cluster GitHub is a mock, so the consent screen gets completed automatically instead of in a browser, but every identity and access-control decision you'll see is real.Here's a quick refresher of what we covered in Part 1 before we run it.I started with the challenges we all phase when agents have to access 3rd party services on behalf of a user. Here I showed how just giving an API token falls short, as you can't tell which user an action was for, it has more access than any single user needs, and you can't revoke it for just one user.Fixing that needed a component that holds each user's own third-party credential, obtained with their consent. The Agentic Identity Broker does exactly that, so I adopted it instead of writing my own.Then I separated the 2 identities that every protected call carries. The is the human the work is being done for, and the is the agent doing the work. This is how the system enforces resource access on the actor and use the subject for what the user personally delegated, which keeps permissions correct when agents call other agents.Finally I made 6 architecture decisions, and 3 of them matter most for what follows:One gateway on every hop, plus a NetworkPolicy so nothing can go around itChecks in the agent runtime, a sidecar per workload, a service meshHow authorization is modelledOne explicit for who may enter an agent, with the agent's own dependencies derived from its spec, all evaluated by KAOS's own Open Policy Agent decision pointA policy language as the authoring surface, or the broker answering the decisionKAOS owns the integration; the broker and the identity provider run as their own releasesThe platform installing and lifecycle-managing its own brokerThat third row is why this walkthrough has both a broker and Keycloak in it. The broker holds the delegated third-party credentials and performs the exchange, and the gateway attaches the returned credential to the outbound request. Keycloak proves who the human is, carries the group membership the rules match on, and registers each agent as its own client so the broker can tell which agent is asking.Now let's build the cluster and see it work.The is the set of components that establish identity and decide the rules. Apart from the gateway, none of them carry your agents' actual traffic; they answer the 3 questions from part 1 about it. Here they are on one map. The greyed pieces belong to section 5 and can be ignored for now.There are quite a few components in this overview, so let's walk through them:: This is the single gateway every request passes through, including agent-to-tool, agent-to-model and agent-to-agent calls, which is what makes it a mesh.: Authenticates users, proves who they are and which groups they belong to; supports OIDC compatible services so we use Keycloak here.: Gives each agent their identity through secure credentials; the default uses k8s Service Accounts, but also supports OIDC compatible services; we also configure Keycloak in this example.: This is the authorization (authz) service that KAOS uses to allow/deny requests based on the "user" calling the "agent" accessing the "resource".Agent Impersonation Service: Lets an agent act on an outside service (like GitHub) as the user by exchanging third-party tokens (github/slack/etc) through a consent mechanism. The concrete tool I use is the Agent Identity Broker (AIB), and it gets its own section, section 5.: This component synchronises auth & identity bidirectionaly; it registers the KAOS resources on upstream auth services, and injects identities and secrets across KAOS resources.Before I show how this all fits together with an example, let's configure the kubernetes cluster with this setup.1.1 Install it in one commandI use the KAOS CLI to install the Gateway Mesh, User Auth, Agent Auth, the KAOS Authz Service, the KAOS Operator, and the Agent Identity Broker (AIB).This command wires everything together in a new cluster:kaos system install \ --gateway-strict \ # Traffic can only go through gateway --authz-enabled \ # KAOS Authorization service enabled --user-auth keycloak \ # Use Keycloak for User auth (alt: OIDC) --agent-auth keycloak \ # Use Keycloak for Agent Auth (alt: Service Accts. or OIDC) --token-exchange-enabled \ # Use AIB for token exchange
# Other flags --wait \ # Block until everything is ready --create-cli-config # In-folder config file for cli kaos system install --help lists everything else (image tags, resource limits, replica counts, realm names, observability backends); the Helm values behind each flag are shown per-component in section 4.Let's confirm the pieces are healthy:gateway ready login service ready (keycloak) access-control ready (2/2 replicas) sync service ready And let's make sure that everything is configured correctly:gateway: address: http://kaos-gateway.kaos-system.svc.cluster.local through_gateway: true auth: issuer: http://keycloak.keycloak.svc.cluster.local:8080/realms/kaos client_id: kaos realm: kaos broker_url: http://aib-agentic-identity-broker.aib-system.svc.cluster.local:8000 broker_admin_url: http://aib-agentic-identity-broker.aib-system.svc.cluster.local:14000/api namespace: kaos-system sessions: {} The is the actual agent traffic, meaning users invoking agents and agents calling tools and models. Everything else is denied, including bob (poor bob).Here's a chart that shows what we'll try to accomplish:2.1 How identity flows through a requestEvery call, a user/agent reaching an agent, or a user/agent reaching a tool or model, travels , which does two checks before letting it through:A is like an ID card issued by the identity provider, and both the user and the agent hold one.User Auth issues signed tokens for human users and it carries their groups ( isn't a core OIDC claim, so the identity provider maps it in; with Keycloak that's a group-membership protocol mapper).Agent Auth also issues signed tokens, but an agent starts from a credential it was given (a mounted ServiceAccount token, or a client secret) and exchanges that for one.The gateway does the two checks in order; first it confirms the token is genuine and unexpired (identity), then it asks the KAOS Authz Service whether that identity is allowed to do this (permission), and only if both pass does the request reach its destination.If the authz service the request is denied. There's no config knob to loosen this, since the operator sets on every policy it generates, and it's the reason the authz service runs highly available.2.2 Deploy the agents and toolsEverything the example needs (both agents, the tool, the model, and the access rule for who may use them) is bundled as a single sample. Each sub-section ends with the actual configuration behind it (declared objects and Helm values).4.1 Agent identity: how does an agent prove who it is?How does the gateway know which agent is calling, even when no person started it? That's Agent Auth's job, and it's the one place on the section 1 map where the KAOS Operator's out-of-band work is easiest to see. Here's the same map from the operator's point of view, with the sync work drawn in:Every agent gets an identity so the gateway knows who is calling. By default that identity is a Kubernetes ServiceAccount. When an agent's pod starts, KAOS mounts a short-lived ServiceAccount token into it, scoped so it's only valid for the gateway (its is ). Every call the agent makes carries that token; the gateway reads it to learn which agent is calling, then checks that agent's grants. The token expires and is refreshed automatically, so there's no long-lived secret sitting in the pod. This is Kubernetes' standard bound, audience-scoped ServiceAccount token mechanism (KEP-1205), not anything KAOS invents. The operator registers each agent so the Authz Service recognises it.I selected at install instead, because delegated third-party access (section 5) needs each agent to hold a login-service identity. With , the operator registers each agent as its in User Auth automatically, using dynamic client registration (DCR), which is the "registers each agent as a client" edge on the chart. No one creates those clients by hand. The stored Kubernetes Secret holding the agent's client credentials is the idempotency key, so if the Secret is present the agent is already registered, and deleting it forces a clean re-registration on the next reconcile. Timing differs by subject too, as the chart's other edges show; users and groups are provisioned once at install, while each agent's client is created when the agent is reconciled. For everything in sections 1 to 4, is simpler and I'd prefer it; only section 5 requires .An agent (like ) has no user behind it, so it acts . Its own identity is the "who asked", and it can reach only what that identity was granted. A user-facing agent (like ) instead carries the identity through to whatever it calls, so downstream checks see the real person.Agent identity is a single choice under security.agentAuth.identity. The default provider is Kubernetes-native:security: agentAuth: gatewayJwtOptional: true identity: provider: serviceaccount # the default serviceAccount: audience: kaos-gateway expirationSeconds: 3600 tokenPath: /var/run/secrets/kaos-agent/token means that for agent tokens, the Authz Service performs the full identity check; the gateway's own user-token check does not block agent calls. Autonomous agents need this, because their Kubernetes-issued ServiceAccount token isn't a user login token, and the user login provider would otherwise reject it before the access check ever runs. The block is the short-lived mounted token described above, valid only for the gateway (), auto-refreshed () and read from .Switching the provider is the whole difference between the two modes, and this is what sets:security: agentAuth: identity: provider: keycloak # each agent becomes its own login-service client With this provider the operator registers each agent's client via dynamic client registration and stores its credentials in a Kubernetes Secret (the idempotency key described above; delete it to force re-registration on the next reconcile). This is heavier than , and needed only when the agent must present a login-service identity to the Agent Identity Broker (section 5).4.2 User identity: who is this person, and what groups are they in?Who is this person, and which groups are they in? When a person is behind a request, User Auth (Keycloak in this example) proves who they are and they're in. That group membership is what access rules match on, so isn't granted access personally, her is. The intuition in one picture: ran the standard login exchange and cached alice's token; the groups it printed are the same ones the gateway will read on every request. The one thing KAOS requires of the login service is that issued tokens carry a claim (and a stable claim naming the user). Everything else about your identity provider, how people actually authenticate, where the groups come from, is up to you.The installer creates a realm with the users, the / groups, and a set of that stamp the right claims onto every issued token. Without the groups mapper, tokens wouldn't carry group membership and group-based AccessGrants couldn't match. This is the shape KAOS provisions (trimmed to the relevant pieces):{ "realm": "kaos", "enabled": true, "groups": [{ "name": "researchers" }, { "name": "support" }], "users": [ { "username": "alice", "email": "alice@example.com", "enabled": true, "groups": ["researchers"], "credentials": [{ "type": "password", "value": "...", "temporary": false }] }, { "username": "bob", "email": "bob@example.com", "enabled": true, "groups": ["support"], "credentials": [{ "type": "password", "value": "...", "temporary": false }] } ], "clients": [ { "clientId": "kaos", "publicClient": false, "secret": "kaos-dev-secret", "directAccessGrantsEnabled": true, "standardFlowEnabled": true, "protocolMappers": [ { "name": "kaos-groups", "protocolMapper": "oidc-group-membership-mapper", "config": { "claim.name": "groups", "full.path": "false", "access.token.claim": "true" } }, { "name": "kaos-subject", "protocolMapper": "oidc-usermodel-property-mapper", "config": { "user.attribute": "id", "claim.name": "sub", "access.token.claim": "true" } }, { "name": "kaos-audience", "protocolMapper": "oidc-audience-mapper", "config": { "included.client.audience": "kaos", "access.token.claim": "true" } } ] } ] } The gateway is told where to find this realm and what audience to expect through two Helm values:security: userAuth: issuer: http://keycloak.keycloak.svc.cluster.local:8080/realms/kaos audience: kaos # tokens must be minted for this audience In production you point at your own OIDC provider instead, and map your existing directory groups into the claim. KAOS doesn't care the claim gets populated, only that it's there.4.3 Access control: the rules and their enforcementThis is where "is it allowed?" gets answered, and there are two kinds of rule: An binds a (or user) to a resource: may use ." This gates a person reaching an agent. An binds an to tools/models: may reach and ." This gates movement between components.Both are the same object type, and only the subject differs (a group/user vs. an agent). I kept it uniform so there's one rule format to learn, one place to look, and one that shows every explicit grant in the cluster.Enforcement lives at the gateway, which asks the on every request. That service runs in-cluster as its own always-on service with multiple replicas, so it's highly available. It , so if it says no or can't be reached the request is denied (you saw this with ). And resources are only reachable when is set, so a workload can't sidestep it by calling a resource directly.The Authz Service never reads your AccessGrant objects directly. The KAOS Operator is the go-between, so it watches the objects, compiles them into the data the Authz Service evaluates, and keeps that projection current as you add and remove grants. The column you saw earlier is the operator confirming the rule is live.Autonomous agents fit the same model. Their identity is the subject, so needs a grant for anything it touches, exactly like a user does.Enforcement is the KAOS Authz Service (stock OPA behind Envoy's authorization plugin) plus the operator's projection of your grants into it:security: pdp: enabled: true # the KAOS Authz Service image: openpolicyagent/opa:1.18.1-envoy-static replicas: 2 # highly available agentAuth: authorization: # "automated": the KAOS Operator projects grant data from your # AccessGrant objects.
