You never author decision-service policy by hand. policyDataSource: automated projection: # prune removes stale grant data when an Agent or AccessGrant is deleted, # so permissions never outlive the object that declared them. prune: true # the "gateway is the only path" posture, so the check can't be bypassed strictGatewayApi: enabled: true networkPolicy: enabled: true # deny direct workload-to-workload traffic gatewayRouting: enabled: true # route agent -> tool/model/peer calls via the gateway The fail-closed behaviour is how the gateway treats an authorization backend that says no doesn't answer, and denying on "no answer" is the default and can't be relaxed into "allow on error". Fail-closed means treating "no answer" from the authz service as a . That safe default costs availability, which is exactly why the Authz Service runs HA.Further reading on the enforcement model. Checking every hop at a gateway is a standard shape, a policy enforcement point (the gateway) consulting a policy decision point (the Authz Service), in the vocabulary NIST SP 800-207 formalised. The concrete mechanism, an Envoy external-authorization filter calling out to a policy engine, is documented in the OPA-Envoy plugin. And while agents here default to Kubernetes ServiceAccounts, the same workload-identity idea generalises beyond the cluster through SPIFFE/SPIRE and the emerging IETF WIMSE work.5. Agents acting on behalf of users - on outside servicesWhat happens when the researcher agent needs to access GitHub on behalf of the user? Whose GitHub account does it act on?Everything so far focuses on identity for access control, and nothing yet lets an agent reach external oauth services like GitHub as the specific user instead of through a shared bot account.The naive way to let an agent use GitHub is to give it a single bot account's token and let every user's request ride on it (I did exactly this the first time round). People build it because it's the thing to build, one token in a Secret, one HTTP client, done. But it's a shared credential, so GitHub sees one identity for everyone, you can't tell whose request was whose, and revoking one person's access means rotating the token for all of them. Worse, that durable token now lives somewhere the agent can read.Nothing from sections 1-4 can fix it, because an in-cluster can't express "GitHub as alice". The cluster has no authority over GitHub's tokens, so it can decide a request leaves, but it can't make GitHub see alice instead of the bot. Bridging that gap needs a component that holds each user's GitHub credential (issued by GitHub, consented to by the user) and puts the right one on each outbound call.KAOS does the opposite of the shared bot on all 3 counts. When alice asks the researcher to touch GitHub, GitHub receives token and sees alice, and bob's requests go out as bob, so permissions and audit on the GitHub side are per-person, exactly as if each user called GitHub directly. The agent only ever holds its own short-lived in-cluster identity, because the real GitHub token is swapped onto the outbound request at the gateway and the agent code never touches it. And alice can withdraw her approval at any time without affecting anyone else.5.2 Enter the Agent Identity Broker (AIB)The component that holds each user's real credential is the (AIB; deployed from the chart). It runs as its own self-managed Helm release alongside the cluster, much like Keycloak, and the KAOS operator deploys none of it. It holds each user's real third-party tokens in a vault, put there when the user consents (5.4), and the one thing it does with them is . Present it proof of who the user is and which agent is acting, and it returns that user's stored third-party token. It never issues anyone's identity; agents get theirs from Agent Auth, users from User Auth, and the AIB only ever trades one proven identity for a stored credential.Nothing new gets installed here. Every component in this section went in with the single install command in 1.1 (, ). On the section 1 map the greyed pieces light up, and everything goes grey:This is also why the install needed . The AIB must be able to tie an exchange request to a specific agent, and for that the agent needs a login-service identity, which a ServiceAccount can't give it. The KAOS Operator keeps the connection current from the other side, registering each agent in the AIB under a stable () and keeping that record's client id up to date across re-registrations (the greyed operator edge on the 4.1 chart).5.3 Register GitHub and create a permission set is a tool the cluster, a KAOS resource gated by AccessGrants, and GitHub is a service it. You could wrap GitHub in an internal MCP server with a shared bot token, which is exactly the anti-pattern from 5.1. Instead, GitHub is declared , and each call goes out as the real user.Outside services are administered in the AIB itself and not as cluster objects, because the AIB is what actually holds the user's third-party tokens. The declaration has 3 parts: the (GitHub, meaning its API hostname and OAuth endpoints), a (the scopes an agent may request on it), and the (which agent may use that permission set, keyed by the agent's stable logical name). The operator keeps that logical name and the agent's login-service client current, and the declaration into the cluster plumbing it implies. The token swap exists only on the GitHub route, so internal traffic never touches the AIB. This is the same boundary the MCP security best practices draws when it forbids and requires audience validation; a token minted for one hop must never be silently reused on another, which is the classic trap.The declaration is AIB-native. There's no third-party YAML in your Git repo, since the AIB is the config authority and it's where third-party access is audited (the trade-off I accepted for keeping it out of the cluster API).# Administered in the AIB, not as a Kubernetes object. service: name: github hostnames: ['api.github.com'] oauth: authorization_url: https://github.com/login/oauth/authorize token_url: https://github.com/login/oauth/access_token scopes: ['repo', 'read:user']
permission_set: service: github scopes: ['repo', 'read:user']
agent: logical_name: kaos/kaos-system/researcher client_id: <keycloak-dcr-uuid> permission_sets: ['github'] The is the stable agent name the operator maintains; is the agent's login-service client (the DCR UUID from 4.1), kept current across re-registrations. From this declaration the operator materializes the egress route to , attaches the AIB's token-swap filter to that generated route, and injects the exchange target into the bound agent. Nothing here touches the internal access-control path.Inside the cluster nothing about the earlier checks changes, so alice still has to be allowed to use the researcher, and the researcher still has to be granted its tools. The new part is only the , the outbound call to GitHub.5.4 The request and consent flowThe user's identity travels all the way through the agent to GitHub, so every call goes out as the real user and GitHub sees alice.The very first time alice asks for something on GitHub there's no approval on file, so the request is refused with an instruction. alice approves once, the AIB stores her token, and from then on it just works until she revokes it:Walk it for real. The first time, there's no approval yet:kaos agent invoke researcher --user alice -m "list my GitHub repos" [X] needs approval - run: kaos auth connect github --user alice alice approves. The CLI opens GitHub's approval screen, she clicks allow, and the AIB stores her token:kaos auth connect github --user alice [OK] connected - alice can now use github through their agents (On a local demo cluster the approval is completed automatically against a mock GitHub, so the notebook runs without a real browser; in production alice clicks "allow" in her browser. That's the only difference.)Retry. Now it works, :kaos agent invoke researcher --user alice -m "list my GitHub repos" Third-party tool completed. [OK] allowed - acting as alice on github Approval is revocable, and revocation simply returns you to step 1 of the flow, so after a disconnect the agent is refused again until re-approved:kaos auth disconnect github --user alice kaos agent invoke researcher --user alice -m "list my GitHub repos" [OK] disconnected [X] needs approval - run: kaos auth connect github --user alice , that successful call is three moves:The agent runtime re-mints alice's own token so it also names the acting agent. This is a standard OAuth 2.0 token exchange (RFC 8693) against User Auth, authenticated with the agent's own client credentials, and it produces a token with , , aud=token-exchange-broker, one token that proves both who the user is and which agent is acting. This is what it means for the agent to the user, or act (the terms are used interchangeably); the exchanged token keeps identities, so the action stays auditable as and not as an anonymous bot.On the outbound GitHub route, and on that route, the gateway presents the re-minted token, together with the agent's own credential, to the AIB. The AIB validates both, checks that alice consented, and returns alice's real GitHub token from its vault.The gateway swaps alice's GitHub token onto the outbound request. GitHub receives it and sees alice (steps 7-10 on the 5.2 map).The token swap can never leak onto internal paths, because the swap filter is attached only to the egress route the operator generated for the declared service. Only alice's own token ever reaches GitHub, and the agent never sees a long-lived credential. But you don't have to think about any of that, since you once and then as normal.Further reading on acting on behalf of a user. Nothing in this pattern is bespoke to KAOS, and the same shape shows up in a few places:Closing Thoughts: Making Agent Identity BoringBack to Alice and Bob sending the same request and deserving different answers, and Alice asking for GitHub and deserving to be the one GitHub sees. I asked 4 questions at the top, and I can answer all of them now.A user in the wrong group is refused at the door. Same agent and same message, and the only difference is who's behind it. alice's token carries , which the one grant I wrote allows, and bob's carries , which nothing grants, so he never reaches the agent at all.The agent's own hops were authorized by its declaration. I wrote exactly one AccessGrant in the entire walkthrough. The researcher reaching and was authorized by the dependencies I declared on the agent, which the operator projected straight into the enforcement data, so that's one less thing to keep in sync.The autonomous agent acted as itself and was still checked. has no user behind it and is allowed anyway, because it presents its own identity, which is valid, and it can reach only what that identity was granted. The user-facing agent invoked with no user is refused, because that one has no identity behind it at all.And the GitHub endpoint received alice. She consented once, the broker stored her token, and every call after that went out carrying her delegated identity. When she disconnected, the very next request was refused again. The agent never held her credential at any point in that sequence, because the exchange happens at the gateway on one specific egress route and nowhere else. On this cluster the endpoint on the far end is a mock, so what I proved is the delegation path and not GitHub's own behaviour.What I'd take away from building this is that almost none of it is exotic. It's OAuth token exchange, an OIDC provider, a gateway doing external authorization, a NetworkPolicy, and one component holding consented credentials that I can now install instead of writing. What made this expensive for everyone was that the credential vault and the consent surface were homework each team had to do alone, and that piece has just been open sourced.If your agents can act as your users without ever holding their credentials, identity has become the dull part of the platform, and I think that's exactly where it belongs.Part 1: the problem, what to build on, and the broker. The three questions every agent request has to answer, the standards and tools that already exist, what the Agentic Identity Broker does, and the architecture decisions I made on top of it.Part 2 (this post): agent identity in action. A worked example that runs end to end on a cluster, with two users, two agents, a tool, a model and a third-party service, and real allow and deny outputs.

item.title: Physicists Trap a Single Antimatter Particle For a Month
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
Physicists at Northwestern University have successfully trapped a single positron for an entire month, allowing researchers to study its quantum properties with unprecedented precision. "Further investigations using the trap might reveal the secret of why the world around us is made of matter and not antimatter, when things could have presumably gone either way," reports Scientific American. From the report: Every normal particle of matter has an antimatter counterpart with equal mass but opposite charge. To build their trap, physicists started with atoms of sodium 22, a radioactive isotope with a half-life of about two and a half years. When one of these atoms decays, it emits a positron -- the antimatter counterpart of the electron. "The big challenge is to persuade these positrons to slow down and then capture them," says Gerald Gabrielse, a physicist at Northwestern University, who oversaw the project. The team reported its achievement on Wednesday in Physical Review Letters (PDF).
The first step is to send the positrons through the crystal lattice of a sliver of cold tungsten. As the particles go pinballing through the material, they slow down and lose energy. "Every time they bang into something, there's a chance of annihilation, but it doesn't always happen," Gabrielse says. "If they make it to the end, they get popped out." Next, the physicists steer the positrons along a channel using electromagnetic fields. Eventually the particles end up in a vacuum, just three tenths of a degree Celsius above absolute zero, trapped by an electric field on top and bottom and a magnetic field on the sides. "If you want to hold on to antimatter, you have to hold it in a container without walls," Gabrielse says. This method allowed the researchers to isolate and study a solitary, lone positron for a monthâ"and could let them do so indefinitely.
The researchers intend to use their trap to make precise measurements of the positron's magnetic moment -- basically the strength and orientation of its magnetic field. To do this, they must determine two things: the energy needed to flip the direction of the positron's spin and the energy needed to make it jump from its ground state to its first excited state. Using a similar trap setup, Gabrielse and his team have already measured the magnetic moment of an electron to a precision of one part in 10 trillion. Taking the equivalent measurement for a positron will allow them to make a crucial comparison. "We're looking to see if they have an exactly opposite magnetic moment," Gabrielse says. That's the prediction of the Standard Model of particle physics. If the two have different values, however, this could help explain why our universe is made of matter instead of antimatter.

item.title: 1Claw Builds the Security Layer for the Day AI Agents Run Wallets and Sign Trades Autonomously
item.author: Ishan Pandey
item.content:encoded: An AI agent that deploys code, pays an invoice or signs a blockchain transaction usually does it with whatever a human would have used, a private key, an API secret or a cloud credential, sitting in its environment where anything that talks to the model can reach it. One prompt injection or one leaked log hands an attacker everything the agent was allowed to do, at a time when CrowdStrike has watched intruders move from first access to the rest of a network in 27 seconds.1Claw sells a different arrangement in which the agent gets permission to act without receiving the master key, through HSM-backed vaults, per-agent spending limits and an enclave proxy that screens model traffic for prompt injection. It signs transactions across more than 109 EVM chains as well as Bitcoin, Solana, XRP, Cardano and Tron, offers a free tier for developers and has just announced integrations with Bankr, Google Cloud, Circle, Tenderly, Coder and the XRP Ledger.Today we sit down with Kevin Jones, its Founder and CEO and a veteran of Web3 infrastructure, on what security looks like for software that no longer waits for a human to press the button. Hi Kevin, welcome to our "Behind the Startup" series. You went from photography to Web2 infrastructure, then to blockchain and now 1Claw. Tell us about your journey and what problems did you see in the market that made you build 1Claw? Throughout my 25-year career in technology, one thing has always motivated me: figuring out how things work, finding ways to make them better, and solving problems that matter. I've also learned that as technology becomes more powerful, keeping it secure becomes increasingly important.I've worked across companies including Best Buy, Yellow Pages, and NGINX, progressing from Site Reliability Engineer to Solutions Architect. Along the way, I've seen firsthand how complex and fragile technology systems can be, and how a single vulnerability can create serious consequences. Those experiences taught me that security shouldn't be an afterthought. It needs to be part of how we build technology from the beginning.My curiosity about cryptography eventually led me into Web3. I was fascinated by how cryptography, data ownership, and decentralized governance could change the way we establish trust online. I began to see that some of these ideas could also help solve security challenges in traditional Web2 systems. For me, it was never just about blockchain; it was about finding better ways to protect the systems and people who depend on technology.Then AI agents started taking off, and I saw another important challenge emerging. We're moving beyond AI that simply answers questions to AI that can access tools, interact with systems, and take action on our behalf. But these agents often need access to sensitive credentials and APIs to do their jobs. If that access isn't properly controlled, the consequences can be serious. I saw an opportunity to apply what I'd learned over the years to help address a problem that will only become more important as AI evolves.That's what inspired me to create 1Claw. I want to help make AI agents safer to use by giving organizations better control over what they can access and do, while still allowing them to be useful and autonomous. I believe we shouldn't have to choose between innovation and security. We should be able to embrace what AI makes possible while building the safeguards that let people trust it.Ultimately, what drives me is the opportunity to solve meaningful problems and help make technology work better for everyone. AI has enormous potential, and I want to help ensure that potential can be realized safely.Outside of technology, photography has always been my creative outlet. It reminds me to slow down, look at things differently, and appreciate the beauty in the world around us. I think that same curiosity carries over into my work: whether I'm behind a camera or solving a complex technical problem, I'm always looking for a new perspective.How 1Claw Signs a Transaction Without Handing Over the Key You mention that the agent gets permission to act but not the master key. Could you walk us through what actually happens, step by step, when an agent asks 1Claw to sign a transaction or call a paid API on its behalf? The idea is simple: an AI agent should be able to get work done without ever having unrestricted access to the credentials that make it possible.Let's say an agent needs to call a paid API or sign a transaction. Instead of handing the agent a permanent API key or private key, 1Claw acts as a controlled security layer between the agent and the resource it needs.Here's how it works, step by step.First, the agent requests an action. It might need to call an API, access a service, or initiate a blockchain transaction.Second, 1Claw verifies the agent's identity and checks its permissions. Is this agent authorized to perform this action? Does it have access to this particular service? Are there restrictions on what it can do?Third, 1Claw applies the relevant security policies. Depending on the configuration, that could mean limiting which credentials the agent can use, which actions it can perform, or what resources it can access.Fourth, if the request is authorized, 1Claw facilitates access to the required credential or signing capability without giving the agent unrestricted control of the underlying secret. For a paid API, that could mean enabling an authorized API call without exposing the long-lived credential. For a blockchain transaction, it could mean routing a signing request through a protected signing mechanism, subject to the applicable permissions.Finally, the action proceeds within those boundaries, and the organization can maintain visibility into how access is being used.The important distinction is that the agent gets permission to perform a specific action, not a master key that gives it unlimited power.That's the philosophy behind 1Claw: give agents the access they need to be useful, while keeping control of sensitive credentials and permissions outside the agent itself.What Fails First When Attackers Move at Machine Speed CrowdStrike says AI-enabled adversaries increased their operations by 89% last year and the fastest breakout it recorded took 27 seconds. When attackers move at machine speed, which part of a company's security stack fails first? And how do companies build new cybersecurity rails?The first thing that breaks is often the assumption that humans can keep up. Traditional security relies heavily on people detecting unusual activity, investigating alerts, and responding to threats. But when attackers operate at machine speed, manual processes and fragmented security systems can struggle to keep pace.AI agents introduce another challenge: they don't just process information; they can take action across multiple systems using credentials and permissions. If those credentials are compromised or an agent is manipulated, the potential impact can spread quickly.Companies need a new security layer built for autonomous systems. That means giving every agent a verifiable identity, enforcing least-privilege access, protecting credentials, monitoring actions, and being able to revoke access quickly when something goes wrong.At 1Claw, we're focused on this access-control problem: helping organizations manage what AI agents can access and do without exposing sensitive credentials or giving them unnecessary permissions.When threats move at machine speed, security can't depend on humans reacting fast enough. It has to be built into the infrastructure from the start.What Agents Can Safely Do Through Bankr, Circle, Tenderly and Coder Bankr and Circle put agents next to real money, Tenderly simulates transactions before they are signed and Coder hands coding agents a cloud workspace. What can an agent do safely through these integrations today that it could not do a year ago? The big shift is that AI agents are moving from making recommendations to taking real actions. With platforms like Bankr and Circle, agents can interact with wallets and move money. Tenderly lets developers simulate transactions before signing them, while Coder gives coding agents controlled environments to write and execute code.That means agents can now participate in real financial and development workflows with safeguards that weren't as accessible a year ago.But enabling an agent to act is only half the problem. How do you make sure it can do only what it's supposed to do? Simulating a transaction or isolating a workspace helps, but neither automatically prevents an agent from accessing the wrong credentials or exercising excessive permissions.That's where 1Claw comes in. We're focused on helping organizations control which credentials, APIs, and tools their agents can access, limit their permissions, and revoke access when needed.The future isn't about giving agents unlimited autonomy. It's about giving them the authority to get work done without giving them the keys to everything.Protecting the Moment of Approval When an Agent Decides Alone The FBI attributed the $1.5 billion Bybit theft to North Korea after attackers fooled the people approving a transaction rather than breaking the keys. If the weakest point is the moment of approval, how do you protect a decision that an agent makes on its own?The $1.5 billion Bybit theft exposed a critical weakness in security: attackers can exploit the process used to approve a transaction, even when the underlying systems have strong protections. The FBI attributed the attack to North Korea, highlighting how manipulating a trusted workflow can have devastating consequences.With AI agents, the challenge is even greater: how do you secure a decision when the agent makes it autonomously? You can't rely on the agent to recognize every malicious instruction or judge whether its own actions are safe.The answer is to separate the agent's ability to request an action from the authority to execute it. Every request should be checked against independent security policies: What is the agent trying to do? Does it have permission? Is the action within its limits? If not, it should be blocked. High-risk actions can also require human approval.That's what we're focused on at 1Claw: giving agents the access they need to get work done without giving them unrestricted authority over credentials, APIs, and critical systems.The principle is simple: let agents make decisions, but make sure security controls, not the agents themselves, determine what they're allowed to do.Revoking a Misbehaving Agent at 3 AM and Who Is Accountable Imagine an agent starts misbehaving at three in the morning while nobody on the team is watching. How fast can a company revoke it through 1Claw and who is accountable for what it has already done? If an AI agent starts misbehaving at three in the morning, the company shouldn't have to wait for someone to wake up to contain it. Access needs to be revocable as soon as a problem is detected, cutting off the agent's ability to use protected credentials and resources. The exact response time depends on how the system is configured and where the agent is operating.With 1Claw, our focus is giving organizations control over what agents can access and do, including the ability to revoke their permissions when necessary. Just as importantly, revocation doesn't erase what an agent has already done. That's why visibility and auditability matter: organizations need to understand which actions were taken, what resources were accessed, and which permissions allowed them.Revoking access is a technical control; accountability is an organizational responsibility. The company deploying the agent remains responsible for its permissions, policies, and oversight. 1Claw's role is to help make access controllable and actions traceable, so organizations can contain incidents and understand what happened.Autonomous agents may operate around the clock, but security and accountability can't depend on someone being awake to supervise every action.The Key Lesson Crypto Learned That AI Is About to Repeat Last question. Which lesson about keys did crypto learn the hard way that the rest of the AI industry is about to learn all over again? The biggest lesson crypto learned the hard way is that whoever controls the keys controls everything, and if those keys are compromised, the damage can be irreversible. In Web3, we saw billions of dollars lost through stolen private keys, exposed credentials, compromised wallets, and poorly managed access. The technology could be incredibly sophisticated, but security often came down to a simple question: who holds the keys, and what can they do with them?Now we're seeing a similar challenge emerge with AI agents. We're giving agents access to APIs, credentials, databases, and business systems so they can act autonomously. But if an agent has unrestricted access, gets manipulated, or exposes its credentials, the consequences can extend far beyond a single task.The lesson crypto learned is that securing the technology isn't enough. You have to secure access to the technology.That's one of the ideas behind 1Claw. AI agents need credentials to be useful, but they shouldn't have unlimited access to everything those credentials unlock. We need to control what agents can access, limit their permissions, protect their secrets, and be able to revoke access when something goes wrong.Crypto learned that key management isn't a secondary security feature; it's fundamental infrastructure. The AI industry has an opportunity to learn that lesson before compromised agents turn it into another expensive one.Don’t forget to like and share the story!

item.title: We Were Never Asked to Write Code. We Were Asked to Solve Problems.
item.author: Sanya Kapoor
item.content:encoded: In 2000 I was at Deutsche Bank, building a new trading platform, watching friends leave one by one for startups that were going to make them rich. They had stock options. They had retirement mapped out at forty. I stayed at the bank and felt the envy of a man doing sensible work while everyone around him seemed to be getting away with something.Then the crash came, and the turned out to be nothing. Pets.com went from a Super Bowl advert in January to liquidation in November. The Nasdaq lost most of its value. Thousands of companies died; the web did not. It carried on and built Google. I was still at the bank, and I have rarely been so grateful for a boring decision.I mention this because I have seen the current mood before, and I recognise the smell.The oldest trick in the industry“Artificial intelligence” is a marketing term. It was coined in the 1950s by scientists who wanted money from the American military, and it worked—which is the only reason we still say it. Every decade or so the phrase gets dusted off, oversold, and followed by an “AI winter” when the funding leaves. We are on the fourth or fifth turn of that wheel, depending on how you count.The technology underneath is real. Deep learning did something startling at the ImageNet competition in 2012, and within three years your phone could identify what was in a photograph. But real capability and honest expectation are different things, and the gap between them is where the money is made.The pattern never changes. A genuine breakthrough arrives, and capital floods in behind it. The promises inflate to justify the valuations until someone is on a stage telling you half your engineers will be redundant by Tuesday. Then reality turns up, the money leaves, and the people still standing go back to work.The radiologists who never disappearedIn 2016, Geoffrey Hinton—one of the people who built this technology—told a room that we should stop training radiologists because deep learning would beat them inside five years. He was mistaken. Cheaper, faster imaging meant doctors ordered far more of it, and demand for radiologists climbed. When a task gets cheap and quick, we tend to want more of it, not less.I think about that every time someone tells me my profession is finished. The tools have landed for software this time. In 2025 the agentic coding assistants stopped being a party trick and started closing real work—taking an issue, writing the code, and opening a pull request you can then argue with. My engineers use them. They ship faster for it.What has not happened is anyone being replaced. The tool still needs an adult in the room. Someone who can tell a plausible answer from the right one and who is on call when it falls over at 9:31 on a Monday. That adult is an engineer. There is simply more demand now for the problems we can afford to solve.The point we keep forgettingDeepMind did not write conventional software to crack protein folding, a problem that had defeated biologists for fifty years. It built a model that solved it, then published the structures of 200 million proteins for free. New antibiotics and malaria vaccine research have already come out of that one act. Nobody asked how many lines of code it took.That is the lesson under the noise. We were never hired to write code—the code was always the means. The job was to solve someone’s problem, and it still is.I have spent twenty-odd years mistaking the one for the other, and the machines have done me the favour of pointing it out.Richard Forss is CTO of , a global multi-asset prime broker, where he leads a 230-person technology division—none of whom he has yet worked out how to replace with a machine, himself included.

item.title: StealC Is Back, and This Time It's a RAT
item.author: Varonis
item.content:encoded:
Four months after Operation Endgame took it down, StealC's seller returns with Stadia, a remote access trojan that shares StealC's code byte for byte.In June, Europol tore down StealC, a prominent infostealer, as part of Operation Endgame. International authorities seized 326 servers and 142 domains, recovered more than 25 million stolen credentials from 385,000 infected machines, and pulled the plug on one of the most widely sold infostealers of the last three years.Four months later, on October 16, the seller behind StealC resurfaced with Stadia. This time it's not a stealer: it's a full remote access trojan. The RAT’s features include hidden desktop control, a live command shell, a file explorer, a process manager and an in-memory loader, with StealC's stealer welded on as one module among six. The actor behind Stadia is working hard to win back original StealC customers: every former StealC customer is offered a free month on the top ($900) tier.Varonis Threat Labs obtained the build shortly after it was listed, reversed it, and watched its panel operate against a machine of our own. The code inside it is StealC's.Operation Endgame forced the seller to rebuild its infrastructure and start again with a new name, new servers and a new panel. This blog walks through that rebuild from the inside: the listing, the panel running against a host of our own, the agent's code, and the detections that catch it.The listing is titled [RAT] Stadia - Stealer, Log Restore, Loader, HVNC, File Explorer (HVNC is Hidden Virtual Network Computing, remote desktop control the victim cannot see), and the seller pitches it as an agent that embeds itself in the system and hands the operator a full toolkit from a web panel.The module list reads like a remote administration suite rather than a stealer:with two modes, a shared desktop and a hidden desktop, described as self-written and not based on public sourcesa custom solution on the base of their stealc v3.5cmd.exe access with input/output streaminga resident loader that runs files from disk or from memoryremote disk access to browse, download, upload and run filesa process tree with the ability to kill a competitor's processThe stealer collects from 50+ browsers, 120+ crypto plugins, 50+ desktop wallets, messengers (Telegram, Discord, Tox, Pidgin), Steam, Battle.net, Uplay and Roblox sessions, Outlook and Thunderbird, and ProtonVPN and OpenVPN clients. A wallet brute covers MetaMask, TronLink, Trust, Phantom, Rabby, OKX and others.The seller's own screenshots in the listing show the product in use. Their demo dashboard reports 596 hosts and 496 logs, with a world map of infections concentrated in South and Southeast Asia, Africa and Latin America.The logs view carries the StealC heritage on its face: per-victim rows with wallet and extension tags, country, OS and a download button for the archive.The HVNC screenshot is a live remote-desktop session on an infected Windows 11 machine, with a Spanish-language runtime error dialog sitting on the victim's desktop. The seller's toolbar offers Ctrl+Alt+Del, Win+R, quality settings and a full-screen mode.Pricing and the StealC pipelineStadia sells on a monthly subscription, tiered by how many modules and builds you get.up to 5 builds, up to 5 accountsHVNC, Remote CMD, Stealer, Loader, File Explorer, Process Managerno build or account limitA second post, added a minute after the listing, offers every StealC customer a free month on the Pro tier. Customers whose panels and servers went down in June get the fuller toolkit at no cost, and the seller keeps the install base.Buyers run everything from a web panel. It brands itself Stadia and runs at version 1.1.2, matching the agent version baked into the sample. Its news tab is a short changelog. Update 1.0.0 (10 Sep 2026) is the first beta release. Update 1.1.0 (29 Sep 2026) records the Stealer module code updated to stealc 3.5.0.The builder tab compiles agents from the current published version. Operators create a build, download the .exe, and deploy it. Our sample is one such build.The sidebar organizes stolen data by type: passwords, credit cards, messengers, software, session tokens for Chrome, Discord, Steam, Roblox, and Azure, and a crypto section for seed phrases.To see the agent and panel as a pair, we stood up one disposable Windows host of our own and let it register. It appeared in the panel's host inventory within a minute, tagged online.The host overview is a full remote-administration console: live status and heartbeat, the install path under C:\ProgramData\, counters for passwords, cookies, wallets, cards and files, related tasks and logs, and a Start Module menu offering Remote CMD, File Explorer, Process Manager, Remote Desktop, Loader and Stealer.Starting a module opens a confirmation dialog first. Remote Desktop offers a current-desktop or isolated virtual-desktop session.The Loader accepts EXE, PowerShell, CMD and MSI, with disk or in-memory execution for each. A job targets selected hosts or every matching host.The log it produced for our host carried a system profile, a desktop screenshot and build metadata, with zero credentials because the host was clean. The archive layout (build.txt, copyright.txt, screenshot.jpg, system_info.txt) is the StealC log format.The sample we pulled from that builder is a 560,128-byte 32-bit Windows executable, native Microsoft Visual C++ (MSVC), no .NET, no Authenticode signature. It decrypts its own build marker to STADIA_BETA and reports agent version 1.1.2, so the file and the panel agree on what it is.ea928494fd30d88b98141d39a502a4324889fb732e74b44bfee12c72137dd73e028afae8b5e9953e1cd84a003c42fd85There is no packer. The outer file imports only KERNEL32.dll and resolves nearly every operational application programming interface (API) at runtime, so the static picture stays thin until you decrypt the strings.Almost every meaningful literal (module names, command-and-control (C2) fields, the config) is stored under one scheme: stored literal = Base64(RC4(plaintext, "eepkTOgSwdNCgrhITR")) The outer Rivest Cipher 4 (RC4) key sits at file offset 0x6B1A0. Recovering the table is a few lines of Python once you have the key: Base64-decode each candidate, RC4 it with the key, keep anything that comes out printable. def rc4(data, key): s = list(range(256)) j = 0 for i in range(256): j = (j + s[i] + key[i % len(key)]) & 0xFF s[i], s[j] = s[j], s[i] i = j = 0 out = bytearray() for b in data: i = (i + 1) & 0xFF j = (j + s[i]) & 0xFF s[i], s[j] = s[j], s[i] out.append(b ^ s[(s[i] + s[j]) & 0xFF]) return bytes(out)
# stored = Base64(RC4(plaintext, key)); recover with: # plaintext = rc4(base64.b64decode(stored), b"eepkTOgSwdNCgrhITR") That pass returns 542 strings: the command vocabulary, the browser targets, the scheduled-task template and the C2 config. The message key and access token were recovered but are omitted from this write-up.Startup and the locale gateEntry is ordinary MSVC startup into a WinMain-like routine. Early on, the agent calls GetUserDefaultLangID and exits for Russian, Ukrainian, Belarusian, Kazakh, and Uzbek system languages (0x0419, 0x0422, 0x0423, 0x043F, 0x0443), the standard do-not-run-at-home guard. It then checks whether its own path sits under C:\ProgramData\. If not, it installs; if so, it takes a single-instance mutex Local\<username>.<computername> and enters the agent loop.That branch is why our one dynamic run went nowhere. Launched under a Low-integrity token from outside ProgramData, the sample took the installer path, could not create its directory, and exited silently. That result reflects our lab setup and says nothing about whether the sample works.How it talks to the serverOnce installed, the agent calls home. The config carries three hard-coded C2 bases, all plain HTTP on the root path:http://93.152.213.215/http://91.92.43.45/The agent tries its three C2 addresses in a fixed order, starting with the first every time it reconnects. To test each one, it sends a set_online message with a host_token of 72 zeroes and waits up to eight seconds for any reply that contains an opcode. If none of the three answers, it waits 300 seconds and starts again.The traffic is not what its header claims. Each message starts as JSON, is encrypted with RC4 using the embedded message key, and is then Base64-encoded before being sent as the HTTP body. The request still declares Content-Type: application/json, so anything inspecting the header expects JSON and receives ciphertext.Persistence, modules and injectionInstallation drops the agent under a randomized 12-character directory below C:\ProgramData\ and picks a filename from a fixed list of nine that impersonate legitimate updaters:OneDriveStandaloneUpdater.exeThe scheduled task name is selected separately from the same nine names, so the task label and the executable need not match. The task is hidden, runs at logon and every 15 minutes for 3,650 days. When the agent is elevated, it also issues a hidden PowerShell Add-MpPreference -ExclusionPath for its install directory. Our test host confirms the scheme: it installed to C:\ProgramData\wzoHcrvZt9RX\MicrosoftEdgeUpdate.exe, a 12-character directory and one of the nine names.The decrypted module vocabulary matches the panel one-to-one:hidden shell, bidirectional stdin/stdoutlist, read, write, pull, push, run; chunked transferprocess tree, CPU/RAM, kill, protected-process listcurrent or virtual desktop, JPEG frames, full input injectionEXE, PowerShell, BAT/CMD, MSI; disk or memory; hidden or runasbrowser profiles, cookies, logins, walletsThe seller says the stealer is built on StealC 3.5. The binary proves the two share code at the byte level.Inside stadia_x32.exe, at file offset 0x77D48, sits a complete 26,112-byte (0x6600) 64-bit Chromium App-Bound Encryption helper, a mapped portable executable (PE) plus a short reflective loader. That exact blob appears once in each of the StealC v3.5 x86 and x64 builds we hold, byte for byte:0e5337a4cc8ebc772bc50f6e79befd1e8efad3410022e050d08d5269733c4ea4StealC v3.5 build_x32.exe0e5337a4cc8ebc772bc50f6e79befd1e8efad3410022e050d08d5269733c4ea4StealC v3.5 build_x64.exe0e5337a4cc8ebc772bc50f6e79befd1e8efad3410022e050d08d5269733c4ea4Stadia's C2 addresses, RC4 key and access token change with every build. What stays the same is how the agent talks to its server and what it does on the host, and that is where detection should focus.On the network, the agent sends HTTP POST requests to the root path of a bare IP address. The Content-Type header claims the body is JSON, but the body is Base64-encoded ciphertext. That mismatch is a useful signal on its own. The build we analyzed calls 93.152.213.215, 91.92.43.45 and 193.148.56.97 on port 80, and blocking those addresses covers that build only.On the host, the clearest signal is the browser credential theft. An unsigned process running from C:\ProgramData\ starts a genuine Chrome, Edge or Brave process in a suspended state and writes a 26 KB block of code into it. Moments later, a .txt file with a GUID-style name appears in C:\ProgramData\, holds a 64-character hex string, and is deleted. That file carries the key the browser uses to protect saved cookies and passwords.Persistence leaves its own trail. Within a few minutes of infection, look for a new executable in a random folder under C:\ProgramData\, a hidden scheduled task that repeats every 15 minutes, and a Windows Defender exclusion added for that folder through PowerShell's Add-MpPreference command. This Sigma rule flags the scheduled task: title: Hidden Fifteen Minute Scheduled Task Executes From ProgramData status: experimental logsource: product: windows service: security detection: selection_event: EventID: [4698, 4702] selection_xml: TaskContent|contains|all: - '<Interval>PT15M</Interval>' - '<Duration>P3650D</Duration>' - '<Hidden>true</Hidden>' - 'C:\ProgramData\' condition: selection_event and selection_xml level: high The implant registers the task through the Component Object Model (COM) API, so a rule scoped to schtasks.exe would miss it. Start the behavioral rules in alert mode and tune them against your own telemetry before you block on them.Stadia is the StealC operation rebuilding after Operation Endgame. The servers, domains and stolen data are gone, and the response has been to come back under a new name with a broader product and a free month to pull former customers across. The stealer is still there, now as one module in a remote access trojan that adds hidden VNC, a command shell, a file explorer, a process manager and in-memory loading.StealC took credentials and left. Stadia stays, watches the screen, runs commands, moves files and loads whatever comes next, and it is priced for teams rather than individuals. A disrupted stealer has come back as a platform, and the four-month turnaround shows how quickly a seller with an existing customer base can rebuild once the code survives the takedown.ea928494fd30d88b98141d39a502a4324889fb732e74b44bfee12c72137dd73estadia_x32.exe, agent 1.1.21ba76d2029744cc6e2f7209c96a696b32962b1f17739a8d0d101ca82b93bbd0acdb6d9af028afae8b5e9953e1cd84a003c42fd850e5337a4cc8ebc772bc50f6e79befd1e8efad3410022e050d08d5269733c4ea40x6600-byte App-Bound helper blob, shared with StealC 3.5outer RC4 string key, per builddesktop-session object nameLocal\<username>.<computername>C:\ProgramData\<12 alphanumeric>\<name>.exeRuntimeBroker.exe, SecurityHealthHost.exe, SearchHost.exe, TextInputHost.exe, MicrosoftEdgeUpdate.exe, GoogleUpdate.exe, OneDriveStandaloneUpdater.exe, nvcontainer.exe, AdobeARM.exenine candidate install and task nameshidden, PT15M interval, P3650D duration, InteractiveTokenCOM-registered, not schtaskspowershell.exe ... Add-MpPreference -ExclusionPath C:\ProgramData\...C:\ProgramData\<GUID>.txt containing 64 lowercase hextransient App-Bound key dropseller alias, signed stealc / stadia

item.title: MEXC Account Types Explained: A Guide to Spot, Futures, RealStocks, Fiat, and Copy Trade Accounts
item.author: MEXC Learn
item.content:encoded: ● MEXC organizes accounts by function, including Spot, Futures, Fiat, Copy Trade, Earn, RealStocks, Prediction Markets, and Trading Bot accounts.● Spot, Futures, Fiat, and Copy Trade are the four core account types beginners are most likely to use.● Funds can be transferred between different accounts depending on how you use them, with the Fiat account used for fiat-to-crypto and crypto-to-fiat conversions.● Transfers between MEXC accounts are free, allowing you to move funds whenever needed.● Both the MEXC website and App support quick fund transfers and let you view your transfer history at any time.1. What Account Types Does MEXC Offer?MEXC organizes its accounts by function. The main typesinclude Spot, Futures, Fiat, and Copy Trade accounts, as well as Earn, RealStocks, Prediction Markets, and Trading Bot accounts. Of these, Spot, Futures, Fiat, and Copy Trade are the four core account types beginners are most likely to use.2. What Is Each Account Used For?** This account is used for Spot trading. When you buy or sell crypto on MEXC’s Spot market, the assets used for trading are held in your Spot account. This account is used for Futures trading, including contracts with different margin types. Funds used for Futures trading are held in this account. This account is used to move funds into and out of MEXC. Conversions from fiat currency to crypto, or from crypto back to fiat currency, are handled through this account. This account holds funds used for copy trading. When you follow a lead trader, the system automatically places orders for you based on that trader’s strategy, and the trader can receive a share of your profits. Although copy trading is a form of Futures trading, its assets are held separately in the Copy Trade account.MEXC also offers for assets allocated to Earn products, for RealStocks trading, Prediction Markets accounts for prediction market trading, and for automated strategy trading, supporting a range of asset management needs.3. How Are the Different Accounts Connected?To understand how the accounts are connected, follow how funds move between them:When you start trading, you first convert fiat currency into crypto. The converted assets are held in your Fiat account.For Spot trading, transfer funds from your Fiat account to your Spot account. For Futures trading, transfer them to your Futures account. The same principle applies to Earn, RealStocks, Prediction Markets, and Trading Bot activities, withfunds transferred directly between your Spot account and the relevant account as needed.To trade RealStocks or participate in market predictions, transfer funds to your RealStocks or Prediction Markets account. Both support direct transfers to and from your Spot account.For copy trading, first transfer assets from your Futures or Fiat account to your Spot account. Once you confirm your copy trading settings, the system automatically transfers the specified amount from your Spot account to your Copy Trade account.When you subscribe to an Earn product, the system transfers the specified amount to your Earn account. After redemption, the funds are returned to the corresponding account.To use a trading bot for automated strategy trading, create and start a strategy, such as grid trading. The system then transfers the specified amount to your Trading Bot account.When you stop trading and are ready to cash out, transfer the crypto in your accounts back to your Fiat account, then convert it into fiat currency to complete the withdrawal.4. Are There Fees for Transfers Between Accounts?No. Transfers between MEXC accounts are free. You can move funds as needed for trading without paying any additional transfer fees.5. How to Transfer Funds Between AccountsApp: From the MEXC App home screen, tap Wallets → Overview / Spot / RealStocks / Futures / Fiat / Prediction Markets → Transferto move funds between accounts.Transfers to a Copy Trade account must be made through the copy trading page. Funds remain in your Spot account until you submit your copy trading settings. The system then transfers the specified amount to your Copy Trade account.The same applies to Earn and Trading Bot accounts. The system only transfers the specified amount to the relevant account once you subscribe to an Earn product or participate in grid trading.6. How to View and Manage Each Account’s Funding HistoryWeb: Go to the , then select the tab to view your transfer history.App: From the MEXC App home screen, tap Wallets → Overview → Transfer → to view your transfer history.To view details for an individual account, select it on the page. The account page shows information such as total assets, crypto holdings, and profit and loss analysis, and provides options to deposit, withdraw, and transfer funds.Understanding MEXC’s account types and how to transfer assets between them can help you move funds quickly and trade more efficiently.

item.title: Your Agent Workflow Is Mostly Code and People
item.author: Sakti Bagchi
item.content:encoded: On 3rd October, my astro-coach agent tried to fix a production Supabase environment problem. It kept retrying until a model usage limit stopped it. The tempting summary is “the agent tried to fix production.”That summary hides most of the engineering.Step in the 3 October astro-coach runDiagnose the production Supabase environment problemA diagnosis and a specific fix to attemptBake the environment settings into the application buildA build artifact whose configuration needed verificationAn unresolved execution state the agent could not readDecide to retry the environment fixModel, acting through the agentAnother invocation, without resolving the previous attempt’s stateKeep retrying until a model usage limit stopped the runModel choosing retries; code executing themAn interrupted workflow, without a confirmed outcomeConfirm the login message and whether users could actually log inThe evidence needed to accept the fix or keep the incident openThis was a workflow on my astro-coach repository, now home to Jyotish Coach. It is tempting to summarize it as “the agent tried to fix production.”That description hides most of the engineering.A person supplied the diagnosis. Code performed the environment bake. The model chose to repeat the operation. A person still needed to confirm the result.The agent’s consequential contribution was the decision at the boundary: run that step again.Most of what we call an agent workflow is a chain of ordinary software operations and human decisions, with a model choosing some of the transitions. If you ship agents, those transitions deserve as much attention as the model.Where the loop actually livedThe environment bake was a code operation. Given the intended configuration and a source revision, the build system should produce an artifact and report what happened.The repository makes this distinction concrete. Its Dockerfile passes and NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY into the environment before running the application build.Its operations notes also warn that, in this deployment setup, changing those variables and triggering a redeploy can reuse the previous image. The documented check is to look for an actual application build.That means “the variable changed,” “the deployment completed,” and “the browser received the intended configuration” are separate claims.After the hang in the 3rd October run, the agent could not read the execution state. It kept attempting the production environment fix until a model usage limit stopped it.The loop lived around the code operation: invoke, lose visibility, invoke again.A hang does not tell you whether an operation failed before making a change, completed without returning a response, or remained in progress. Repeating the command does not resolve that uncertainty. It can add another attempt whose relationship to the first is also unclear.The usage limit ended the activity. It did not establish that production was correct.“Agent fixed it” is too coarse to review. Each handoff needs an input, a record of the state left behind, and a next owner.For this workflow, I would name them explicitly:Input crossing the boundaryThe person’s diagnosis, target environment, and intended configuration changeA proposed operation with a defined scopeModel prepares the action; person reviews its scopeApproved inputs and source revisionAn identified build attempt and its logsBuild → deployment approvalArtifact identity and configuration checksA report of success, failure, or unresolved executionApproval → production changeSign-off tied to that artifact and targetA deployment attempt with a recorded identityInterrupted execution → reconciliationAttempt identity and last known statusA read-only determination of what happened, or an explicit unknownCode checks state; person owns unresolved casesDeployment → login acceptanceThe deployed revision and technical checksEvidence from the actual sign-in flowThis is a proposed ownership structure, not a claim that the October run followed it. The run exposed why it was needed.The weakest handoff was interrupted execution to the next decision. The agent had an incomplete observation, but retained the ability to initiate another production attempt.That is where uncertainty became action.A durable attempt record would make a different next step possible: inspect the existing operation. Without that record, the model is being asked to reason about state it cannot observe.Make the environment bake a script that runs once and reportsThe structural fix is to take the repeated environment bake out of the model’s decision loop.I would make it a script that runs once for a specified operation, then reports. Its inputs would identify the source revision, target environment, and intended configuration. Its output would identify the build attempt, resulting artifact, verification results, and final status. It should report configuration checks without exposing secret values.“Runs once” needs enforcement in code. An operation identifier should prevent a second invocation from silently starting duplicate work. If the caller loses its connection, the next action should retrieve that operation’s status.The script also needs to preserve uncertainty honestly. A timeout is an unresolved result until the underlying build or deployment state has been checked.The model can help prepare inputs and interpret the report. The execution contract belongs in code.Before a production change, a person signs off on the concrete artifact, target, and expected effect. That approval must refer to what will actually be deployed. If the artifact changes, the earlier approval no longer describes the action.This gives the workflow a stopping condition tied to the task: a reported result, a verified state, or an unresolved case handed to a person. A model usage limit should never have to serve as the incident’s stopping rule.The step I would not delegateThe final handoff is deployment evidence to user acceptance.A build can succeed with the wrong configuration. A deployment can be healthy while authentication fails. A sign-in message can appear successful without giving the user a usable session.The repository’s authentication environment code documents one such failure mode: sign-in can appear to work while subsequent API calls return unauthorized responses. That is why a reassuring message is insufficient evidence.Automated checks should cover login. They should verify session creation and access to protected routes. But for closing this production incident, I would keep a person responsible for the acceptance decision.I would open the deployed site, use the relevant sign-in method, read the message, and confirm that the session lets me reach the protected experience.The model can assemble evidence. Code can test the path. I would not delegate the final confirmation that users can actually log in.

item.title: How I Migrated a Live Database to a Many-to-Many Relationship
item.author: Gabriela Colombo Alves Longo

item.title: A Successful ETL Job Can Hide Thousands of Data Discrepancies
item.author: RISHI SHRIVASTAVA
item.content:encoded:
A Green Status Does Not Guarantee Correct DataAn ETL workflow completes successfully. The scheduler reports no errors. The expected target tables are populated, and the processing logs indicate that all configured transformations finished.Everything looks fine until someone compares the data.A downstream report contains fewer records than expected. Some identifiers are missing, others appear unexpectedly, and the total record count does not explain the discrepancy.This is a familiar challenge in enterprise data engineering. A pipeline can satisfy its technical execution requirements without satisfying the business requirements associated with its output.In my work involving enterprise data processing, reconciliation and data-quality validation, I have found it useful to distinguish three questions:Did the pipeline execute successfully?Did the expected data arrive?Does the resulting data satisfy the relevant business rules?These questions require different forms of validation.Execution logs can establish whether a workflow ran. Record-count comparisons provide an initial indication of completeness. Identifier-level reconciliation and attribute validation help determine whether the actual data is correct.To illustrate the difference, consider a fictional enterprise dataset undergoing reconciliation between two processing cycles.Note: All dataset names, identifiers and numerical values in the following example are fictional. They are used solely to demonstrate the reconciliation approach.The Problem With Relying Only on Record CountsSuppose an enterprise data pipeline processes records from multiple source systems into a consolidated dataset.During a routine comparison, the engineering team observes the following:Previous successful datasetCurrent processing datasetDifference in total counts Table 1: Dataset Record Count Comparison The obvious conclusion is that 12,330 records are missing.However, the difference between two total counts represents only the net change in dataset size.It does not establish which individual records were removed, which were added or whether those changes were expected.To investigate further, the datasets must be compared using a unique business identifier.Assume each record has a stable and that identifiers are unique within each dataset.A bidirectional comparison produces the following results.Present in previous dataset but missing from current datasetPresent in current dataset but missing from previous datasetTotal distinct identifiers across both exception setsNet record-count difference Table 2: Bidirectional Reconciliation Results The numbers reveal something important.Although the net difference is 12,330 records, there are actually 13,360 distinct identifiers present in only one of the two datasets.The arithmetic is straightforward:Both results are valid, but they represent different measurements.The first measures the net change in record count. The second measures the total number of unique identifiers that differ between the datasets.For engineers investigating missing or unexpected records, the second measurement is often more informative.Why Reconciliation Must Work in Both DirectionsA one-directional comparison identifies records missing from the current dataset.However, it does not identify unexpected additions.Consider a situation in which 5,000 identifiers disappear from one processing cycle and 5,000 different identifiers appear in the next.The total record count remains unchanged.A count-based validation reports zero difference, even though 10,000 distinct identifiers have changed.This is why I prefer bidirectional comparisons when validating record completeness.The first comparison identifies identifiers that existed previously but are absent from the current dataset.For databases supporting the operator, the query is:SELECT RECORD_ID FROM PREVIOUS_DATASET
MINUS
SELECT RECORD_ID FROM CURRENT_DATASET; The reverse comparison identifies newly introduced identifiers:SELECT RECORD_ID FROM CURRENT_DATASET
MINUS
SELECT RECORD_ID FROM PREVIOUS_DATASET; These queries return distinct identifiers because set operators eliminate duplicates.For databases such as SQL Server, the equivalent operation uses .One important limitation is that this approach does not detect duplicate occurrences of the same identifier. Duplicate-key validation should therefore be performed separately.Another consideration is null handling. Business identifiers should be checked for missing or invalid values before interpreting the results.The objective is not simply to produce two lists of differences. It is to establish which differences require investigation.A Missing Record Is Not Necessarily a Data DefectOnce missing identifiers are identified, the next challenge is understanding why they are missing.An identifier present in the previous dataset but absent from the current dataset may have several explanations.The source system may have legitimately removed the record. A transformation may have excluded it according to an established business rule. An inner join may have removed the record because a corresponding reference value was unavailable.Alternatively, the record may have been rejected because of an unexpected null value, invalid code or processing defect.These possibilities cannot be distinguished through record-count comparison alone.The investigation must consider the relevant source data, transformation rules and downstream records.One useful technique is to compare missing identifiers against a separate master dataset.For example, an identifier may be absent from the current processing file but still exist in the enterprise master table.That distinction provides useful information about where to investigate next.Classifying Reconciliation ExceptionsAn exception report becomes more actionable when each identifier is assigned a meaningful classification.Consider the following categories.Missing from current dataset, found in masterMissing from current and master datasets Table 3: Exception Classification Matrix The classification process should distinguish observations from conclusions.For example, a record missing from the current dataset but found in the master dataset does not automatically indicate that the current dataset is defective.It indicates that the identifier is present in one downstream reference and absent from the current processing input.Additional business context is needed to determine whether that condition is expected.Similarly, an identifier missing from both the current dataset and the master dataset may require investigation into upstream extraction, business eligibility rules or downstream processing.The classification helps narrow the investigation without prematurely assigning a root cause.SQL-Based Exception ClassificationThe following query demonstrates how identifiers from the previous dataset can be classified against the current dataset and a master dataset.SELECT P.RECORD_ID, CASE WHEN C.RECORD_ID IS NOT NULL THEN 'Present in both datasets'
WHEN M.RECORD_ID IS NOT NULL THEN 'Missing from current; found in master'
ELSE 'Missing from current and master' END AS RECON_STATUS
FROM PREVIOUS_DATASET P
LEFT JOIN CURRENT_DATASET C ON P.RECORD_ID = C.RECORD_ID
LEFT JOIN MASTER_RECORDS M ON P.RECORD_ID = M.RECORD_ID; This example assumes non-null, unique identifiers in all three datasets.The query classifies identifiers originating from the previous dataset. Newly introduced identifiers must be obtained through a separate reverse comparison.In an actual implementation, I would also validate key uniqueness before joining the datasets. Otherwise, duplicate records can multiply join results and create misleading exception counts.The advantage of this classification approach is that it converts a raw list of identifiers into information that can guide investigation.Why Matching Identifiers Is Only the First Validation LayerA record can exist in both datasets and still contain incorrect information.Suppose a record has the same identifier in both processing cycles but its status code, effective date or organizational assignment has changed unexpectedly.An identifier-level comparison would classify the record as matched.Yet the data may still violate an important business rule.This is where attribute-level validation becomes necessary.In a typical enterprise data environment, validation can include checks for missing mandatory fields, invalid reference values, duplicate identifiers, unexpected status changes and inconsistent relationships between records.The rules must reflect the actual meaning of the data.A changed status code may be legitimate when it reflects an approved business event. The same change may be problematic if it results from an incorrect mapping or transformation.For that reason, field-level comparisons should not automatically treat every change as an error.They should identify differences that require evaluation against documented business expectations.Making Reconciliation Repeatable With PythonSQL works well for database-level comparisons.However, enterprise reconciliation often involves CSV files, external extracts, intermediate outputs and multiple processing environments.Python provides another option for performing repeatable identifier comparisons.Consider the following example using pandas.import pandas as pd
previous = pd.read_csv( "previous_dataset.csv", dtype={"RECORD_ID": "string"} )
current = pd.read_csv( "current_dataset.csv", dtype={"RECORD_ID": "string"} )
previous_ids = set( previous["RECORD_ID"] .dropna() .str.strip() )
current_ids = set( current["RECORD_ID"] .dropna() .str.strip() )
missing_ids = previous_ids - current_ids
new_ids = current_ids - previous_ids
common_ids = previous_ids & current_ids
print("Previous unique records:", len(previous_ids)) print("Current unique records:", len(current_ids)) print("Matched identifiers:", len(common_ids)) print("Missing identifiers:", len(missing_ids)) print("New identifiers:", len(new_ids)) print( "Total distinct exceptions:", len(missing_ids | new_ids) ) The script separates missing, new and matched identifiers.Using the pandas string data type helps preserve identifiers that contain leading zeros.However, several practical issues still require attention.First, blank identifiers should be handled explicitly. A blank string and a missing value are not necessarily treated identically.Second, duplicate identifiers should be measured before converting the values into sets. Set operations retain only distinct values.Third, data normalization must follow documented rules. Automatically changing letter case or stripping leading zeros can create incorrect matches when those characteristics are meaningful.Finally, memory usage matters. Loading multiple large datasets into pandas may not be appropriate for high-volume processing. Database-side comparisons or distributed processing may be better choices.A reconciliation implementation should be selected based on data volume, processing environment and operational requirements.What I Would Validate Before Trusting a Reconciliation ScriptOne lesson from working with data validation is that reconciliation logic itself requires testing.A script can run successfully and still produce incorrect results because its comparison assumptions are wrong.I would test the reconciliation logic with several deliberately constructed datasets.For example, one test should contain identical identifiers in both datasets. Another should contain missing identifiers. A third should introduce new identifiers while removing an equal number of old ones.The third scenario is particularly valuable because it verifies that the process does not depend solely on net record-count differences.Other useful test cases include duplicate identifiers, blank keys, null values, inconsistent data types and unexpected whitespace.For attribute-level validation, test records should include both legitimate business changes and intentionally invalid values.The expected result of each test should be defined before execution.This makes it possible to determine whether the reconciliation logic is behaving correctly rather than merely producing plausible-looking output.When reconciliation is performed repeatedly, the long-term objective should be to reduce unnecessary manual investigation.That does not mean automating every decision.Some differences require business interpretation, particularly when source-system changes, eligibility rules or effective dates determine whether a record should be included.Instead, automation should handle the repetitive technical work.A practical validation framework can separate checks into several stages.Stage 1: Dataset-level checksValidate source availability, file structure, expected columns, processing dates and overall record counts.Stage 2: Identifier-level reconciliationIdentify matched, missing, newly introduced and duplicate identifiers.Stage 3: Attribute-level validationCompare important fields and evaluate configured business rules.Stage 4: Exception classificationCategorize discrepancies using available source and master-data information.Stage 5: Investigation and resolutionProduce an exception report that includes sufficient information to investigate each discrepancy and document its disposition.This layered approach provides a more complete view of data quality than any single validation query.It also creates opportunities for consistent reporting across different pipelines.What I Learned About Enterprise Data ReliabilityThe most important lesson is that data correctness cannot be inferred from execution success.A pipeline may complete every technical step while producing an incomplete dataset.Likewise, a dataset may have the expected number of records while containing the wrong identifiers.These conditions require different controls.I have also learned that reconciliation results need context. A list of missing identifiers is useful, but understanding whether those identifiers should be present is what makes the information actionable.Another important consideration is the design of exception reports.When an exception report contains thousands of records, clear classifications and reproducible comparison rules make the investigation more manageable.Finally, I would avoid treating reconciliation as an activity performed only after a production issue occurs.Defining validation rules early in the development lifecycle makes it easier to test assumptions, detect unexpected changes and establish reliable acceptance criteria.What I Would Do Differently When Designing a New PipelineFor a new enterprise data integration project, I would begin by identifying the business keys and documenting their uniqueness requirements.I would then establish which transformations are expected to add, remove, consolidate or modify records.This matters because a one-to-one reconciliation is not appropriate for every pipeline.Next, I would define the validation rules before implementing the final reporting layer.The rules would include volume checks, bidirectional identifier comparisons, duplicate detection and selected attribute-level controls.I would also define what constitutes an acceptable exception.Some discrepancies may be expected because of approved business changes. Others may require investigation before downstream data is released.The objective is to establish validation criteria that reflect the actual business use of the data.Only after those rules are clear would I decide which checks should be automated and which require human review.The Real Measure of a Reliable Data PipelineEnterprise data platforms are often evaluated through execution time, throughput, availability and successful workflow completion.These measurements remain important.However, none of them independently proves that the resulting data is complete or accurate.The fictional reconciliation example demonstrates why this distinction matters.Two datasets can differ by 12,330 records in total count while containing 13,360 distinct identifier-level exceptions.Without bidirectional reconciliation, part of that difference remains hidden.The broader engineering lesson is straightforward: pipeline reliability must include data correctness, not only execution success.A reliable data pipeline should make it possible to establish which records were processed, which records changed, why exceptions occurred and whether the resulting dataset meets its intended business requirements.That is the difference between a workflow that finishes successfully and a data process whose output can be trusted.

item.title: Investigating Feature Leakage and Proxy Variables in a Clash of Clans ML Model
item.author: oteope
item.content:encoded:
Welcome, guys, to another ML article.In this one, I want to talk about a problem I ran into while working on my Clash of Clans ML lab.While preparing the dataset for the ML problem, I found something strange. A group of trophy-related features seemed to contain a huge amount of predictive information about the target. At first, that sounds great, because a highly predictive feature is usually exactly what we want in a machine learning model. But something about these features made me want to look a little closer.When a feature is too predictive, there is always a question worth asking: Maybe the feature contains information the model shouldn't have. Maybe it's indirectly encoding the target. Or maybe it's simply a very strong signal that the model is completely justified in using.This is where comes into the picture. Leakage happens when information that shouldn't be available to the model ends up in the training data, so the model makes predictions using something it wouldn't have in the real prediction scenario. The result can be a model that looks incredibly strong during evaluation but performs much worse once that information is no longer available.There's another possibility, though: the feature could be acting as a . A proxy doesn't directly contain the target, but it's strongly related to it, so it gives the model a very powerful shortcut for making predictions.The tricky part is that a feature can be extremely predictive without necessarily being leakage. So how do we tell the difference? That was the question I wanted to investigate:When does a highly predictive feature stop being useful information and start becoming a proxy for information the model should not have?To answer it, I took a closer look at one particular case from my Clash of Clans dataset: .2. The Clash of Clans DatasetNow let’s talk about the dataset and, more importantly, what exactly we are trying to predict. is the target of this problem. It represents the position a player has within their clan according to the game’s ranking system.If you don’t play Clash of Clans, don’t worry. I’ll explain how the ranking system works, because it matters a lot for understanding this problem.In the past, Clash of Clans had a simpler trophy-based system: players earned trophies, and the more trophies they had, the higher they were placed within the clan. The current system is different, though.I thought this was an interesting ML problem because I wanted to find out which features actually matter for getting a higher position in the clan. In other words, could we use a player’s data to understand what makes them rank higher?All the raw data was extracted from the official Clash of Clans Developer API, which provides a lot of useful player and clan information and makes it a pretty good source for an ML project.Each row in the raw data represents a player, with around 33 features depending on the dataset. From that raw data, I built a specific dataset for this problem using feature engineering, so the final set of features is not just a copy of the original API data.For this particular problem, the dataset contains around .I also created features that describe a player’s position relative to the rest of their clan. For example, instead of only looking at a player’s trophies, we can also look at their difference from the clan average, their ratio to the clan average, or their percentile within the clan. This gives the model some information about how strong a player is compared with the other players around them.I went with regression.
