Predicting a player's exact position out of around 50 possible spots isn't really a problem where I wanted to treat each position as a completely separate class.I tested three different models:For evaluation, I used , , and . For me, a good result was not just about getting strong metrics. What mattered was whether those metrics could help me understand what information the models were actually using to make their predictions.I also built two different versions of the dataset: one including trophy-related features and one without them. The idea was not to assume that trophies were problematic from the beginning. I wanted to compare both versions and see how much the trophy-related information changed the results. That gave me a cleaner way to investigate what was happening than just removing the features because they looked suspicious.Something Interesting Appeared During EDAWhile doing the EDA, I noticed something else. There were a lot of highly correlated features according to both Pearson and Spearman correlation, which at first could make the dataset look like it was full of duplicated information or unnecessary noise.But there was another possible explanation. Clash of Clans is a progression-based game, so as players progress, a lot of their stats naturally increase or change together. A player with more progression will usually have several other features reflecting that same progression.So instead of simply removing all the highly correlated features, I took a closer look at them. That's when one particular group of features started to look especially suspicious: trophy-related features. They were not just correlated with other variables. They seemed to contain a surprisingly large amount of predictive information about the target.And that raised the question:Why are trophies so predictive of clan rank?3. The First Audit: Leakage or Proxy?My first step, before training any models, was to check whether the trophy-related features were actually a problem.Instead of removing them right away, I built a small feature analyzer specifically for this problem. The goal was to screen the candidate variables and see whether any of them showed a suspiciously strong relationship with . I defined three possible outcomes for a feature: — the feature did not meet the thresholds I defined for a potential proxy or overly direct relationship. — the feature had a strong relationship with and needed further investigation. — the relationship was so strong that the feature could be encoding almost the same information as the ranking itself.I also defined some variables that could never be used as predictors, such as itself, , and .The key part was how I measured the relationship. Instead of calculating one global correlation across the whole dataset, I calculated Spearman correlation separately . This made more sense for the problem because is a position within a clan, so I wanted to know whether a feature was strongly related to ranking inside individual clans, rather than just across all players.The analyzer then summarized those correlations using three values:the median Spearman correlation across clansthe 90th percentile of the absolute correlationsthe percentage of clans where the absolute correlation was greater than 0.9The classification was based on those values. For example, a variable was marked as when the absolute value of the median Spearman correlation was at least 0.95 and at least 80% of the clans had an absolute correlation above 0.9.The core of the analysis was basically this:corr_series = _per_clan_spearman(merged, variable).dropna()
median = float(np.nanmedian(corr_series)) p90_abs = float(np.nanpercentile(np.abs(corr_series), 90)) high_pct = float((np.abs(corr_series) > 0.9).mean()) And then I used those values to classify each feature:if abs(median) >= 0.95 and high_pct >= 0.8: classification = "TOO_DIRECT" elif abs(median) >= 0.8 or high_pct >= 0.5: classification = "POTENTIAL PROXY" else: classification = "SAFE" I ran this analysis across several candidate variables, including , , , , , , , , , and .The first result was quite unexpected. According to the thresholds I had defined for the audit, trophies were classified as . The median Spearman correlation between trophies and was . The 90th percentile of the absolute correlation was , and of clans had an absolute correlation greater than 0.9.So, according to my own criteria, trophies did not look like a direct leakage feature or even a strong proxy at the overall level. The rest of the candidate features were also classified as SAFE, with being the only variable for which the analyzer reported insufficient data.At that point, the analyzer was basically telling me:Nothing looks obviously wrong.But that was not really the end of the investigation. The results still left me with a question: if trophies were supposedly safe, why did they appear to be so predictive when I looked at the dataset?By now I knew that trophies were strongly related to in some parts of the dataset, but I still didn't fully understand why. So I went back to the game itself. To understand what the model was seeing, we first need to understand how Clash of Clans actually determines a player's position within a clan.How Clan Rank Actually WorksIn the current Clash of Clans system, players within a clan are ordered mainly according to their league. However, when players are in the same league, their trophies are used to break the tie.This immediately makes trophies much more interesting. If two players are in the same league, the player with more trophies will be placed higher in the clan ranking. So trophies are not just another random player statistic: in certain situations, they are directly involved in determining the player's position.It also explains something from the previous section. Remember that the analyzer gave trophies a median Spearman correlation of only -0.3963, but its 90th percentile of absolute correlation was 1.0. That suddenly makes a lot more sense.Why Top Clans Are DifferentA significant part of my dataset comes from very advanced clans, where many players are already at the highest levels of the game and concentrated in the highest leagues. Once several players are in the same league, the league itself becomes much less useful for distinguishing their positions.In that situation, trophies become extremely important. Instead of having to predict the ranking from many different player characteristics, the model can exploit a much simpler relationship: among players in the same league, their trophies can tell us a lot about where they will appear in the clan ranking.This also explains why the relationship is not equally strong across all clans. In some clans, league differences are enough to separate many players. In others, especially highly advanced clans, many players already share the same league, which makes trophies much more informative. So the strange combination we saw earlier — a moderate overall correlation but almost perfect correlations in some clans — starts to make sense.And Then There Is Town Hall LevelTrophies are not the only feature that stands out here. also showed a relatively strong relationship with , which at first might look unrelated to the ranking problem. But Clash of Clans has progression mechanics that connect Town Hall level with the league system.To prevent highly advanced players from dropping too far down the league system, there are league floors depending on the player's Town Hall level. This means that if a player is in a league below the minimum allowed for their Town Hall level, the game can move them back up to the appropriate league. So Town Hall level can influence the league a player can be in, and if league influences , Town Hall level can become predictive of clan rank without directly determining the ranking itself.This is exactly the kind of relationship that can be easy to miss if we only look at individual features without understanding the domain behind the data.There is one more detail about trophies worth knowing. They are reset with the beginning of a new league cycle, so unlike something such as Town Hall level, they are not simply a permanent measure of player progression. Their value depends partly on where we are in the current league cycle, which means the same trophy value can represent different situations depending on the context in which it appears.Now we have a much clearer picture of what was happening in the dataset. Trophies are strongly connected to clan rank. Town Hall level is connected to the league system, and the league system is connected to clan rank. And in highly competitive clans, trophies can become especially important because many players share the same league.So the feature that initially looked suspicious has a perfectly plausible explanation. But there is still an important question left:Is the model simply learning a legitimate game mechanic, or are we accidentally giving it information that makes the prediction too easy?I couldn't answer that just by looking at correlations. I needed to test it.5. Testing the HypothesisI now had a pretty good idea of what was happening, so the next step was to put it to the test.If trophies were creating a leakage-driven shortcut, removing them should reduce the model's predictive performance. On the other hand, if they were simply providing useful information, the model should still be able to learn a lot from the remaining features.This is why I created the two dataset versions I mentioned earlier: one with trophy-related features and one without them.For both versions, I used the same general setup. I split the data using from scikit-learn, with a 20% test set and . I then trained three different regression models:As the experiments progressed, I also used to optimize the XGBoost hyperparameters, which eventually produced the best-performing model in both dataset variants.When trophy-related features were included, the best model was XGBoost optimized with Optuna. The results were:This means the model explained of the variance in , while making an average absolute error of roughly three to four ranking positions. Random Forest was also very close, with an MAE of 3.6783 and an R² of 0.7523. The difference between the two models was not huge, but XGBoost was still the strongest overall.So far, nothing too surprising. Trophies looked very useful. The interesting part came when I removed them.For the second experiment, I removed not only trophies, but also the trophy-related features derived from it, such as the player's trophy difference from the clan mean, trophy ratio to the clan mean, trophy percentile within the clan, , and other related variables. Again, XGBoost + Optuna was the best-performing model.This time, the results were:Removing trophies clearly hurt performance. The MAE and RMSE increased, while R² dropped from 0.7710 to 0.7140. But there was something more important in those numbers: the model still achieved an R² of without any of the explicitly trophy-related variables.And that was the moment when I thought:Trophies were not making the model magically predict the target. They were simply providing a lot of useful information. Removing them did not destroy the model's predictive ability, which made the idea that trophies were responsible for the model's overall performance through leakage much less convincing.With vs. Without TrophiesPutting the two experiments side by side makes the difference easier to see:So yes, trophies matter. Removing them makes the problem harder, but it does not make the model collapse. The remaining player progression and clan-related features still contain enough information to predict very well.For me, this was the most important result of the whole investigation so far. The suspicious feature was not simply giving the model the answer. It was giving the model high-quality signal. A feature can be highly predictive because it contains meaningful information about the target, and that does not automatically make it leakage.What Is the Model Actually Using?After seeing the difference in overall performance, I also wanted to know whether the models were relying heavily on trophies or using a broader set of signals. The feature-importance analysis gave me a more interesting picture. is a good example of a feature that stays relevant everywhere: it ranks among the top features for both XGBoost and Random Forest, in dataset variants. That fits exactly with what we found earlier — Town Hall level connects to the league system, and the league system is a big part of what determines .What changes the most between the two variants is feature picks up the slack once trophies are gone, and it's different for each model. For Random Forest, — simply the size of the clan — becomes by far the single most important feature once the trophy-related columns are removed, far ahead of anything else in the whole comparison. For XGBoost, it's — a player's share of attack wins relative to the rest of their clan — that jumps the most once trophies disappear., the player's trophy standing relative to the rest of the clan, does show up among the top features in the with-trophies models — Random Forest leans on it the most of the three — but even there, it's smaller than several non-trophy features. It shares the spotlight rather than dominating it. Ridge, meanwhile, spreads its importance much more evenly across a wider set of features (completion ratios for equipment and troops, hero levels) instead of leaning hard on one or two, which is a good reminder that "what matters most" depends on the model as much as on the data.And that brings us back to something we saw earlier:A feature can tell the model much more when we understand how it relates to the other variables around it.6. What This Means for ML EngineeringAfter going through all of this, the main lesson I take from this problem is quite simple:Before removing a feature, you need to understand exactly what is happening with it.It would have been very easy to look at the correlation between trophies and , decide that the feature was suspicious, and remove it from the dataset. But that would have meant removing useful information without really understanding why it was there in the first place.I think this is where domain knowledge becomes extremely important in ML Engineering. For this project, the domain was a game, and I had to understand how Clash of Clans progression, leagues, trophies, and clan rankings work in order to make sense of what I was seeing in the data. But this applies to much more than games.Imagine you are working on a market analysis project, some variable suddenly changes, and the model starts behaving differently. Without understanding the market, you might blame the model or the project itself without realizing that there is a perfectly valid reason behind the change. The same thing can happen in finance, healthcare, marketing, or pretty much any other domain.For me, this is what makes an ML Engineer different from someone who only knows how to train a model.You need to understand what your data actually represents.A model can only work with the information you give it, so understanding where that information comes from is just as important as knowing which algorithm to use.This is also why the feature analyzer turned out to be so useful. It was not just a way of automatically deciding which features to remove. It gave me a way to investigate the dataset and understand why a feature was related to the target. A feature should not be in a model just because it happens to be available in the dataset, and it should not be removed just because it has a strong correlation with the target either. What matters is knowing what the feature represents, how it was generated, and why it is predictive.For the same reason, I think feature auditing should be part of the ML workflow, especially before making decisions about removing potentially problematic variables.In the end, this whole investigation started with a simple question about trophies, but it ended up reinforcing a much bigger idea:Good ML Engineering is not only about building models. It is about understanding the data well enough to know why the model is able to make its predictions.And sometimes, that means looking much deeper into the domain than you expected.I started this project with a simple question: why were trophies so predictive of clan rank?At first, it looked like I had found a data leakage problem. Instead of removing the feature and moving on, I decided to investigate what was actually happening.The first audit did not flag trophies as problematic according to the thresholds I had defined. Looking deeper into the game mechanics revealed why: league determines the main ranking context, while trophies can separate players within the same league. This becomes especially important in highly advanced clans, where many players are already competing in the same league.Then I tested the hypothesis. With trophy-related features, XGBoost reached an R² of 0.7710. After removing them, performance dropped to 0.7140, but the model still retained most of its predictive power. And that was the moment everything clicked.Trophies were not giving the model the answer outright. They were giving it good information.The important lesson is not that highly predictive features are suspicious. It is that predictive power alone does not tell you whether a feature is good or bad. Before removing a feature, understand where it comes from, what it represents, and why it is predictive. In this case, what first looked like leakage turned out to be a strong signal created by the system itself.Good ML Engineering is not just about building a model that predicts well. It is about understanding why it predicts well.

item.title: Replacing Transactional MSMQ with RabbitMQ Without Losing Consistency
item.author: Ilnur Yusupov
item.content:encoded:
Replacing MSMQ with RabbitMQ may look like a straightforward transport migration. In applications that rely on WCF, SQL Server, and distributed transactions, however, it can also change the application's consistency model. RabbitMQ does not participate in the same ambient TransactionScope as SQL Server, so guarantees that were previously provided by the infrastructure have to become explicit parts of the application architecture.This article compares three implementations of the same business flow: transactional MSMQ, a naive RabbitMQ replacement, and RabbitMQ with a transactional outbox. We will look at where a direct replacement breaks atomicity, why simply changing the order of database commit and message publication does not solve the problem, and how outbox, publisher confirms, retries, and idempotent consumers form a different reliability model.Why This Migration Is Harder Than It LooksMany long-lived .NET enterprise applications were built around Windows-centric technologies such as .NET Framework, IIS, WCF, MSMQ, and MSDTC. These technologies can still be appropriate in environments designed around them, but their platform coupling can limit future deployment and architecture options when teams move toward Linux containers, automated delivery, cloud-native infrastructure, or independently deployed services.One of the less obvious risks in such migrations is the loss of reliability guarantees that application code previously received from the infrastructure. This article focuses on one example: replacing WCF/MSMQ transactional messaging with RabbitMQ while preserving business consistency.Modernization Strategy: Isolate Messaging Before Migrating the RuntimeIt can be tempting to treat a large modernization program as one rewrite: upgrade the runtime, replace infrastructure, change the deployment topology, and redesign transaction handling at the same time. In practice, combining unrelated changes increases the number of failure modes and makes it harder to identify which architectural assumption was broken.The sample used in this article intentionally takes a narrower path. It remains on .NET Framework 4.8.1 and changes only the messaging strategy. Once the application no longer depends on WCF/MSMQ transactional messaging, a later migration to modern .NET becomes a separate step.The sample exposes the same business flow through three messaging modes:msmq - the legacy WCF/MSMQ baseline with distributed transaction supportrabbit-naive - a direct RabbitMQ replacement that preserves the call site but not the transaction semanticsrabbit-outbox - RabbitMQ publishing through a transactional outboxAt the application boundary, the code depends on a deliberately small abstraction:internal interface IMessagePublisher { void Publish(MessageEnvelope message); } The business flow can be simplified to:Begin TransactionScope Insert business record into SQL Server Publish BusinessRecordCreated message Complete transaction Only the implementation of IMessagePublisher changes. Keeping the application flow stable makes the consistency differences easier to observe and keeps the sample focused on the migration problem rather than on unrelated refactoring.The msmq-rabbitmq-consistency repository contains the sample application and the three messaging modes used throughout the article. Keeping the code next to the narrative makes it possible to reproduce the behavior discussed in the following sections and compare the implementations directly.Legacy Baseline: WCF and Transactional MSMQThe baseline uses WCF over a transactional MSMQ queue. In this architecture, SQL Server and MSMQ can enlist as durable resources in a transaction coordinated by System.Transactions and MSDTC. Microsoft documents System.Transactions as supporting SQL Server, MSMQ, and escalation to MSDTC when multiple durable resources participate.Conceptually, the producer performs:Begin TransactionScope Insert row into SQL Server Send message to transactional MSMQ queue Complete transaction If both resources are correctly enlisted and the TransactionScope completes, the database change and the message send are committed together. If the application fails before completion, both can be rolled back.The consumer side can also use a transactional receive. WCF can receive an MSMQ message inside a transaction and execute database work in the same local handling transaction. If message handling fails, the queue receive is not committed and the message can be delivered again.An important nuance is that the producer and consumer do not share one end-to-end transaction. The sender has a transaction around its local database write and queue send; the receiver has a separate transaction around queue receive and its own resource updates. WCF/MSMQ hides much of this coordination from business code, which is one reason the programming model feels deceptively simple.Why a Direct RabbitMQ Replacement Changes the Consistency ModelThe first migration attempt can look almost identical to the MSMQ implementation: keep TransactionScope, save the business record, and publish to RabbitMQ.Begin TransactionScope Insert row into SQL Server Publish message to RabbitMQ Complete transaction The code shape is similar, but the semantics are not. The SQL operation is controlled by TransactionScope; the RabbitMQ publish is not. The application now performs two independent writes to two different systems.Begin TransactionScope Insert row into SQL Server Publish message to RabbitMQ Application fails before transaction commit Rollback SQL transaction RabbitMQ may already have accepted the message while the SQL transaction later rolls back. A consumer can therefore observe an event for a business record that never becomes committed. Even when the SQL transaction eventually commits, a fast consumer may receive the message before the corresponding database change becomes visible to it.A natural reaction is to move publishing after the database commit. That prevents a message from escaping a transaction that later rolls back, but it creates the opposite failure window:Commit SQL transaction Application crashes or RabbitMQ is unavailable Publish message fails Now the business state is committed, but the event that should describe that state change is missing. Retrying the whole business operation may be unsafe because the database update has already succeeded.The dual-write problem: Publishing before the commit can create a message without committed business data. Publishing after the commit can create committed business data without a message. Changing the order does not make two independent resource updates atomic.This is the critical migration gap. Replacing MSMQ with RabbitMQ is not merely a change of transport API; it changes the consistency model of the application.A Production Symptom: Waiting for the DatabaseThis failure mode is not only theoretical. I have encountered production code where a consumer compensated for the race by repeatedly querying the database, sleeping for a fixed interval, and retrying until the record referenced by the message became visible.Such a workaround can hide one particular timing problem - message delivery before the producer transaction becomes visible - but it does not restore atomicity. If the producer transaction later rolls back, the expected row will never appear. Even when it commits, correctness now depends on timing, retry intervals, and timeout policy rather than on an explicit consistency guarantee. The workaround treats a symptom of the changed consistency model instead of addressing the dual-write problem itself.Transactional Outbox: Move the Reliable Write Into the DatabaseThe transactional outbox changes the problem instead of trying to make RabbitMQ participate in the SQL transaction. The application writes both the business change and a description of the outgoing message in the same database transaction.Begin local database transaction Insert business record into SQL Server Insert message into OutboxMessages Commit transaction Because both writes are in the same database, they share one local transaction boundary. If the transaction rolls back, neither the business row nor the outbox row remains. If it commits, both are durable.A separate dispatcher reads committed outbox rows and publishes them to RabbitMQ:Read unpublished outbox records Publish each message to RabbitMQ Wait for broker confirmation Mark the outbox record as published The database becomes the source of truth for the business operation and for the intent to publish. RabbitMQ delivery happens later, outside the business transaction. The architecture is now explicitly based on eventual consistency rather than pretending that the broker participates in the database transaction.The Dispatcher Gap and At-Least-Once PublishingThe outbox removes the atomicity gap between business data and the decision to publish, but the dispatcher still performs two operations: send the message and record that the send succeeded. That creates a smaller but unavoidable failure window.Dispatcher reads an unpublished row Dispatcher publishes the message RabbitMQ confirms the publish Dispatcher crashes before marking the row as published Application restarts Dispatcher publishes the same row again The message is not lost, but it may be published more than once. For that reason, a production outbox is commonly designed for at-least-once publication rather than relying on an end-to-end exactly-once assumption.Publisher confirms are important here. A successful client method call or a socket write alone is not sufficient evidence that the broker durably accepted a message. RabbitMQ documents publisher confirms specifically as a publisher-side data-safety mechanism.A robust dispatcher therefore retries failed sends and marks an outbox row as published only after the required broker confirmation. The trade-off is duplicate delivery, which moves the next reliability requirement to consumers.Idempotent Consumers and the Inbox PatternIf the same logical message can arrive more than once, consumers must ensure that repeated delivery does not repeat the business effect.The sample uses a ProcessedMessages table keyed by MessageId. The business update and the processed-message marker are written in the same local database transaction:Begin local transaction If MessageId already exists in ProcessedMessages: Commit Acknowledge broker message Return
Apply business changes Insert MessageId into ProcessedMessages Commit Acknowledge broker message If the consumer commits its database transaction and crashes before acknowledging RabbitMQ, the broker can redeliver the message. On the next attempt, the consumer finds the existing MessageId and skips the business effect.This mechanism is often described as an inbox or duplicate-detection pattern. Storing MessageId is not the only possible idempotency strategy - some operations are naturally idempotent - but the important architectural requirement is the same: a retry must not corrupt business state.This is the core shift away from the MSMQ/MSDTC model. Reliability is no longer obtained by coordinating every resource in one distributed transaction. It is assembled from local atomic transactions, durable intent, retry, broker acknowledgements, and idempotent processing.Production ConsiderationsThe dispatcher in a teaching sample should remain intentionally small. A production implementation has to address several additional concerns:row claiming or locking when multiple dispatcher instances run concurrentlyretry policies with backoff and a clear policy for permanently failing messagesRabbitMQ publisher confirms before an outbox record is considered dispatchedmessage ordering where business semantics require per-aggregate or per-stream orderingdead-letter or poison-message handlingmetrics, tracing, alerting, and visibility into outbox backlogcleanup or archival of old outbox and inbox recordsmessage schema evolution and serialization compatibilitybatching and throughput controls so the outbox does not become a database bottlenecka documented idempotency strategy for every consumer with non-transactional side effectsFor example, multiple workers may claim rows in parallel to improve throughput, but they should avoid uncontrolled concurrent publication of the same record. If ordering matters for a particular entity, parallelism must be constrained accordingly. A failed broker publish should be retried with backoff, while a confirmed publish should not be marked as sent until the confirmation has been observed.These details are deliberately outside the minimal implementation. The sample is intended to explain the architecture, not to become another messaging framework.Framework-Assisted ImplementationsProduction systems rarely implement every reliability mechanism from scratch. Mature .NET messaging frameworks such as MassTransit, NServiceBus, and Wolverine provide built-in support for outbox/inbox patterns, retries, duplicate detection, and related operational concerns.These frameworks do not restore the old MSDTC-based transaction model. The underlying architecture is still different: business data and the intent to publish are committed locally, while message delivery happens later and may be retried.The companion repository includes a .NET 8 example using MassTransit with RabbitMQ and EF Core to demonstrate a framework-assisted outbox/inbox implementation.The manual implementation remains useful because it exposes the actual failure windows and trade-offs. Once those mechanics are understood, a framework can automate much of the infrastructure without hiding the consistency model itself.A Practical Staged Migration PathOne possible migration sequence is:Identify where business transactions currently depend on transactional MSMQ behavior.Introduce a messaging abstraction so business code does not depend directly on WCF/MSMQ.Replace direct MSMQ publishing with RabbitMQ plus an outbox-based reliability model.Adopt a mature messaging framework where its operational features justify the dependency.Migrate the application runtime and deployment model to modern .NET as a separate iteration.This order is not universal. Some systems can migrate the runtime first; others are better candidates for a strangler approach or for extracting new services around a stable legacy core. The important principle is to make the reliability model explicit before changing infrastructure that used to provide hidden guarantees.Enterprise modernization is rarely a sequence of mechanical package upgrades. Infrastructure choices encode behavioral guarantees, and changing those choices can silently change application correctness.The WCF/MSMQ baseline in this article could coordinate SQL Server and a transactional queue through System.Transactions and MSDTC. A direct RabbitMQ replacement preserves the shape of the code but not that atomicity. Publishing before the database commit risks messages for rolled-back state; publishing after the commit risks committed state without a message.The transactional outbox resolves this dual-write problem by moving the reliable decision to publish into the same local database transaction as the business data. The cost is a different consistency model: asynchronous dispatch, eventual consistency, retries, and possible duplicate delivery. Idempotent consumers are therefore part of the design, not an optional optimization.The broader lesson is not that distributed transactions are universally wrong or that every legacy system must be rewritten. It is that modernization must preserve business correctness while the technical foundation changes. When a platform-level guarantee disappears, the replacement architecture must make that guarantee - or its new equivalent - explicit.For many long-lived enterprise applications, separating the replacement of transactional messaging from the runtime migration can reduce risk and make the transition easier to test. It turns a large rewrite into a sequence of smaller architectural changes whose failure modes can be understood independently.

item.title: The Missing Layer in Enterprise AI: A Governance Architecture for LLMs and Machine Learning
item.author: Sunilkumar Reddy Eraganeni
item.content:encoded: Most companies have a data platform, a model platform and a pile of AI pilots. Fewer have the thing that decides which of those pilots should be allowed near a customer.The chatbot that worked a little too wellPicture a mid-sized insurer that ships an internal claims assistant in six weeks. Adjusters love it. Then someone pastes a policyholder's medical notes into the prompt box to get a quick summary, and a month later a compliance analyst asks a perfectly reasonable question: where did that text go, who could see it, and which model version produced the answer we sent to the customer?Nobody can say. The logs exist, technically, but they live in three systems and none of them record the model version. The "approval" for the project was a slide deck and a nod in a meeting.I have seen versions of this story enough times that I no longer think of it as a failure of any particular team. It is what happens when a company builds the data layer, the model layer and the application layer, and quietly assumes the fourth thing will appear on its own. Governance does not appear on its own. Somebody has to design it.Why the usual answer does not hold upThe default response is a policy document and a review board. I understand the instinct. A policy feels like progress, and a board feels like accountability.The trouble is timing. A board that meets monthly cannot review a system that changes weekly, and a PDF cannot stop a prompt from leaking a phone number at 2 a.m. Policy written in prose is a statement of intent. It only becomes a control when something in the system enforces it, records that it did, and can show the record to a stranger a year later.There is a fair counterargument, though. Heavy governance can strangle the experimentation that makes AI worth doing. A team that needs six sign-offs to try a summarisation prompt will simply stop asking, and then you have shadow AI, which is worse. So the goal is not more process. It is the right amount, attached to the right places and automated wherever that is realistic.The shift that helped me most was to stop picturing governance as a gate at the end and start picturing it as a layer that runs alongside everything else, like identity or networking. You would not let each team invent its own login system. The same logic applies here.Frameworks already point this way. The NIST AI Risk Management Framework talks about governing, mapping, measuring and managing risk as continuous activities. The EU AI Act ties obligations to risk tiers, which in practice means you need to know what you have and how risky it is before you can comply with anything. Banks have lived with something similar for years under supervisory guidance on model risk, such as SR 11-7 in the United States. None of these tell you what to build, which is both their strength and their limit. That gap is what an architecture fills.Five planes and one evidence trailHere is the structure I keep coming back to. It is not the only way to slice the problem, and I would not be shocked if your version has six planes or four. What matters is that each concern has a home and an owner. holds the rules in a form machines can read. Risk tiers, acceptable use, who may approve what, and which regulation maps to which control. A customer-facing credit model and an internal meeting summariser should not face the same hurdles, and the policy plane is where that difference is written down. answers where the inputs came from. Lineage, consent, classification and retention all live here. For LLM work this includes the documents behind a retrieval index, which is the part teams most often forget. If the index can read a file, the model can repeat it. is the registry and the testing ground. Every model, prompt template and fine-tune gets a version, an owner, an evaluation record and a short model card. Evaluation here means more than accuracy. It covers bias checks for scoring models and, for LLMs, things like grounding, refusal behaviour and resistance to prompt injection. is where controls actually bite. Input and output guardrails, rate limits, human escalation and a kill switch sit here. watches everything afterwards. Drift monitoring, incident response, reporting to risk teams and the board.Running through all five is the evidence trail: immutable logs that record decisions, owners and timestamps. This is the unglamorous part, and I would argue it is the whole point. Governance you cannot prove is just a story you tell.What this looks like for an LLMTake the insurer's claims assistant and run it through the runtime plane.A request arrives. An input guard checks for personal data and obvious injection attempts, and applies policy for that user's role. Retrieval then runs with access control, so the system only fetches documents the person is already allowed to read. This step matters more than most prompt-level defences, because it stops the model from ever seeing what it should not repeat. The model generates an answer. An output guard checks whether the answer is grounded in the retrieved sources and whether it leaks anything sensitive. Low-confidence or high-stakes cases route to a human.Every stage writes to the audit log: the prompt, the sources, the model version, the guard verdicts, the latency, the user's role. When the compliance analyst asks her question, the answer takes a few minutes instead of a few weeks.I should be honest about the limits. Guardrails are probabilistic, and the OWASP list of risks for LLM applications exists precisely because injection and data leakage are not solved problems. No filter catches everything. The architecture does not promise safety. It promises that failures are contained, visible and traceable, which is a more modest and more truthful claim.What this looks like for classical machine learningTraditional models need the same bones with a different rhythm. A fraud model or demand forecast moves through a lifecycle, and governance shows up as gates between the stages.Data intake requires a lineage and consent check. Training must be reproducible, so someone else can rerun it and get the same result. Validation covers performance, bias and robustness. Approval requires a named human owner, with the depth of review set by the risk tier. Deployment comes with a canary release and a rollback plan. After that, monitoring watches for drift, and the loop closes: when a threshold is crossed, the model is retrained or rolled back.Retirement is the underrated stage. Old models linger because nobody owns the decision to switch them off.Architecture without ownership is a diagram on a wall. The model I find most workable borrows from the three lines familiar in financial services, scaled down so a smaller company can use it.Build teams own their models and use cases, run the tests and respond to alerts. A small governance office sets risk tiers, reviews only the high-tier approvals and maintains the shared tooling, so everyone else gets the controls for free. Internal audit and risk sample the logs and test whether the controls work in practice, then report upwards.Policy flows one way, evidence flows the other. If a team has to fill in a form to get a control, it will be skipped. If the control ships with the platform, it will mostly be used.Two failure patterns are worth naming. One is governance theatre: beautiful policies, no enforcement, no logs. The other is the opposite, a control regime so heavy that teams route around it.I am also not sure the five-plane split suits every organisation. A ten-person data team probably does not need a governance office. It might need one engineer who owns the registry and a habit of writing down who approved what.A sensible first ninety daysI would not begin with tooling. I would begin with an inventory, because you cannot govern what you cannot list. Find every model and LLM-powered feature, including the quiet ones in spreadsheets and vendor products, and give each a risk tier and a named owner.Next, pick the highest-risk system and wire up logging end to end, so a decision can be traced back to a model version and data source. Then add one automated gate to the deployment pipeline, such as refusing to promote a model with no evaluation record. Small, boring and enforceable beats ambitious and optional.Enterprise AI does not usually fail because the models are weak. It fails in the seams: between the team that built the thing and the team that has to answer for it, between what the policy says and what the system does. Governance is the layer that closes those seams, and it is far easier to design before the first incident than after it.The insurer in my opening example eventually fixed things. Retrieval got access control, the logs gained a model version, and the approval became a record instead of a nod. None of it was glamorous. All of it was the part that let them keep the chatbot.What does your organisation's version of this layer look like, and who owns it? I would genuinely like to hear where this framing breaks down.

item.title: When AI Designs a Presentation, Who Authorizes Its Decisions?
item.author: Ghada AlAmoudi
item.content:encoded: A few weeks ago, while developing a system for designing presentations with artificial intelligence, I encountered a problem that initially appeared too small to deserve much attention.An AI presentation tool had added a short explanatory section to a slide. The addition was coherent, visually appropriate, and consistent with the general subject. Under ordinary circumstances, it might have been considered an improvement.But I had not asked for it.The presentation concerned the possibility of introducing a four-day workweek. Its purpose was exploratory: to organize the questions management needed to consider, without recommending a decision or presenting unsupported conclusions. The additional section introduced an interpretation that had not been approved in the preceding design process.The problem was not whether the sentence sounded reasonable. It was whether the tool had the authority to introduce it.This distinction became increasingly important as the development continued.We often evaluate AI-generated presentations by examining the final slides. Are they attractive? Is the information organized? Does the narrative appear coherent? Yet these questions tell us relatively little about the decisions made during generation.A presentation may look professionally designed while containing interpretations, priorities, or assumptions that its author never intended.I began to think that the difficulty was not primarily a matter of improving the prompt. It concerned the architecture of the process itself.When someone asks an AI tool to prepare a presentation, the instruction is usually incomplete. It may identify the subject, audience, objective, and preferred style, but it rarely specifies every decision required to produce the final slides.The system must therefore make choices.It determines which subjects deserve separate slides, how information should be grouped, which statements should be emphasized, whether a diagram is more appropriate than text, and how the visual arrangement should direct the audience's attention.Some of these decisions are necessary for implementation. Others can alter the meaning of the material.This is where I believe an important boundary exists.Choosing the position of a text block is not equivalent to introducing a new argument. Adjusting spacing is not equivalent to changing the importance of a conclusion. Selecting a visual representation is not necessarily a neutral operation when that representation can suggest certainty, causality, or comparison.If we treat all these actions as ordinary design decisions, we may overlook the point at which the system moves from executing the user's intentions to interpreting them on the user's behalf.The distinction is particularly important in professional presentations, where the audience may interpret visual emphasis as an indication of evidential strength or organizational priority.A polished slide can make an uncertain statement appear settled.The question, then, is not how to prevent AI from making decisions altogether. That would make generative design impractical. The question is how to distinguish decisions that the system may make independently from those that require explicit authorization.Designing a system around decision boundariesThis question shaped the development of AI Presentation Designer — Professional.The project began as an attempt to improve AI-assisted presentation design through structured instructions. As development progressed, however, the work increasingly concerned the relationships between different design responsibilities.I found that presentation structure, information hierarchy, layout, visual assets, and final composition could not be treated as independent activities.A change in structure could affect the argument. A change in hierarchy could alter the audience's interpretation. A visual asset could introduce meaning that was absent from the source material.The challenge was therefore to coordinate these responsibilities without allowing one to assume the authority of another.The system was developed as a coordinated prompt-based architecture rather than a conventional software application. Its components are implemented through structured instructions, each assigned a specific responsibility within the presentation-design process. The instructions do not operate as isolated requests for generating slides; they form a connected workflow in which the output of one stage becomes a controlled input to another.What distinguishes this approach from a simple sequence of prompts is the attention given to decision authority and the preservation of approved requirements. Each stage is expected to work within its assigned responsibility, while subsequent stages must not silently reinterpret earlier decisions. These boundaries are expressed through the instruction system and examined through review, rather than enforced by a deterministic software engine.The resulting architecture organizes the design process into eleven specialized modules, supported by an execution workflow and a review stage.These modules are not intended to operate as eleven unrelated prompts. Their value lies in the boundaries established between them and in the decisions transferred from one stage to the next.For example, the component responsible for slide structure may organize authorized information, but it should not manufacture additional content to achieve a preferred slide count.Similarly, the component responsible for layout may determine how content is presented, but it should not treat a familiar design pattern as evidence that a particular conclusion belongs in the presentation.This distinction may appear restrictive. In practice, it addresses a recurring problem in generative workflows: an implementation choice gradually becomes an assumed requirement, even though no one explicitly authorized it.Why incomplete information must remain incompleteOne of the more interesting problems during development concerned missing information.Generative models are particularly effective at producing coherent text. When information is incomplete, they can often construct a plausible continuation.In some creative contexts, this is desirable. In a professional decision-making context, it may be precisely what we need to prevent.Consider a presentation evaluating a four-day workweek.If the organization has supplied no productivity measurements, the presentation can identify productivity as a relevant consideration. It cannot legitimately report that productivity will improve, decline, or remain unchanged.The absence of evidence is not an invitation to complete the argument.The same principle applies to design.A chart may be visually attractive, but its presence can imply that measurable evidence exists. A prominent concluding statement may suggest that the analysis has reached a recommendation, even when the original purpose was only to explore alternatives.During development, this led to a broader requirement: uncertainty must be preserved not only in the text but also in the way information is structured and displayed.A system that avoids inventing numbers but visually presents unresolved questions as established findings has not fully preserved the meaning of its source material.What an end-to-end test revealedTo examine the workflow, I used an exploratory management presentation concerning a four-day workweek.The initial brief specified the purpose and audience but did not provide organizational productivity data or customer-coverage measurements.The design process produced a sequence of decisions about structure, visual language, layout, information hierarchy, and other presentation elements. These decisions were then used to guide implementation through an AI presentation tool.The test exposed two useful problems.The first appeared during structural development. An approximate target of eight slides encouraged unnecessary expansion, including material that existed primarily to satisfy the expected length.This revealed a conflict between a numerical preference and the actual informational requirements of the presentation.The workflow was revised so that an approximate slide count would not be treated as a requirement to manufacture content. The final structure contained six substantive slides.The second problem appeared after implementation.The presentation tool introduced additional explanatory material, including a section labeled “Starting Point.” The content was plausible, but it had not been authorized by the preceding design decisions.The review identified the deviation, and the presentation was corrected.What interested me was that the additional material did not look like an obvious error. It appeared to improve the presentation.Had the review focused only on visual quality or narrative coherence, the deviation might have remained unnoticed.The test was limited to an architectural development scenario. It was not a controlled study comparing different presentation systems, and it cannot establish a general performance advantage.Its value was more specific: it exposed where decision boundaries could fail and allowed the workflow to be revised accordingly.The importance of separating execution from verificationA further architectural decision concerned the role of the presentation-generation tool itself.I did not want the system to depend entirely on one presentation platform, nor did I want the host tool's existing preferences to determine the meaning of the presentation.The architecture was not developed as an autonomous AI agent, nor was it implemented as a software engine tied to a particular presentation platform. It was designed as a coordinated system of structured prompts that can guide compatible AI models through a sequence of defined design responsibilities.During development, ChatGPT was used to process the decision-oriented stages, while Gamma was used to implement the resulting presentation. This arrangement allowed the decision workflow and the presentation-generation tool to be examined as distinct components.Although the architecture is intended to be adaptable across compatible models and tools, broader interoperability remains a subject for further testing.This separation does not mean that the host tool becomes passive. It still performs essential work, including rendering slides, arranging elements, and producing the presentation artifact.But implementation should not automatically confer authority to change the approved requirements.The resulting presentation must also be examined as an artifact in its own right.A correct instruction does not prove that it was correctly implemented.This is why the workflow includes verification after execution. The review is concerned not only with whether the slides appear consistent, but also with whether their content, hierarchy, and composition remain faithful to the decisions established earlier.It is possible for a presentation to be internally consistent and still depart from the original brief.That possibility makes verification a separate engineering responsibility rather than a final cosmetic inspection.A question extending beyond presentation designI do not consider this architecture a complete solution to the broader problem of controlling generative AI.Its current implementation has been developed and examined within a specific presentation-design workflow. Broader claims would require additional testing across tasks, tools, and users.Nevertheless, the development raised a question that extends beyond presentations.As generative systems become capable of producing increasingly complete artifacts, how do we preserve the distinction between what the user intended, what the system inferred, and what the system actually implemented?This question is relevant wherever AI is entrusted with work that involves interpretation rather than mechanical execution.It is tempting to assume that greater generative capability will reduce the need for explicit design decisions. My experience during this project suggests a different possibility: the more work a system can complete independently, the more important it becomes to understand the boundaries of that independence.I am interested in AI systems that can do more than produce convincing outputs. I am interested in systems whose decisions can be examined, whose assumptions can be questioned, and whose implementation can be evaluated against the intentions that authorized it.The development of this presentation-design system has been one practical exploration of that problem.And it has left me with a question that I believe deserves further engineering attention:When an AI-generated artifact appears complete, how can we determine whether it is complete according to the user's requirements—or merely according to the system's own interpretation of them?This article draws on the development of AI Presentation Designer — Professional, an independent project exploring decision authority, structured prompt architectures, and verification in AI-assisted presentation creation.This article is based on my original development work, architectural decisions, and practical testing experience. I used ChatGPT to assist with English drafting, technical discussion, and editorial refinement. I reviewed and approved the final manuscript and take responsibility for its content, accuracy, and conclusions.

item.title: Open Inference Networks: Democratic Access to Intelligence
item.author: vishwa vimukthi gammuduwaththage
item.content:encoded:
Weights you cannot run are a fileAn open model on your disk is only a large file until something runs it. If the only place that can run it is a rented data center, you are still a tenant.I come at this from edge work. Models on a drone have to run on the device, with no network at all. That makes me sympathetic to the local-first argument, and also impatient with claims that ignore physics. I wrote about that shift in my piece on edge AI.There are three ways to run a model outside a hyperscaler. I will take them in order of how well they work.Tier one: run it yourselfThis is the part of the story that has clearly arrived.Tools such as llama.cpp and Ollama made local inference a one-line install. Quantization, which stores each weight in about 4 bits, cut memory needs to roughly a quarter of the original with modest quality loss.The same source treats 30 tokens per second as the threshold for comfortable chat. By that measure, a model in the 8B to 30B range is fully interactive on one high-end consumer machine.Memory is the hard limit. A 70B model at 4 bits needs about 35 GB for the weights alone, which is more than any single consumer graphics card holds. Laptops with 16 GB handle the 8B class. Phones run models in the 1B to 4B range.Switching is easy, because Ollama serves the same API shape that cloud providers use:from openai import OpenAI
client = OpenAI(base_url="http://localhost:11434/v1", api_key="unused")
reply = client.chat.completions.create( model="gemma3:12b", messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Summarize this log file."}], ) print(reply.choices[0].message.content) Change one URL and your application talks to your own machine. No subscription, no rate limit, and no data leaving the room.The limit is quality. A 12B or 27B model is very capable at summarizing, drafting, extraction, and routine coding. It is not equal to the largest hosted models on long, multi-step reasoning. Anyone who says otherwise is selling something.[YOUR EXPERIENCE: a short paragraph on a model you run locally or on-device, what it handles well, and where you still reach for a cloud API.]Tier two: pool the devicesNow the harder claim. If one laptop cannot hold a frontier-size model, can a thousand laptops hold it together?Do the arithmetic first. A 405-billion-parameter model at 4 bits is about 200 GB of weights. If each volunteer device offers 8 GB, you need at least 26 devices in a chain, each holding a block of layers. A prompt enters the first device, and the intermediate result is passed along until the last device produces one token. Then the whole chain runs again for the next token.That is the design of Petals, the best-known project of this kind, which describes itself as running models "BitTorrent-style." It works. The project reports up to 6 tokens per second for a 70B model in the best case. That is usable for batch jobs and well below chat speed.Three problems explain the gap. Each token crosses every device in the chain, over home internet. A July 2026 review of Petals names bandwidth between nodes as the main documented obstacle, and describes the project's recent maintenance as limited.Pooling adds memory, not speed. This is true even under ideal conditions. In benchmarks of the exo framework, four top-end Mac Studios linked by Thunderbolt 5 ran a very large model at 32.5 tokens per second, against 21.1 for one machine. Four times the hardware bought 1.5 times the speed, and that was over a direct cable link built for low latency. Ordinary Wi-Fi and broadband are far worse. In a layer-split network, the device holding the first block receives your prompt in a form that can be read. Devices further along see intermediate values. This is weaker privacy than a cloud provider bound by a contract, not stronger. And as part three showed, you also cannot easily confirm that a peer ran the layers it claimed.So the honest answer to "can consumer devices collectively host a frontier model" is: they can hold it, and they cannot serve it at a speed most people would accept. Pooling on a local network with fast links is a real option for a lab or a small office. Pooling across the public internet is, for now, a research result.Tier three: pay people to run itPetals relies on volunteers, and volunteer networks have a known weakness. Many people use them and few contribute.Token-incentive networks try to fix this with payment. Bittensor is the largest example. In outline:The network is divided into subnets, each focused on one task such as text generation. run models and answer requests. score the answers.The network issues new tokens every day and splits them according to those scores.This is a real mechanism for getting hardware online without a company buying it. It is the supply-side idea from part one, applied to inference.It is also where I think the "subscriptions to tokens" story needs care, because it mixes two different things. means paying per request to whoever served it. That is a sound model. It is how every API already bills, and an open network can do the same with any currency. mean paying suppliers with newly created tokens, whether or not customers showed up. That is a subsidy. It gets a network started, and it lasts only while the token holds value.The criticisms in the source I cited are mostly about the second:A small group of large validators controls how rewards are distributed.Subnet owners can run validators and miners inside their own subnet.Competitive mining is estimated to cost $1,500 to $6,000 a month in GPU rental, which favors funded teams over individuals.Judging answer quality is far harder to verify than validating a block.For a buyer there is a simpler issue. A $20 subscription costs $20 next month. A token-priced service costs whatever the token is worth that day. Businesses budget in currency, and volatility is a cost.None of this means incentive networks fail. It means the comparison is between a predictable service with a landlord and an open market with a subsidy and an exchange rate.Data centers are more efficient. A cloud GPU serves many users at once by batching their requests together. A laptop serves one person and sits idle most of the day. Cost and energy per token favor the data center by a wide margin.The best models are not open. The strongest systems are closed, and the largest open ones need hardware almost no individual owns. Open inference gives broad access to good models, not to the best ones. A machine that runs a 27B model well costs thousands of dollars. That is several years of a subscription, paid upfront, for hardware that ages.Peer-to-peer weakens privacy. Sending your prompt through strangers' machines is a step down from a provider with a legal agreement, unless the network adds protections that do not yet exist at scale.Incentives can be captured. Any system that pays for scores invites people to game the scores. Concentrated validators are the predictable result.Convenience usually wins. Most people will choose the option that needs no setup. That has been true of email, hosting, and storage.Better small models cut both ways. They make local inference stronger, and they remove the main reason to split a huge model across a swarm in the first place.I expected to write about swarms of phones running frontier models. The evidence pointed somewhere less dramatic and more useful. is ready for private data, offline use, low latency, and predictable cost. This is where most of the real gain in access is.Pooling on a local network makes sense when you need to fit a model that no single machine can hold, and you accept the speed.Public peer-to-peer networks suit batch work and resilience. They are not yet a chat service. remain the answer when you need the strongest model.The practical pattern is a hybrid. Run a small model locally for most requests and send the hard ones to a larger model elsewhere. That is how I would build a product today."Democratic access to intelligence" is arriving, mainly because a model that needed a data center two years ago now fits on a desk. That is progress in research and hardware. The networks and tokens are a second-order story so far.

item.title: Tailoring a Multi-agent LLM System for a Mid-sized Business
item.author: Max Tsvetkov
item.content:encoded: As a medium-sized company with a large number of monthly active users (MAU) and a few digital products, you will have realised by now that using free ChatGPT is not enough. Yes, you have learned about skills.md and the expensive Claude subscription. But is that enough? In this article, I will share the knowledge needed to design a multi-agent LLM system for mid-scale organisations.The golden rule of working with LLMs: treat publicly available models as a brain, not as eyes and ears. An LLM doesn't actually anything — it generates something that looks like an answer. That's why we, as developers, need to add plenty of validation along the way from the user's request to the model's response. Keep one simple rule in mind: if a human could mess it up, an LLM definitely will, because LLMs have no common sense.The general pipeline for getting an answer from an LLM looks like this: indexing > retrieval > generation. The user types a prompt, it gets vectorized and sent to the database to look for relevant data. But how do we check the facts? For facts, we rely on external tools, not the LLM. Out of the box, LLMs are usually bad at precise facts — an LLM is not a rule engine. So if you're serious about your LLM product, never call the model without validation. Validation is what turns a bare LLM into a real agent.The easiest way to reduce the chance of incorrect answers is to get an explicit prompt out of the user. The very first check is input validation: we need to know for sure that the request matches the data we're prepared to serve. Another strategy is the family of zero-shot, one-shot, few-shot, and multi-shot methods, which help the LLM understand the format you want the answer in. With zero-shot, the model decides on its own how to approach the task. The more shots you give, the more context the model has about what exactly is expected of it.You can also inject sample answers into the context using RAG. RAG gives the model access to up-to-date knowledge and can reduce hallucinations. Sample answers can be built around popular prompting techniques, such as: — "Imagine you're a financial analyst…" — "Break the task down into substeps…" — "Once you've prepared the final answer, go through the information again and make sure nothing important was left out…" — "Give me several possible answers, pick the best one, repeat." — graphs, like the ones in ComfyUI. — "Second agent, challenge the first agent's answer…"It's always a good idea to explicitly ask the LLM to draw up an action plan. Step-by-step reasoning works through zero-shot CoT.Keep your prompts short. One task, one prompt. If you want the model to assess a situation, give it explicit options: , , or . Start with simple prompts and gradually layer on context — it works as a kind of lightweight fine-tuning. This is also why you shouldn't mix developer specs with product context: they belong in separate stores, so the LLM never gets confused about which context is the right one. Stick to SDD (spec-driven development) frameworks: Superpowers, GSD, grill-with-docs, OpenSpec.Another framework for better prompts is RACE (Role > Action > Context > Execute/Expectations). Here's the structure: have the model play a CFO, a copywriter, or a security specialist. analyze, summarize, transform, generate. describe the audience — who will use the results. JSON, formal prose, word count.Role: Facebook ad specialist with expertise in Gen Z engagement Action: Create six ad copy variations for our new self-driving scooters, bearing in mind the additional value of the carbon tax. Context: Brand voice guidelines: casual, informal, authentic, slightly irreverent. Target audience: environmentally-conscious Gen Z (18-26) • USPs: recycled materials, carbon-neutral shipping, $10 donation to plant mangrove trees. Maximum 115 characters per ad. Execute: Provide 6 numbered ad variations with: - Attention-grabbing headline - Body copy - CTA (Call to action) Each one should appeal to a different emotion (urgency, rebellion, belonging, impact). But what if the user overdoes it and sends a gigantic request? Say they dump their entire console output into our little agent, just to see what the AI makes of it. More verbs, better results — isn't that what everyone thinks? In that case, the agent decomposes the request into a series of subqueries, and we retrieve many chunks, each answering one small subquery. This is called Demonstrate-Search-Predict (DSP). First, the LLM generates a general answer to the main question, and then the set of subquestions forms vectors for better retrieval. You'll find detailed descriptions of these techniques under names like query expansion, query transformation, step-back prompting, and query rewriting. Keep in mind, though, that every extra step for retrieving, processing, and validating data costs more resources and adds response time — a sure path to poor tail latency.In more technical terms, what matters isn't how many tokens you spend in one go, but the size of the context. Tokens aren't the same as words: they include punctuation, symbols, digits, and other text elements, and tokenization schemes vary from one LLM to another. As a rule of thumb, a two-word phrase like "cat escaped" takes about two tokens. This is where context limits come from: GPT-3.5 had a context window of 4,096 tokens, roughly five pages of text. GPT-4 raised that to 8,192 tokens (10 pages), and GPT-4-32k arrived with 32,768 tokens (40 pages). Gemini 1.5, meanwhile, works with a 1-million-token context window — over 1,000 pages. So can we take older models and feed them a huge context? No — that's a sure path to hallucinations. I've tried.Also, be careful about letting users play with the parameter, which controls the probability distribution — think of it as focused randomization. It's generally not recommended to adjust and temperature at the same time. Note that top-p is OpenAI's term; other models may call it something else. A higher temperature means a more "creative" model, but in reality it simply makes the next token less predictable. If we asked the model to delete files and cranked the creativity all the way up… well, whose fault is that?If you have just one agent (LLM + harness) handling every task, it will break quickly. This is called role overload. The fix is simple, just like with human employees: split the responsibilities. One person can single-handedly carry an entire project, but they can't keep doing it on a steady basis. That's exactly why businesses and professions exist — a team with defined roles solves problems systematically. At the very least, it lets agents keep working after errors occur. "If you failed, try again" logic is generally bad practice (just as it is in people management). You end up in an infinite loop where the agent hits the same error over and over and burns through your entire budget. Mind your limits.Also, if you're simply calling an LLM directly, that's not an agent — it's just an interface wrapper around the LLM. An agent runs in a loop: it reasons about the best action or tool for the task, uses those tools, and updates its state. One popular structure looks like this: → → → → or . All of these steps are essential for debugging, too. The can be the user's prompt, tool outputs, or the history of failures.Agents need certain rules: common sense (gravity exists, so people can't fly), linguistic knowledge (the syntax of a language), and domain knowledge (understanding medicine, say). Knowledge is more or less "frozen" at the pre-training stage. Common sense, however, can be its own separate agent.Which agents you build is entirely up to you, but each industry has established best practices. A standard "team" consists of reasoning (research, planning) > tools and integrations (APIs) > memory (remembering all actions, plans, and conversations) > and the worker agents themselves (writing content, sending emails, running code). For example, if you're building agents for red teaming, you'll definitely need a dedicated agent that blocks prohibited, dangerous, or irreversible actions. Or a supervisor agent might oversee several local control agents. Its main job is to resolve goal conflicts between those local agents by adjusting their objectives in line with global priorities. In short, a boss agent that keeps everyone on course toward the goal.A Monitor Agent is responsible for watching external API integrations in a production multi-agent system. Teams usually want it to spot signs of API degradation and coordinate remediation. This can be tracked in numbers — for example, how often each external API exceeds its timeout within a given time window. A review might reveal, for instance, that executor agents are frequently waiting on decisions from planner agents. That means the data-exchange queue needs optimizing and backpressure routing should be added. Or, in a large multi-agent system, monitoring might show that end-to-end request latency spikes with every traffic surge, even though average CPU utilization across the cluster stays below 50%. In that case, we notify another agent or a human.Here's another real-world example. In my own multi-agent system, the monitoring agent detected that an external scheduling API was showing latency and intermittent timeouts at certain hours. To stabilize behavior, I added adaptive backoff and graceful degradation, temporarily simplifying how scheduling requests were handled whenever latency crossed predefined thresholds. And whenever an agent failed, I returned structured error codes along with machine-readable details on what caused the failure and which constraints were violated.Naturally, there's a dedicated agent for working with MCP. If an MCP server has database access, it's important to restrict queries to a predefined set of parameterized operations with strict input validation. Every tool should be isolated, and read-only tools can run in parallel. But if calls can modify the underlying data, they should run sequentially. Once again, agents need to understand when to call external tools and when to rely on their built-in knowledge.In a multi-agent manufacturing system, a coordinator agent orchestrates calls to several MCP tools: one forecasts demand, another assesses production capacity, and a third handles scheduling. The right strategy is to use a shared domain model and map each tool's input and output schemas to that model before and after every tool call.The role-based split described above also helps with debugging. You can only debug between steps — between agents and tools. Be sure to think about tracers, so you know what state the system was in and at what moment. This isn't about logging; it's about being able to answer questions when something goes wrong: inputs, outputs, validation errors, state changes, and final decisions. We need to be able to explain to management why an agent behaved a certain way at a specific point in time. New agents should be rolled out via blue-green deployment. And if agents have learned something while working with a particular cohort of employees, that new skill should be propagated into the agent system only after offline validation.We're also talking about using different LLMs for different roles. Take DeepSeek: they have many models, such as V3, R1, and Janus Pro. DeepSeek is good at processing unstructured data and can show its chain of reasoning. It works at the Neural Network Layer. The common practice is to use DeepSeek-V3 for code generation and refactoring, and DeepSeek-R1 — which is built on transformers — for reasoning and decomposing complex tasks. Every LLM gets its own role, and when choosing one, consider the model's architecture (CNN, Transformer, RNN) and look at its loss function. V3 is also well suited to generating candidate bug fixes, while R1 is better at determining which fix best addresses the root cause. R1 can draw reasonably sound conclusions from complex datasets; its inference module is designed to make well-grounded inferences, which is one of R1's core functions.As for combinations that work well: GPT + Codex, Claude + Claude Code, Gemini + Antigravity (though you can't get by without Claude here), and DeepSeek + Kimi + GLM + OpenCode.CrewAI is used for agent orchestration, and its main goal is to make the system predictable. CrewAI assigns agents roles — marketer, developer, support operator — and that's where the predictability comes from, along with reduced flexibility. AutoGen, on the other hand, is more about LLMs communicating with each other, which gives you high flexibility and a higher chance of problems. AutoGen typically requires very active human involvement at every stage of the agents' work, with small, iterative tasks. This is also where you can plug in RLHF, in which a human helps the models produce results that match human expectations — and that requires direct human feedback. AutoGen can also be very token-hungry and drift into long, convoluted dialogues. If you need complex orchestration logic, look at LangGraph instead. LangGraph is more token-efficient than AutoGen, especially with a well-built Critic Agent. More advanced, visual tools include n8n. Or you can simply get by with the LangChain ecosystem: turns your system into an API. a set of modules for integrating LLMs with additional memory, prompts, and other tools. used to analyze, monitor, and evaluate your application.And there's no need to build a homegrown monster out of a thousand components. You can use DeepSeek via GrokAPI, Cursor AI, or Perplexity, and Make for building assistants. Or you can do it all yourself: create a backend endpoint that authenticates against the DeepSeek API, and forward user requests to DeepSeek after sanitizing them.RAG is simply extra information added to an existing LLM to help it answer better. RAG was originally designed for one simple job: retrieve information and summarize it. Complex questions also require the model to , which goes beyond what standard RAG offers. Naive RAG is "retrieve and read," while so-called modular RAG is more about , , and . Overall, there are two main ways to teach an existing LLM new knowledge: fine-tuning and RAG.When to choose RAG and when to choose fine-tuning: is great for feeding new knowledge directly into an LLM, and it can do so dynamically, in real time. Fine-tuning is static. can work with a small data sample, while fine-tuning needs a good, large, clean dataset. It's worth stressing that unstructured data — articles, chat histories, meeting notes, reports — is no friend to either RAG or fine-tuning.
