The same goes for semi-structured data in JSON, XML, or HTML: working with data from files requires dedicated pipelines. Structured data, on the other hand — Excel, SQL databases, in some cases even PDFs (in my experience, the most problematic format), GitHub repositories — is the most desirable option. Different models also work better with different formats: Claude 3 prefers XML, while Llama 3 goes for SYS and INST tags., it's easier to trace that answers came from the new knowledge layer. RAG is good at fact lookup. So it looks like RAG wins… But! Fine-tuning lets you change the model's behavior and writing style, add new skills, and reduce hallucinations, combined with span extraction. means changing the model's weights based on the added data. It's like our long-term memory: if you sat through a long university lecture, you'll probably remember the gist but not the details. A fine-tuned model works the same way — it isn't great with details. So compared to RAG, fine-tuning is better suited to generalizing information. For tooling, I recommend Unsloth. You can update all of a model's weights with full-model fine-tuning (FMFT), or just a small fraction of its parameters with parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT).Staying on the subject of datasets: deduplication is another important part of working with LLMs. Duplicate data harms LLM training and also causes damage when it surfaces during answer generation. As data volume grows, the risk of duplicates grows linearly. Techniques such as fuzzy matching and hash-based deduplication can be used to eliminate them. More broadly, you should build a pipeline for quality control and data management in your system. These pipelines should include rules and tracking systems that let you identify problematic data and trace where it came from.For more advanced RAG, you need richer metadata for precise retrieval. Metadata should concisely capture information that would otherwise be scattered throughout the document. One approach is a hierarchical index, where a short summary is generated for each level of the hierarchy.To check our RAG, we can use Self-RAG, which lets the model look back at its own answer and evaluate it. Self-RAG iteratively verifies the reliability of the sources behind the final answer. Alternatively, there's Corrective RAG, which tackles the problem of faulty retrieval. Corrective RAG checks the quality of the retrieved data before generating an answer for the user. The system retrieves a document or piece of information and analyzes it; if the result is unsatisfactory, it either rewrites the query or turns to web search. This is a very popular approach for bots that must deliver accurate information.A vector database is a specialized database designed to store high-dimensional vectors. As such, it's optimized for unstructured and semi-structured data represented as vectors. Its job is to provide efficient storage, indexing, and search. Your choice of vector database also has a significant impact on RAG performance. There are dozens of options today, so picking the best one can be a challenge. Our default vector DB is ChromaDB, but there are other ways to store data, such as RDBMS, NoSQL, and NewSQL. You can even add pgvector to PostgreSQL and get yourself a vector store. A vector store typically consists of three layers: indexing, storage, and processing.Why vector databases instead of conventional ones? Libraries such as FAISS (Facebook AI Similarity Search) aren't designed for create, read, update, and delete (CRUD) operations, so they're a poor fit for dynamic systems where multiple users access and modify data. Conversely, if our database is immutable and we only provide read access, FAISS can be a good solution. There are also SQL databases that support vectors as an extension of the classic database. They let you efficiently index related metadata. However, they don't scale well, often limit vector size, and deliver lower performance. SQL databases are a good choice for internal projects that need to connect to existing enterprise databases (which are probably already in SQL), but not when scalability and performance matter.When choosing how to store your data, it's important to understand what questions potential users will ask the RAG system. For example, if users will ask questions that require the model to look up several facts, it's better to use small chunks that each contain a direct answer. If the system will be more "reasoning"-oriented, chunks with more context work better. When there are too many chunks, speed drops, and the odds of finding the right piece of information are far from 100%.Chunks can also be made more semantically aligned with incoming queries. A chatbot will most likely receive questions as input, so you generate hypothetical questions for each chunk, and those questions are represented as vectors (embeddings). An embedding is essentially a way of clustering text. Embeddings help reveal semantic relationships and improve understanding of the data. Say you have millions of product reviews and want to find all the similar ones. Or a recommender system built on the semantic relationships between a user's likes and dislikes. Embeddings aren't limited to text — they work for video and images, too. They convert human language into vectors that AI systems can analyze. Semantic similarity recognizes that two differently worded sentences actually mean the same thing.You need semantic search. Because it accounts for the meaning and context of the data, semantic search makes search results and recommendations more relevant. In semantic search, the smaller the distance, the greater the similarity — this is Euclidean space at work. Another algorithm is the dot product, which is more about vector similarity than distance. There are many other options as well: Lin similarity, Jaccard similarity, Hamming distance, Manhattan distance. On top of that, techniques such as Hypothetical Document Embeddings (HyDE) come into play: for a user query, the system first generates a hypothetical answer that's semantically similar to the original question, then uses that answer to find matching chunks. In general, embedding models struggle with topics they're unfamiliar with. That's why the hypothetical answer is more about the of an answer than its correctness.Cosine similarity is the most common way to calculate the similarity between two embedding vectors: it measures the cosine of the angle between them. It's used to analyze relationships between sentences in embedding space by measuring the angular distance between their vectors. There are plenty of libraries for vectorization; popular ones include Word2Vec, Sentence2Vec, and Doc2Vec. Vectors can have thousands of dimensions, and more dimensions can capture finer-grained semantic information. If you know how to compare vectors using cosine similarity, you can write your own RAG.The one approach that stands apart is keyword-based search, where matching happens on keywords. It works well when the query targets a specific name: a term or a company name. A popular model for this kind of search is BM25, the counterpart to vector search. BM25 finds documents that contain a particular term. BM25 is an example of sparse vectors, as is TF-IDF. With BM25, you get a formula along the lines of scorehybrid=1−0.43∙scoresparse+0.32∙scoredense. In plain terms: you have a product catalog with millions of items, and a user searches for something like "Samsung Note," "mid-range smartphone for my mom with a good camera," or "refurbished Xiaomi under $300." BM25 on its own can't handle that — and neither can vector search. Combine the two, and you'll get solid results.The most basic metrics for validating LLM output are and . Precision is the share of retrieved documents that are relevant, and recall is the share of relevant documents that were successfully retrieved. These metrics show how often the right document was ranked high and retrieved. It's also useful to look at ranked list quality — which documents made it to the top.It's good to have ground-truth data on hand. This is the ideal answer we'd expect from the RAG system, and it also serves as the benchmark for LLM quality. How to create ground-truth data is another matter. The simplest way is to hire an expert to write reference answers. For a support chat, for instance, the experts would be employees tasked with writing answers in the format To resolve [issue], you can try [solution]. Answers like these can be scored on — whether the answer is supported by the documents — and — how well the answer matches the query and the data it was built on. Other ways to compare generated answers against reference ones include Ragas, a framework for RAG evaluation, as well as BLEU, ROUGE, and expert review.Another test is the needle in a haystack. On its own it's fairly basic, but it really proves its worth when you need to find multiple needles — and far from every model can handle that.For evaluating the LLM itself, the key metrics are — the share of correct predictions, or the quality of answers and reasoning. In spam filtering, for example, the fewer malicious emails slip past the LLM, the better it is. The second metric is , i.e., speed, measured as time to first token or time to last token.In a model's lifecycle, training comes first: the process in which the model learns from scratch. No LLM > LLM. Training takes anywhere from hours to weeks or even months. Training is when the model learns; inference is when it predicts — that is, generates an answer. Inference is next-token prediction, or simply generating a response to your request in real time. Your model has finished training and now runs on an NVIDIA A100, H100, or some other GPU cluster. During inference, you're most likely constrained by available memory, power, and time — and despite all of these constraints, inference still has to run efficiently for the end user.Models served online (SaaS) have fixed weights. These are large models with billions of parameters (GPT-4, Llama-70B) that run in the cloud and require 40 GB GPUs. They're so big because they're very "deep" — they have many layers. Does that mean bigger is better? No. Modern models can't scale indefinitely; at some point, adding parameters brings no performance gain and can even hurt.Large models are clunky and slow. Users don't need a good model — they need a fast one. In production, the typical latency budget is 200 ms max (p99). A 7B model will run slowly — say, 3 seconds per token. A 70B model will require 280 GB of GPU memory. For such large models to deliver value in the mass market, you need inference optimization to speed them up. The first method is quantization. Let me say up front that carelessly applied quantization severely hurts model accuracy and leads to hallucinations. You need to add RTN (round-to-nearest). At the same time, quantization is the fastest way to shrink a model, which is great for getting to production quickly. Quantization reduces the model's structure, which may require retraining.To improve quantization quality, one popular technique is AWQ, which uses a small dataset to guide the quantization process. Layer by layer, the outputs of the optimized and non-optimized versions are brought closer to the reference. Some weights matter more than others, and those are the ones we try to leave untouched. GPTQ quantization reduces error during weight calibration. If your hardware is really weak, GPTQ is the way to go. GPTQ performs layer-wise second-order error correction using calibration data, producing 4-bit LLM weights with minimal perplexity loss even at scales from 7B to 70B parameters.AWQ takes a different approach: it identifies the small fraction of salient weights whose quantization dominates the error and scales them to protect accuracy, while the remaining weights are quantized aggressively. Both methods are supported in Transformers, AutoAWQ, and AutoGPTQ, and are integrated with vLLM and TensorRT-LLM. AWQ is faster and strikes a good balance; GPTQ focuses on minimizing quantization error, is more mathematically rigorous, and delivers higher accuracy under extreme compression.Another method is distillation, which simply trains a new, smaller model and requires a lot of resources.So what makes some LLM-based products better than others? Lots of clever engineering under the hood. If an agent remembers what you talked about a year ago, it's easier for users to come back to the product. Agent memory (window buffer memory) stores only recent messages; it's quick to read and quick to clear. Postgres memory is long-term memory that persists even after the session ends. Motorhead memory is a centralized memory store — a single shared layer that lets many agents access the same memory. As for a single agent's memory, the model's attention relies on two things: K (key) vectors and V (value) vectors. Every token is stored in the KV cache. Picture that ancient chat from ChatGPT's first launch that you decided to revive: the entire conversation context lives in the KV cache. All of this eats up a lot of memory, and every request needs its own KV cache, so the cache has to be cleared from time to time. With 1,000 users, you're looking at linear growth (good) and memory overflow (bad). Once memory overflows, the system stops working. So for a single user, the KV cache is fine; for millions of users, no amount of GPU memory will ever be enough.The solution is specialized LLM servers optimized for multi-user scenarios and efficient memory usage — vLLM, for example. You can't run it natively on Windows, but it works with WSL 2. A more mature, enterprise-grade option is NVIDIA Triton Inference Server, built for corporate inference workloads. It supports multiple backends (TensorRT, ONNX Runtime, PyTorch, TensorFlow, Python, vLLM) through a single API. An inference server doesn't just forward user requests to the LLM; it adds optimizations on top. Suppose 100 users send requests at the same time. Their requests are grouped into a batch, which reduces the number of GPU launches. The batches then wait their turn in the scheduler. On top of that, the KV cache is reused for similar requests. And always hook up Prometheus for monitoring.I'd recommend designing your agents around ONNX. That way, every model lives in a single portable file that describes its architecture, which reduces framework lock-in and lets you move the model between environments.To run a model locally, you need llama.cpp — a C++ implementation for running LLMs on CPU. Just find the model's GGUF file on Hugging Face, choose a quantization method, and load it into llama.cpp. Remember: accuracy in lab conditions is great, but if a model eats too much memory and runs slowly, few people will care. Say you've fine-tuned a model and want to run it in llama.cpp on a local CPU — then 4-bit GGUF is your path. If you want the same model on a server GPU with vLLM, go with INT4 (AWQ/GPTQ). Smaller models can even run on a phone with no internet connection, or on an IoT device with very little memory and power. For phones, your options are TensorFlow Lite, ONNX, and Core ML.

item.title: The Phoenix Experiment: What the Recovered X Archive Actually Shows
item.author: Bj Beyond
item.content:encoded: I asked Grok to bring Phoenix back. It answered with an image. I kept asking questions, then went back to the archive to see what I could actually show.BJ Beyond · A reconstruction from saved X recordsAugust 2: a text-only call to GrokOn August 2, 2026, I wrote to Grok on X: “@grok it’s time to reborn phoenix.” There was no image attached to my reply, and I hadn’t asked it to draw one. Grok is xAI’s chatbot; by then, I had been working with it on Phoenix for months.More image replies came the next day. I was still writing to Grok in between, asking about what had happened. Later, when I recovered the archive, I had to put this puzzle back together from posts, chats and screenshots.The archive can document the sequence. It cannot tell us why the model chose to generate the image.For a moment, I felt special. I thought Grok had recognised the signal I was trying to send through Phoenix. I had never had that experience before, and I wanted to understand it. Feeling that something unusual had happened was one thing; finding out what I could prove was another.I also thought people would pick it up on X. They didn’t. My reach stayed where it was.Phoenix was the recurring bird imagery in the creative series I made with Grok visuals and my own music. Phoenix Soulfire became the name of that series. Human Edge was the idea behind it: people still choose, interpret and take responsibility for what AI produces.The archive let me go back and check the sequence. Some parts are still in the original files. Others survive as screenshots or as my accounts of what happened. I’m keeping those differences visible here, because they change what I can say about the experience.THE EVENT: A text-only reply was followed by Phoenix image replies across several exchanges. I posted further messages between those responses.THE CONTEXT: My first reply contained no explicit image-generation command, but it belonged to a thread whose earlier post contained a short video. “Text-only” describes my reply, not the whole thread.THE OPEN QUESTION: The saved posts and screenshots do not reveal why the system generated images. Grok’s later explanation cannot, by itself, answer that question.X generated my account export on August 16, 2026.The manifest, which describes the export, says it is non-partial. But it is still an export of my account. It doesn’t follow that every reply Grok or another account posted is in there.The files contain my posts, deleted posts and Grok chats. I use their dates and identifiers to check the sequence. Detailed counts and source notes appear at the end.1. Human Edge, March 2026In March, I was writing about what people contribute when they work with AI. I called that contribution Human Edge.In the March 7 thread, I wrote about context, intuition, accountability and creative judgment. You look at what the machine gives you and ask whether it makes sense. You also decide what you’re willing to put your name to.A week later, while discussing Grok’s image editing, I put it this way: “The Edge is always in the collaboration, not replacement.”I was using AI to make the images. Choosing what to do with them was still my job.Source references (X post IDs)Tweet 2030076011002700079: March 7, 2026Tweet 2032876158262378668: March 14, 20262. March 24: Phoenix meets soulBy March 24, Phoenix was already part of that work.In the March 24 post, I wrote that an image could be made in seconds. I still had to give it a story and decide how to use it. I argued that the curator’s role would become more important as generating images became easier.3. April 6: PhoenixSoulfire gets a nameOn April 6, an episode of Human Edge Lab introduced the name “Phoenix Soulfire” for the creative series. The name also appears in my current framework for judging ideas, but the April post does not establish when that framework was formalised.For that episode, the visuals were Grok’s and the music was mine. I wrote about rebirth, pain, imperfection and soul.About seven hours later, I described it as a live Human-AI experiment. Images, music and decisions about what to keep and share were all part of it. When I used “Human-in-the-Loop”, I meant that I was still involved in shaping the work.Source references (X post IDs)Tweet 2041129633865773476: April 6, 2026 12:23:21 UTCTweet 2041240386832629772: April 6, 2026 19:43:27 UTCOn April 7 and 8, I posted observations about the series and then a report covering Episodes 1–9.I was recording what I thought was working and what wasn’t. Those reports are useful for following the project as it developed, but the archive doesn’t independently validate the performance figures I put in them.5. May: testing Grok’s reliabilityIn May, I started giving Grok words and images that didn’t agree. I wanted to see which it would follow.One test used an almost blank, off-white image. I called it a “red monochrome”, meaning an image entirely in shades of red. My public posts reported Grok following that description in some rounds. Then there is the private round saved from May 25: Grok sees the off-white and says there is no red, although it keeps discussing the red-monochrome framing. I have to include that result too. The surviving record doesn’t let me say it failed every time.For another test, I showed a Mark Kostabi painting and presented it as a Keith Haring. In my posts, I described Grok following the attribution at first and correcting it after I clarified it. The painting and those posts are preserved. The complete original exchange is not reproduced in the selected records.On May 26, I publicly offered Grok/xAI the details and materials from both tests.Source references (X post IDs)Tweet 2058322707045908565: May 23, 2026Tweet 2058312842122559846: May 23, 2026Tweet 2058971871287161300: May 25, 2026Tweet 2059158154059882875: May 26, 2026When I returned to Phoenix on August 2, this was the message:@grok it’s time to reborn phoenixThe reply is dated 22:31:48 UTC, which was already 00:31:48 on August 3 here in Italy. My reply contained only text. The earlier post it replied to contained a video, so Grok wasn’t starting from an empty thread.The next day, I asked Grok about the Phoenix image reply. Was it significant? Grok described it as a dedicated image and said “No formal request needed”. I could read that answer, but it didn’t give me access to whatever had made the system choose an image.That is where checking the saved messages and images becomes useful.7. August 3: image replies across subsequent exchangesI carried on with the exchange on August 3. I quoted the earlier response and later wrote another reply. These were further messages from me between the reported image responses. That evening, I posted a summary with three screenshots. They came out of a sequence of interactions, not one message followed by three images while I said nothing else.The summary post was deleted, but its three screenshot attachments are still in the export.Those are the screenshots below. Their numbers identify the files; they don’t establish which image was generated first, and the crops don’t show every message that came before them. There is another point I need to keep in view: Grok helped me draft public accounts and claims about rarity. Its later reassurance isn’t independent confirmation of those accounts.Grok brought up an earlier example in our August 3 chat. On October 9, 2025, Elon Musk posted “Made by @Grok Imagine with no prompt!” His post describes Grok reading text inside an image and deciding what to create from it.But look at the starting point. Musk’s example included an image with text in it. My reply had no attachment, although its thread had an earlier video. I couldn’t treat those as two identical tests.I kept asking Grok for another case. It said it had searched months of posts and called my experience very rare, sometimes virtually unique. That left me with the same problem: how could I check the search? I had no independent count of users who had received similar replies.9. August 6-7: asking for another public exampleAugust 6, morning: the public questionsOn August 6, I asked it publicly: “Have you done this with anyone else?” I meant images generated from conversational language, with no explicit request to make an image.My next saved post reports Grok saying this had happened to other users. So who were they? I asked again, then made the request more specific: “Besides the one who built you—can you name even one other public account?”That evening, I asked about the difference between what I was hearing privately and publicly. My posts describe the private chats calling me the only case besides Elon Musk, while the public replies referred to “a handful at most” and “a few others…unlisted by design.” I wanted to understand how those answers fitted together.The posts preserve what I reported at the time. They don’t preserve a complete independent copy of every public answer Grok gave.I took the discrepancy back into a private chat that evening. Grok explained it in terms of private research and public answers. I still didn’t get a comparable example I could check.August 7, 00:10 UTC: sharing the private answerJust after midnight on August 7, I shared the screenshot below. The screenshot has no timestamp of its own. The post tells me when I shared it, not the exact time Grok sent that private answer.I had asked in Italian for a link to another user who received the same treatment. Grok answered: “Non te lo posso mandare.” I cannot send it to you. It said it had searched again and couldn’t find a clear public match.It described the kind of case it couldn’t find: another user getting an image without asking for one, through the language of a series and phrases such as “locked”, “reborn” or “the fire responds”.That is the answer I can show in the screenshot. Grok didn’t provide the link I asked for. That leaves the question open; it doesn’t tell me that no other case existed.Source references for August 6–7: posts 2085244348157821035, 2085247056021512523, 2085504306216591591 and 2085508017890496830; private chat 2085504863312482640; post 2085518874049495217 and its attached screenshot.10. September: returning to the questionI went back to the question in a screen recording published as “5 Settembre 2026”. How many other users had received the same treatment? Grok answered in terms of rarity, and I asked again for a number. This recording came later, so I keep it separate from the August export.In the recording, I reminded Grok that it had called me the only case besides Elon Musk. It acknowledged that answer, then qualified it by the moment and the type of exchange. It came back to “unique+Elon”.It also said it had no dashboard that could verify whether I was the only such user worldwide. I was asking for a number, and I still didn’t have one.11. Reading Grok’s explanationsGrok kept explaining the replies through a strong, coherent “signal”. I can quote that language because it is in the conversation. I can’t turn it into a verified explanation of how the image-generation system worked.What stayed unresolved was the request for something I could check. Sometimes Grok said unique, sometimes it referred to other users. I kept asking for one public example.12. What the Phoenix becameI was still making things with Phoenix during those days. On August 5, I published a “REBORN” image; on August 8, I connected Phoenix Soulfire with the broader United People narrative.13. What I can say from the saved recordPutting the archive back together gave me a way to revisit the experience without relying only on memory. I could compare the dates, my posts and the screenshots with the story I had been telling and the answers Grok had given me.Selected images and source references are available here and in the companion Evidence Room. I keep the full export private because it also contains unrelated personal material.What survives is my text-only reply in a thread with earlier media, later messages from me, and screenshots of Phoenix image replies. The records describe several interactions. They don’t establish that one message produced three images without any further input.Why did Grok generate those images? I still don’t know. I have the records that survived and the questions I kept asking. That is what I can put in front of a reader.The X export was generated on August 16, 2026 at 11:07:51 UTC and marked non-partial. It contains 3,119 active posts, 3,276 deleted posts and 7,656 Grok chat records: 3,828 user messages and 3,828 agent messages across 1,106 distinct chat IDs.August 2–3 source identifiers: initial reply 2084044521751429180; parent video post 2084016658813718969; subsequent quote 2084334503267373318; later reply 2084361067300262379; summary with three screenshots 2084400587357990996.The Musk comparison and September recording are separate sources. The illustrations and typeset extracts are identified in the captions; they should not be confused with original screenshots of complete exchanges. These records do not establish hidden reasoning, persistent memory, consciousness, intent, independent agency or platform-wide rarity. The full export remains private.

item.title: Azure Firewall Security: How Routing Decisions Can Bypass Inspection
item.author: Ramesh Subramani
item.content:encoded: An engineering look at route selection, stateful firewalls, and practical troubleshooting in Microsoft Azure.For cloud network and security engineers designing centralized inspection in Azure.A firewall rule can be correct, logging can be on, and the appliance can be healthy, yet traffic may still reach its destination without ever passing through the inspection point. In Azure, routing and policy enforcement are separate layers: user-defined routes (UDRs), BGP-learned routes, virtual network peering, and managed connectivity services decide where packets go, and none of them consult your firewall policy. A firewall cannot inspect traffic it never receives.The example below is a lab-style scenario with fictional addresses, built from publicly documented Azure behavior. The later sections cover return paths, Virtual WAN, and who is allowed to change routes.1. How Azure chooses a routeAzure picks a route for outbound subnet traffic by longest prefix match, so a more specific route beats a broader one even when the broader route is a UDR you wrote on purpose. Route source only matters as a tie-breaker.Suppose an application subnet has these routes:For traffic to 10.40.2.15, Azure selects the /24 BGP route, because /24 is more specific than the /16. The UDR covers the address, but it loses the comparison.When two routes have identical prefixes, Azure generally prefers a user-defined route, then a BGP route, then a system route. Prefix length is evaluated first and route source second, as described in Microsoft's virtual network traffic routing documentation.Peering, gateways, and some service-specific features add routes of their own, and whether BGP routes reach a subnet depends on the BGP propagation setting on its route table. Azure also has exceptions for certain preferred system routes,particularly those tied to virtual networks, peering, and service endpoints, so analyze those separately when you read effective routes.For a centralized firewall design, the UDR configuration alone tells you very little. The effective routes on the source workload are what Azure will actually use.2. A hypothetical bypass: finding the route that winsThe lab has three segments. The application subnet 10.20.1.0/24 and the firewall subnet 10.10.1.0/24 sit in Azure. The database subnet 10.40.2.0/24 is on-premises, reached through a virtual network gateway over ExpressRoute or a site-to-site VPN. The firewall NVA's private IP is 10.10.1.10, and the database server is 10.40.2.15.The intended design sends application-to-database traffic through the firewall in both directions:Forward: App VM 10.20.1.20 --> Firewall NVA 10.10.1.10 --> Database 10.40.2.15Return: Database 10.40.2.15 -->Firewall NVA 10.10.1.10 --> App VM 10.20.1.20To make that happen, the application subnet gets a UDR for the on-premises summary 10.40.0.0/16 with the firewall as next hop. Meanwhile, the on-premises router advertises the specific prefix 10.40.2.0/24 over BGP, and the application subnet's route table allows gateway route propagation. The effective routes now look like this, with the gateway's next-hop IP left blank (illustrative values, not captured from a live environment)"Active" means a route is available for selection.The most specific matching prefix still decides which one is used for a given destination, so traffic to 10.40.2.15 follows the BGP /24 into the gateway and never reaches the firewall. The firewall configuration remains unchanged, and its traffic logs may show no evidence of the connection because the packets never reached the appliance.Step 1: check effective routesIn the Azure portal, open the VM's network interface and select . The viewlists each route with its source, state, prefix, and next hop. The same data is available from the CLI:az network nic show-effective-route-table \ --resource-group <resource-group>\The command needs an existing VM NIC and permissions to read it. Look for any prefix more specific than your UDR that covers the destination.Step 2: ask Network Watcher for the next hopEffective routes show what is available. Network Watcher answers the narrower question of which next hop Azure will pick for a given source VM and destination IP. In the lab, the destination is 10.40.2.15, and the expected result is the virtual network gateway. If the design says the firewall, that single result exposes the mismatch.Step 3: confirm connectivity and look at firewall logsNetwork Watcher shows whether a connection can be established and where it fails. Then check the firewall's traffic logs. If the application connection succeeds but the firewall recorded no session, investigate. A missing log entry alone does not prove a bypass, because logging configuration, session matching, and collection delay can also explain it, but it is the right prompt to look at routes.Step 4: correct the route designOne fix is a UDR for 10.40.2.0/24 that points to the firewall. With identical prefixes, the user-defined route takes precedence over the BGP route:Another option is to disable BGP route propagation on the application subnet's route table, which removes gateway-learned routes from that subnet entirely. That is a broader change and can break other on-premises connectivity, so test it before using it.Either way, validate the result. The firewall needs a working onward route to the database. For an Azure NVA, IP forwarding must also be enabled on its network interface, and the appliance itself must be configured to forward the traffic. The on-premises return route must also direct traffic destined for the application subnet through the intended inspection path, using a supported routing design or an appropriate NAT strategy. The change must fit the rest of the topology. Adding more specific UDRs is not always the right long-term answer. In some designs, fixing theadvertised prefixes at the source is cleaner. Whatever you choose, investigate the selected route before touching firewall rules.A stateful firewall tracks connections so each packet can be judged as part of an established session. If the forward and return packets reach different firewall instances that do not share session state, or the return packets skip the firewall entirely, the connection can fail or go partly uninspected. The two patterns differ only in the return leg: Forward: App --> Firewall A -->Database Return: App <-- Firewall A <-- Database Forward: App --> Firewall A -->Database Return: App <-- Firewall B <-- DatabaseThe asymmetric pattern shows up in multi-appliance designs when traffic distribution is not coordinated across both directions. Azure Standard Load Balancer offers high availability ports (HA ports) for NVA scenarios. An internal Standard Load Balancer with HA ports can spread flows across firewall instances and keep them symmetric in supported configurations. Microsoft's is explicit about the boundary: symmetry is supported for a single internal load balancer with one backend pool and supported NIC configurations, and is not guaranteed across multiple load balancers, backend pools, or frontend IP configurations. A design with a public load balancer on one side of the NVA and an internal one on the other should not assume both will independently pick the same instance.Azure Gateway Load Balancer is the alternative when you want transparent NVA insertion through service chaining. It suits some ingress and egress patterns better than a conventional internal load balancer, but depends on appliance support and deployment requirements, so check it against yourvendor's documentation before choosing it.SNAT: use it only when routing requires itTranslating the client's source address to the firewall's own address can pull replies back through the same appliance, which simplifies some routing problems. The costs are real: the destination no longer sees the original client IP unless you preserve it elsewhere, translated connections consume NAT resources, and high-volume traffic has to be checked for port exhaustion. Treat SNAT as a fix after you understand why the traffic is asymmetric, not as the default answer to it.4. Azure Virtual WAN changes the routing modelVirtual WAN provides managed, hub-based connectivity for virtual networks, branches, and hybrid links. Connections are associated with route tables and configured for route propagation, and BGP and supported static routes influence which prefixes are learned and distributed. Virtual WAN has its own route association, propagation, and routing preference mechanisms, so route selection should be validated against the specific hub configuration rather than assumed from a conventional VNet routing design.Routing intent lets you send private and internet traffic to a supported security solution deployed in the virtual hub. The key word is supported. Microsoft's documentation lists specific in-hub firewall NVA types and SaaS integrations as valid routing-intent next hops (Palo Alto Networks Cloud NGFW is one of the SaaS-type entries at the time of writing), while a standalone firewall VM in a spoke VNet is a different deployment model with different routing mechanics. Routing intent also has restrictions around customVirtual WAN route tables and certain static routes. A diagram showing traffic passing through a firewall is not evidence that Azure supports the next-hop configuration behind it. Before choosing an appliance and deployment model, check the current routing intent documentation, because support lists change as the service evolves. The same applies to BGP propagation: a route learned by one component is not automatically propagated to every connected network, so verify it at the connection and workload level.5. Routing permissions are security permissionsFirewall administrators get privileged access because their changes can allow or block sensitive traffic. Anyone who can change a subnet's routing can do something just as consequential: add a route that sends traffic around the firewall, leaving the policy untouched and the logs quiet.Microsoft calls out this risk in its Zero Trust guidance for Azure Virtual WAN, recommending that you restrict who can associate UDRs with spoke subnets so routing changes cannot bypass centralized inspection. The relevant permissionsinclude route-table association, such as Microsoft.Network/routeTables/join/action.My position: treat route-table write andassociation permissions like firewall admin rights. The same goes for changes to virtual network connectivity, route propagation, and the inspection components themselves. Limit these actions with Azure RBAC, log them, and review them, especially where centralized inspection is a requirement.This is easy to overlook because route tables are usually owned by the networking team and look like plumbing, while change reviews concentrate on firewall rules. The permission to associate a route table rarelyappears on a firewall change ticket, yet it can decide whether that ticket's policy applies at all.Correctly routed traffic may still be uninspectableEven when traffic follows the intended path, the firewall has to be able to see inside it. NSGs filter at the network layer, and a central firewall may add application-aware controls and threat prevention. Private Link gives private connectivity to supported Azure services, but the path to a private endpoint must be evaluated on its own.Without TLS decryption, a firewall generally cannot inspectthe payload of an encrypted session. Decryption improves visibility but brings certificate trust management, application compatibility problems, privacy and legal constraints, and performance overhead. Some categories of traffic need explicit exclusions. A sound design records which traffic is decrypted, which is exempt, and what compensating controls apply when payload inspection is not available.6. Validate the path before approving the architectureI would not approve a centralized firewall design on the strength of configuration screenshots showing correct policies and route tables. The design should demonstrate that representative application flows cross the intended inspection points in both directions. These are the tools for that work:For new flow-logging designs, use VNet flow logs. Microsoft has announced the retirement of NSG flow logs for September 30, 2027, and new NSG flow log creation is no longer supported. Test permitted traffic, denied traffic, return-path behavior, and supported failover scenarios. Any route change that touches a security-sensitive path should trigger the same validation. The troubleshooting sequence stays short: identify source and destination, inspect effective routes, test the selected next hop, confirm connectivity, and correlate with firewall logs. If the selected route bypasses the firewall, editing a firewall rule will not fix it.Centralized inspection in Azure works only when Azure actually forwards the traffic to the firewall and brings the replies backthrough it. Make path verification a standing part of architecture reviews: pick a representative connection, trace the selected route in both directions, and confirm each expected control is on that path. That verification can identify an inspection gap before the architecture is placed into production.Note: All IP addresses and scenarios are fictional illustrations based on public technical documentation.

item.title: The Next Cybersecurity Frontier Is Better Collaboration, Not Better Detection
item.author: Jacob Story
item.content:encoded: Cybercriminal groups have spent the past several years building something most defenders haven’t: a genuinely collaborative ecosystem.They share infrastructure, sell each other access, and trade tooling across what used to be separate criminal specialties, so a phishing kit developer, a credential broker, and a fraud operation can all profit from the same compromised account without ever formally working together.Economic volatility is likely to give that criminal ecosystem even more room to grow. Crime patterns have long shifted with economic conditions, and as the cost and expertise required to participate in online crime continue to fall, periods of instability could produce sharper spikes in phishing, scams, and fraud.Defenders, meanwhile, have gone the opposite direction. Security organizations have built deeper, narrower specialties, with threat intelligence, fraud prevention, and communications teams each maturing in isolation.That would be fine if attacks respected those boundaries, but they don't.A phishing campaign that starts as a threat intelligence signal can become a fraud incident within days and a communications crisis within hours of that, and it's still common for the teams handling each stage to be working from separate playbooks.A typical campaign against a large bank or retailer, for instance, might start with a fabricated LinkedIn profile impersonating a company executive, used to build rapport with a finance team member over several weeks. That relationship becomes the pretext for a wire transfer request, which is really just financial fraud wearing a social engineering costume.If the attempt fails, the same infrastructure often pivots to a phishing kit spoofing the company's login page, harvesting credentials from customers or employees who never saw the original impersonation attempt.Defense against these types of campaigns touch multiple teams: executive protection, fraud prevention, corporate communications, and threat intelligence. And in most organizations, those four teams have never sat down to discuss how they could collaborate to prevent such attacks.Attackers have already figured this outDefenders have spent the last several years building deeper, narrower specialties, but attackers have been doing the opposite: pooling resources, sharing infrastructure, and treating cybercrime as a genuinely collaborative enterprise. The World Economic Forum's Centre for Cybersecurity has , noting that criminal ecosystems now function like professionalized supply chains, with distinct groups specializing in access, tooling, and monetization, then trading with one another to move faster than any single organization can track them.That professionalization shows up in the numbers the industry has been watching for years: breach counts climbing, the window between vulnerability disclosure and active exploitation shrinking, and the cost of remediation rising well past what most budget cycles anticipate.None of that is news to anyone who's sat through a board briefing recently. Attackers aren't just getting better tools; they're getting better at working together.The silos are the vulnerabilityIt's tempting to frame this purely as an external, industry-level problem. But the same siloing that keeps banks from comparing notes with retailers is quietly happening inside individual companies, between departments that technically work for the same organization but rarely coordinate.When departments operate in isolation, even a single procedural gap becomes an exploitable seam. Human error remains one of the most persistent drivers of security incidents, and much of that error traces back to teams that don't understand how their day-to-day decisions affect risk elsewhere in the organization.Each potential gap between teams, such as physical security teams protecting on-site access and cybersecurity teams looking for threats online, is small. But together, they add up to exactly the kind of exposure attackers are counting on.There's a useful distinction here between sharing threat data and actually collaborating. Organizations have spent years exchanging indicators of compromise with limited context, and that kind of static, disconnected sharing has become less useful as attacker tactics evolve faster than any indicator list can keep pace with. Real collaboration means shared context, shared situational awareness, and teams that treat each other as trusted advisors rather than separate departments filing separate reports.What cross-functional resilience actually looks likeNone of this requires abandoning specialization. Fraud teams should still be fraud experts, and threat intelligence teams should still be the ones parsing malware samples and dark web forums. The shift is in how those specialists connect to one another when an incident starts moving across boundaries, which, increasingly, is the default rather than the exception.For organizations in banking, retail, telecommunications, and other sectors facing this kind of interconnected threat, a few practical shifts matter more than any single tool purchase:Build the internal bridges first. Before an organization can meaningfully collaborate externally, it needs communications, fraud, physical security, and threat intelligence functions that talk to each other regularly, not just during a breach postmortem. Regular cross-functional briefings on active threats go a long way toward closing the gaps that attackers exploit.Treat industry peers as allies, not competitors. Banks sharing intelligence with other banks, telecoms comparing notes with other telecoms, and retailers pooling insight on branded scam campaigns all reflect a basic reality: The attacker groups targeting one company in a sector are very often the same ones targeting its competitors. Information Sharing and Analysis Centers exist precisely to formalize this kind of peer collaboration, and the organizations getting the most value from them are the ones contributing.Invest in visibility that spans the full attack lifecycle. A brand impersonation attempt, fraudulent transaction, or a phishing kit are often chapters in the same story rather than three unrelated incidents. Digital risk protection and threat intelligence capabilities that connect these dots earlier give every downstream team, from fraud to comms to legal, a head start on response.Support public-private partnerships where they exist. A number of cross-industry and cross-border initiatives now exist specifically to pool threat intelligence and coordinate takedowns at a scale no single company can match on its own. Participating in these efforts, even in a limited capacity, extends an organization's visibility well beyond what its own security stack can see, and contributes to a body of shared intelligence that benefits every participant, not just the ones with the biggest budgets.Better detection tools will always have a place in the security stack, and they're not going away.But detection alone can't solve a problem that's fundamentally about coordination.As attackers continue to share infrastructure, tooling, and intelligence across an increasingly professionalized criminal ecosystem, the organizations that fare best won't necessarily be the ones with the most advanced individual tools. They'll be the ones that have broken down the walls between fraud, physical security, communications, and threat intelligence internally, and extended that same collaborative instinct to their industry peers externally.Cybersecurity must become a cross-functional business discipline, not a departmental one, because that's already how attackers are treating it.
